Bells_Vireo.Description: Small vireo, grayish above with two wing bars and pale eye ring. Yellowish sides and flanks. About 5 inches.
Bells_Vireo.Behavior: Skulks in dense scrub. Song a fast rambling chatter. Declining due to Brown-headed Cowbird parasitism.
Bells_Vireo.Habitat: Dense willow and mesquite scrub along streams. Breeding range from Great Plains to California.
Bells_Vireo.Similar Looking Birds: White-eyed Vireo has white iris. Bell's Vireo has dark eye and faint wing bars.
Bells_Vireo.Best Ways to Identify: Small secretive vireo in dense low scrub. Faint wing bars, yellowish wash. Fast chattering song.

Belted_Kingfisher.Description: Large-headed blue-gray bird with shaggy crest, heavy dagger bill, white collar and underparts; male has single blue breast band; female adds rusty band.
Belted_Kingfisher.Behavior: Hovers over water then plunges headfirst to catch fish; rattling call in flight; excavates nesting burrows in earthen banks; solitary and territorial.
Belted_Kingfisher.Habitat: Along rivers, streams, ponds, lakes, and estuaries throughout North America; needs clear water for hunting and earthen banks for nesting.
Belted_Kingfisher.Similar Looking Birds: No other kingfisher species regularly overlaps in most of North America; the much rarer Green Kingfisher is tiny and lacks the shaggy crest.
Belted_Kingfisher.Best Ways to Identify: Large blue-gray head with shaggy crest, dagger bill, rattling call in flight, and habit of hovering then diving into water headfirst.

Bendires_Thrasher.Description: Medium thrasher, gray-brown above with lightly spotted breast, yellow eye, relatively short bill. About 10 inches.
Bendires_Thrasher.Behavior: Forages on ground in desert scrub. Early nester. Song varied and melodious. Uses specific desert plant communities.
Bendires_Thrasher.Habitat: Desert grassland and sparse desert scrub in Arizona, New Mexico, and southeastern California.
Bendires_Thrasher.Similar Looking Birds: Curve-billed Thrasher heavier bill more curved. Sage Thrasher smaller, streaked, different habitat.
Bendires_Thrasher.Best Ways to Identify: Shorter bill than other thrashers. Yellow eye. Lightly spotted breast. Desert scrub and grassland in Southwest.

Bermuda_Petrel.Description: Medium gadfly petrel, gray-brown above, white rump and underparts, gray breast band, dark cap. Critically endangered. About 15 inches.
Bermuda_Petrel.Behavior: Critically endangered; once thought extinct, rediscovered 1951. Breeds only on Bermuda. Forages in Atlantic Ocean.
Bermuda_Petrel.Habitat: North Atlantic Ocean; breeds only on Bermuda islands. One of world's rarest and most endangered seabirds.
Bermuda_Petrel.Similar Looking Birds: Black-capped Petrel has more white on head. Bermuda has gray cap with white forehead.
Bermuda_Petrel.Best Ways to Identify: Gray cap and back with white underparts. Rump patch. Only breeds on Bermuda. Very rare Atlantic seabird.

Berylline_Hummingbird.Description: Medium hummingbird. Iridescent green head and breast, gray-brown belly, rufous wings and tail with purple gloss. About 4 inches.
Berylline_Hummingbird.Behavior: Feeds on nectar and insects in mountain forests. Rare summer visitor to mountain canyons of southeastern Arizona.
Berylline_Hummingbird.Habitat: Pine-oak mountain forests of Mexico and Central America. Rare visitor to Huachuca and Chiricahua mountains of southeastern Arizona.
Berylline_Hummingbird.Similar Looking Birds: Broad-billed Hummingbird in similar habitat. Berylline's rufous wings distinctive in flight.
Berylline_Hummingbird.Best Ways to Identify: Rufous wing panels flash distinctively in flight. Green head and breast with gray-brown belly. Rare in Arizona mountain canyons.

Bewicks_Wren.Description: Small wren with rich brown back, clean white eyebrow (supercilium), white underparts, and long tail with white spots on outer corners.
Bewicks_Wren.Behavior: Active and curious; cocks tail up; explores brush piles and low shrubs; males sing complex varied songs; common in gardens and brushy yards.
Bewicks_Wren.Habitat: Brushy areas, open woodlands, chaparral, and suburban gardens; common in the western U.S.; formerly widespread in the East but declined there.
Bewicks_Wren.Similar Looking Birds: House Wren is smaller with shorter eyebrow and browner overall; Carolina Wren has rich buff underparts; Marsh Wren has streaked cap and back.
Bewicks_Wren.Best Ways to Identify: Bold white eyebrow, white-spotted tail corners when spread, clean white belly, and energetic tail-cocking behavior in brushy western habitats.

Bicknells_Thrush.Description: Small thrush, brown above with spotted breast, yellow base to bill. Extremely similar to Gray-cheeked. About 6.5 inches.
Bicknells_Thrush.Behavior: Breeds in dense stunted forest on high mountain peaks. One of most restricted breeding habitats in North America.
Bicknells_Thrush.Habitat: Dense balsam fir krummholz on mountaintops of northeastern United States and southern Canada. Winters in Caribbean.
Bicknells_Thrush.Similar Looking Birds: Gray-cheeked Thrush nearly identical; best separated by range and breeding habitat. Call note and song differ.
Bicknells_Thrush.Best Ways to Identify: High mountaintop stunted forest breeder. Nearly identical to Gray-cheeked. Yellow lower mandible. Specific call.

Bishops_Oo.Description: Small Hawaiian honeyeater, black with yellow ear tufts and yellow undertail coverts. Long bill. About 8 inches.
Bishops_Oo.Behavior: Foraged for nectar in native Hawaiian forest flowers. Extinct since approximately 1904. Last recorded on Maui.
Bishops_Oo.Habitat: Native forests of Molokai and later Maui. Extinct due to habitat destruction and introduced avian diseases.
Bishops_Oo.Similar Looking Birds: Other Oo species on different islands. All Hawaiian Oo now extinct.
Bishops_Oo.Best Ways to Identify: Extinct species from Molokai and Maui. Black with yellow ear tufts. No longer exists in nature.

Black-and-white_Warbler.Description: Boldly striped black and white overall; male has black cheek and throat; female has white cheek; both have black-streaked white underparts.
Black-and-white_Warbler.Behavior: Creeps along tree trunks and branches like a nuthatch, probing bark for insects; one of the earliest spring warblers to arrive; "wee-see" thin high song.
Black-and-white_Warbler.Habitat: Deciduous and mixed forests of eastern North America; nests on the ground among tree roots; winters in Florida, Caribbean, and Central America.
Black-and-white_Warbler.Similar Looking Birds: Blackpoll Warbler (fall) has similar streaking but lacks the creeping behavior; Black-throated Gray Warbler has yellow spot near bill; Downy Woodpecker has red patch.
Black-and-white_Warbler.Best Ways to Identify: Creeping along bark like a nuthatch; bold black-and-white stripey pattern; thin squeaky song; one of the earliest spring warblers.

Black-backed_Oriole.Description: Medium oriole, orange with entirely black back, black throat and wings, white wing bars. About 8.5 inches.
Black-backed_Oriole.Behavior: Forages in flowering trees. Very rare vagrant to southwestern United States from central Mexico.
Black-backed_Oriole.Habitat: Pine-oak forests and highlands of central Mexico. Very rare vagrant to southwestern United States.
Black-backed_Oriole.Similar Looking Birds: Streak-backed Oriole has streaked back. Bullocks Oriole different pattern.
Black-backed_Oriole.Best Ways to Identify: Entirely black back contrasting with orange body. Very rare vagrant from highland Mexico.

Black-backed_Woodpecker.Description: Medium woodpecker with solid black back (no white stripe). Males have yellow crown patch. Heavily barred flanks. White face with black cheek stripe. About 9.5 inches. Three toes instead of four.
Black-backed_Woodpecker.Behavior: Specializes in foraging on recently burned forest, stripping bark for wood- boring beetle larvae. Hitches along trunks. Drums loudly. Usually solitary.
Black-backed_Woodpecker.Habitat: Recently burned boreal and montane conifer forests of northern and western North America. Often appears in forests 1–5 years after fire.
Black-backed_Woodpecker.Similar Looking Birds: American Three-toed Woodpecker has barred black-and-white back. Hairy Woodpecker has white back stripe. Black back is unique to this species.
Black-backed_Woodpecker.Best Ways to Identify: Solid black back with no white stripe is diagnostic. Found in burned forest. Males show yellow crown. Three-toed foot (check if possible). Loud rapping.

Black-bellied_Plover.Description: Large plover; breeding adult has striking black face, neck, and belly contrasting with speckled silver-gray back; nonbreeding birds are gray overall.
Black-bellied_Plover.Behavior: Forages on tidal flats and beaches by running and pausing; loud mournful three-note whistle call; gathers in large flocks on migration.
Black-bellied_Plover.Habitat: Breeds on Arctic tundra; migrates along both coasts and interior; winters on beaches, mudflats, and estuaries of both coasts.
Black-bellied_Plover.Similar Looking Birds: American Golden-Plover has golden-speckled back in breeding plumage and lacks the black "wingpit" (axillaries) visible in flight.
Black-bellied_Plover.Best Ways to Identify: Large plover with silver-gray speckled back, breeding black belly, and black "wingpits" visible in flight; loud mournful whistle call.

Black-bellied_Storm-Petrel.Description: Dark storm-petrel with white belly patch bisected by dark central streak, white rump. About 8 inches.
Black-bellied_Storm-Petrel.Behavior: Swims and feeds on ocean surface, different from other storm-petrels. Very rare vagrant to North American Atlantic coast.
Black-bellied_Storm-Petrel.Habitat: Southern Ocean and south Atlantic. Very rare vagrant to North American Atlantic coast.
Black-bellied_Storm-Petrel.Similar Looking Birds: White-bellied Storm-Petrel similar but lacks dark central streak on belly.
Black-bellied_Storm-Petrel.Best Ways to Identify: White belly with black central streak. White rump. Swims on surface rather than pattering. Very rare southern vagrant.

Black-bellied_Whistling-Duck.Description: Distinctive duck with bright orange-red bill, chestnut breast, black belly, and bold white wing stripe. Long pink legs. Upright posture. About 21 inches. Adults have gray face with white eye ring.
Black-bellied_Whistling-Duck.Behavior: Perches in trees; nests in tree cavities. Highly social in large flocks. Makes loud, whistling calls in flight. Nocturnal feeder on seeds and grains.
Black-bellied_Whistling-Duck.Habitat: Ponds, lakes, marshes, and flooded fields in southern Texas, Louisiana, Arizona, and Florida. Expanding northward. Tropical species common in Central America.
Black-bellied_Whistling-Duck.Similar Looking Birds: Fulvous Whistling-Duck is tawny overall without black belly. No other duck has combination of orange bill, chestnut breast, and black belly.
Black-bellied_Whistling-Duck.Best Ways to Identify: Orange bill and bold white wing stripe in flight are unmistakable. Black belly visible at rest. Loud whistle calls. Tree-perching behavior unusual for ducks.

Black-billed_Cuckoo.Description: Slender long-tailed bird with brown upperparts, plain white underparts, all-black bill, narrow red eye ring, and small white tail spots below.
Black-billed_Cuckoo.Behavior: Skulks in dense vegetation; eats caterpillars including hairy tent caterpillars other birds avoid; secretive but vocal with repetitive "cu-cu-cu" calls.
Black-billed_Cuckoo.Habitat: Dense thickets, deciduous forests, and shrubby edges of eastern North America; winters in South America; often responds to rainy weather (rain crow).
Black-billed_Cuckoo.Similar Looking Birds: Yellow-billed Cuckoo has yellow lower mandible, rusty wing panels in flight, and larger tail spots; Mangrove Cuckoo has buff belly and is coastal.
Black-billed_Cuckoo.Best Ways to Identify: All-black bill, narrow red eye ring, small white tail spots, and plain white belly; skulking behavior in eastern thickets; distinctive hollow calls.

Black-billed_Magpie.Description: Bold black-and-white bird with iridescent blue-green wings and long wedge-shaped tail; black head, breast, and back; white belly, scapulars, and wing patches.
Black-billed_Magpie.Behavior: Intelligent and curious; caches food; builds a domed stick nest; loud chattering calls; omnivorous; often forages on the ground near livestock.
Black-billed_Magpie.Habitat: Open country, shrublands, forest edges, and rural areas of western North America from Alaska to the Great Basin; common near farms and ranches.
Black-billed_Magpie.Similar Looking Birds: Yellow-billed Magpie is nearly identical but found only in California's Central Valley; American Crow lacks white patches and long tail.
Black-billed_Magpie.Best Ways to Identify: Large black-and-white bird with enormously long iridescent tail and bold white wing patches flashing in flight; loud chattering calls.

Black-browed_Albatross.Description: Most common mollymawk albatross. White body and head, dark back and wings, yellow-orange bill, black eyebrow stripe. About 35 inches.
Black-browed_Albatross.Behavior: Most likely mollymawk to reach North America. Follows ships, feeds on fish and squid. Southern hemisphere breeder.
Black-browed_Albatross.Habitat: Southern Ocean. Rare vagrant to North Atlantic and Pacific; occasional off Atlantic coast of North America.
Black-browed_Albatross.Similar Looking Birds: Atlantic Yellow-nosed Albatross has slimmer bill and thinner dark eyebrow stripe.
Black-browed_Albatross.Best Ways to Identify: Yellow-orange bill with black tip, black eyebrow stripe. White body, dark back. Most frequently seen mollymawk vagrant.

Black-capped_Chickadee.Description: Small energetic bird with black cap and bib, white cheeks, gray back and wings, and buffy sides; white edging on wing feathers.
Black-capped_Chickadee.Behavior: Bold and acrobatic; hangs upside down to forage for insects and seeds; caches food; visits feeders; gives "chick-a-dee-dee" alarm calls.
Black-capped_Chickadee.Habitat: Deciduous and mixed forests, parks, and suburban areas across the northern United States and Canada; year-round resident; forms winter flocks.
Black-capped_Chickadee.Similar Looking Birds: Carolina Chickadee has less white on wing and different call; Mountain Chickadee has white eyebrow; Boreal Chickadee has brown cap and sides.
Black-capped_Chickadee.Best Ways to Identify: Black cap and bib, white cheeks, gray back, and lively "chick-a-dee" and two-note whistled "fee-bee" song; very common at feeders.

Black-capped_Gnatcatcher.Description: Tiny gnatcatcher, blue-gray above, white below. Male has large black cap extending below eye. About 4.5 inches.
Black-capped_Gnatcatcher.Behavior: Active and vocal in dense scrub. Rare visitor to Arizona from Mexico. Pairs forage together year-round.
Black-capped_Gnatcatcher.Habitat: Dense thorn scrub and thorny woodland of Mexico. Rare visitor to extreme southern Arizona near border.
Black-capped_Gnatcatcher.Similar Looking Birds: Black-tailed Gnatcatcher has less extensive cap. Blue-gray Gnatcatcher much whiter below.
Black-capped_Gnatcatcher.Best Ways to Identify: Large black cap extending well below eye. White underparts. Southern Arizona rare visitor from Mexico.

Black-capped_Petrel.Description: Medium gadfly petrel, dark gray-black back, black cap, white collar and rump, white underparts. About 16 inches.
Black-capped_Petrel.Behavior: Breeds on Caribbean island cliffs. Forages in Gulf Stream; regular offshore Atlantic from Florida to New England.
Black-capped_Petrel.Habitat: Gulf Stream waters off Atlantic coast. Breeds on Haiti and Dominica; ranges widely in western North Atlantic.
Black-capped_Petrel.Similar Looking Birds: Bermuda Petrel smaller with gray cap. Black-capped has bold black cap and white collar.
Black-capped_Petrel.Best Ways to Identify: Bold black cap with bright white collar and rump. Dark back. Gulf Stream specialist off Atlantic coast.

Black-capped_Vireo.Description: Small vireo with male showing glossy black cap, white spectacles, olive-green back, and yellow-white underparts with yellow sides. Females have slate gray cap. Red eye. About 4.5 inches. Endangered species.
Black-capped_Vireo.Behavior: Forages actively in dense shrubs, gleaning insects from leaves. Secretive and hard to observe. Males sing persistently from dense cover in spring.
Black-capped_Vireo.Habitat: Scrubby oak and juniper thickets on rocky hillsides and canyons in Oklahoma, Texas, and Coahuila, Mexico. Requires shrubs with patchy openings. Threatened by Brown-headed Cowbird parasitism.
Black-capped_Vireo.Similar Looking Birds: Blue-headed Vireo has blue-gray head without black cap. Ruby-crowned Kinglet is smaller. No other vireo has solid black cap with white spectacles.
Black-capped_Vireo.Best Ways to Identify: Black cap with white spectacles on male is unmistakable. Female's gray cap also distinctive. Harsh, rapid song. Found in cedar-oak scrub in Texas.

Black-chinned_Hummingbird.Description: Small hummingbird with metallic green back; male has black throat with a narrow iridescent purple lower band; female is pale green-gray below.
Black-chinned_Hummingbird.Behavior: Pumps tail while hovering; males perform a J-shaped pendulum display dive; visits flowers and feeders; catches insects in flight; highly territorial.
Black-chinned_Hummingbird.Habitat: Streamside thickets, mountain canyons, dry woodlands, and suburban areas of the western United States; winters in Mexico.
Black-chinned_Hummingbird.Similar Looking Birds: Ruby-throated Hummingbird overlaps little in range; Calliope Hummingbird is smaller with streaked gorget; Costa's has purple crown and long side tufts.
Black-chinned_Hummingbird.Best Ways to Identify: Purple throat band below black chin on males; western range; tail pumping while hovering; J-shaped dive display; common at western feeders.

Black-chinned_Sparrow.Description: Medium sparrow with gray head, breast, and upperparts. Males have black chin and face patch. Back streaked brown and black. Pink bill. About 5.5 inches. Females lack black chin, have paler gray faces.
Black-chinned_Sparrow.Behavior: Forages on ground and in shrubs for seeds and insects. Secretive, often staying low in dense chaparral. Males sing from exposed perches in spring.
Black-chinned_Sparrow.Habitat: Dense chaparral, sagebrush, and mountain scrub on brushy hillsides in California, Arizona, and New Mexico. Winters in southwestern deserts.
Black-chinned_Sparrow.Similar Looking Birds: Dark-eyed Junco has white outer tail feathers. Chipping Sparrow has rufous cap. Other gray sparrows lack the combination of all-gray head and pink bill.
Black-chinned_Sparrow.Best Ways to Identify: Gray head and breast with pink bill in chaparral habitat. Males show black chin patch. Plaintive, accelerating trill song. Brushy mountain slopes in west.

Black-crested_Titmouse.Description: Small titmouse with distinctive black crest, gray body, white forehead patch, rusty flanks. About 6 inches.
Black-crested_Titmouse.Behavior: Active forager in oaks and mesquite. Visits feeders readily. Loud and vocal. Replaces Tufted Titmouse in Texas range.
Black-crested_Titmouse.Habitat: Oak woodlands, mesquite thickets, and suburban areas of central and southern Texas and northeastern Mexico.
Black-crested_Titmouse.Similar Looking Birds: Tufted Titmouse has gray crest, not black. Overlaps with Tufted Titmouse in narrow hybrid zone in Texas.
Black-crested_Titmouse.Best Ways to Identify: Black crest contrasting with white forehead. Central Texas range. Rusty flanks. Very similar to Tufted Titmouse.

Black-crowned_Night-Heron.Description: Stocky heron with black crown and back, white face and underparts, gray wings, and red eyes; short thick neck; long white head plumes in breeding season.
Black-crowned_Night-Heron.Behavior: Most active at dusk and dawn; roosts in trees during the day in groups; gives a barking "quok" call in flight; nests in colonies.
Black-crowned_Night-Heron.Habitat: Freshwater marshes, swamps, estuaries, and lake edges throughout North America and much of the world; very widespread distribution.
Black-crowned_Night-Heron.Similar Looking Birds: Yellow-crowned Night-Heron has black-and-white head pattern and yellow crown; adult herons in flight may be confused with other species.
Black-crowned_Night-Heron.Best Ways to Identify: Black crown and back, white face, red eyes, stocky short-necked profile; active at night and dusk; loud "quok" call in flight.

Black-faced_Grassquit.Description: Tiny finch. Male dark olive with black face and breast. Female plain olive-brown. About 4 inches.
Black-faced_Grassquit.Behavior: Forages for grass seeds. Rare visitor to Florida from Caribbean islands. Can be locally established.
Black-faced_Grassquit.Habitat: Grasslands, gardens, and open areas. Caribbean resident. Rare visitor to southern Florida.
Black-faced_Grassquit.Similar Looking Birds: Yellow-faced Grassquit has yellow on face. Blue-black Grassquit male all blue-black.
Black-faced_Grassquit.Best Ways to Identify: Male dark olive with black face. Tiny size. Rare Florida visitor from Caribbean. Female plain olive-brown.

Black-footed_Albatross.Description: Large seabird, mostly dark sooty brown with white around bill and eye, and white at base of tail. Long narrow wings spanning 7 feet. Black feet. Hooked bill. About 28 inches long.
Black-footed_Albatross.Behavior: Soars effortlessly on ocean updrafts. Follows ships for refuse. Breeds on Hawaiian islands, returning to same nest site each year. Long-lived species.
Black-footed_Albatross.Habitat: North Pacific Ocean, common off the west coast of North America. Pelagic, coming to land only to breed. Abundant on pelagic birding trips offshore.
Black-footed_Albatross.Similar Looking Birds: Laysan Albatross is white-bodied with dark back and wings. Short-tailed Albatross is larger with pink bill. Black-footed is the common dark albatross.
Black-footed_Albatross.Best Ways to Identify: Large, all-dark albatross with white around bill and eye. White tail base. Long gliding flight on stiff wings. Common on North Pacific pelagic trips.

Black-headed_Grosbeak.Description: Male has black head, orange-cinnamon breast and collar, black and white wings, and large pale bill; female is streaked brown with buff eyebrow.
Black-headed_Grosbeak.Behavior: Eats seeds, insects, and berries with powerful bill; one of few birds that can safely eat toxic Monarch butterflies; robin-like rich melodious song.
Black-headed_Grosbeak.Habitat: Mixed and deciduous forests, orchards, and wooded parks of western North America; winters in Mexico; common at feeders during migration.
Black-headed_Grosbeak.Similar Looking Birds: Rose-breasted Grosbeak (eastern) male has rosy-red breast triangle; female grosbeaks are similar — look for bold eyebrow and large bill.
Black-headed_Grosbeak.Best Ways to Identify: Male's orange-cinnamon breast and black head are distinctive; large pale conical bill; robin-like song in western forests; common at feeders.

Black-headed_Gull.Description: Small gull. Breeding adult has dark brown hood, red bill and legs, gray back, white underparts. About 15 inches.
Black-headed_Gull.Behavior: Common in Eurasia; rare but regular vagrant to eastern North America. Flocks with Bonaparte's Gulls on Atlantic coast.
Black-headed_Gull.Habitat: Coastal and inland waters of Eurasia. Regular but uncommon vagrant to Atlantic coast of North America.
Black-headed_Gull.Similar Looking Birds: Bonaparte's Gull similar. Black-headed has dark brown hood and larger size.
Black-headed_Gull.Best Ways to Identify: Dark brown hood in breeding. Red (not black) bill. Slightly larger than Bonaparte's Gull. Regular vagrant on Atlantic coast.

Black-headed_Nightingale-Thrush.Description: Small thrush with black head and back contrasting with gray underparts. Orange bill. About 6.5 inches.
Black-headed_Nightingale-Thrush.Behavior: Forages in dense forest undergrowth. Rare vagrant to Texas from Mexico. Beautiful song.
Black-headed_Nightingale-Thrush.Habitat: Dense humid mountain forest of Mexico and Central America. Very rare vagrant to southern Texas.
Black-headed_Nightingale-Thrush.Similar Looking Birds: Orange-billed Nightingale-Thrush lacks black head. Other spotted thrushes have spotted underparts.
Black-headed_Nightingale-Thrush.Best Ways to Identify: Black head contrasting with gray body. Orange bill. Very rare Texas vagrant from mountain Mexico.

Black-legged_Kittiwake.Description: Medium gull with clean white head and body, gray back and wings, and solid black wingtips (no white spots). Yellow bill, black legs. In winter, gray smudge behind eye. About 17 inches long.
Black-legged_Kittiwake.Behavior: Feeds by plunge-diving for small fish and marine invertebrates. Highly pelagic outside breeding season. Nests colonially on narrow cliff ledges.
Black-legged_Kittiwake.Habitat: North Atlantic and Pacific oceans. Breeds on Arctic and sub-Arctic cliffs. Winters offshore, regularly seen from shore during storms. Most oceanic gull.
Black-legged_Kittiwake.Similar Looking Birds: Ring-billed Gull has ring on bill and pale wingtips. Mew Gull is smaller. Bonaparte's Gull is smaller with black head in summer. Kittiwake has clean solid black wingtips.
Black-legged_Kittiwake.Best Ways to Identify: Clean solid black wingtips with no white mirrors. Yellow bill, dark legs. Buoyant, tern-like flight. Most commonly seen gull far offshore in winter.

Black-necked_Stilt.Description: Elegant long-legged shorebird with black back and head, white underparts, and remarkably long bright pink-red legs; red eye; straight thin bill.
Black-necked_Stilt.Behavior: Wades in shallow water probing for invertebrates; aggressively defends nest by dive-bombing intruders; loud "kek-kek-kek" alarm calls; gregarious.
Black-necked_Stilt.Habitat: Shallow freshwater and saltwater wetlands, flooded fields, and sewage ponds throughout the West, Gulf Coast, and Florida; increasingly common inland.
Black-necked_Stilt.Similar Looking Birds: American Avocet has upturned bill and rusty head; Black Oystercatcher is all black with red bill; Willet is gray with white wing stripe.
Black-necked_Stilt.Best Ways to Identify: Extremely long pink-red legs (one of longest-legged birds relative to body), bold black and white pattern, and loud alarm calls at wetlands.

Black-tailed_Gnatcatcher.Description: Tiny long-tailed bird, blue-gray above, pale below. Male has black cap in breeding. Much black on tail. About 4.5 inches.
Black-tailed_Gnatcatcher.Behavior: Active forager in desert scrub, constantly flicking tail. Pairs remain together year-round. Harsh insect-like calls.
Black-tailed_Gnatcatcher.Habitat: Arid desert scrub, washes, and thorny thickets of the Sonoran and Chihuahuan deserts in southwestern United States.
Black-tailed_Gnatcatcher.Similar Looking Birds: Blue-gray Gnatcatcher has more white in tail. California Gnatcatcher coastal with different call.
Black-tailed_Gnatcatcher.Best Ways to Identify: Mostly black tail from below (white-sided in Blue-gray). Desert scrub habitat. Harsh calls. Black cap on male.

Black-tailed_Godwit.Description: Large godwit. Breeding adult has orange-red head and neck, black and white tail, bold white wing stripe. Long straight bill. About 16 inches.
Black-tailed_Godwit.Behavior: Forages in shallow water for invertebrates. Rare vagrant to eastern North America from Eurasia. Wades deeply when feeding.
Black-tailed_Godwit.Habitat: Breeds on European and Asian wet meadows. Winters on African and South Asian coasts. Rare vagrant to Atlantic coast.
Black-tailed_Godwit.Similar Looking Birds: Hudsonian Godwit has similar wing stripe pattern. Black-tailed has straight bill.
Black-tailed_Godwit.Best Ways to Identify: Black and white tail pattern and bold white wing stripe distinctive. Straight (not upturned) bill. Rare vagrant on Atlantic coast.

Black-tailed_Gull.Description: Medium gull, pale gray back, white body, distinctive black tail band, yellow bill with red and black tip. Yellow eyes. About 18 inches.
Black-tailed_Gull.Behavior: Common in Asian coastal waters. Rare vagrant to North American coasts. Rests on rocks and jetties; scavenges widely.
Black-tailed_Gull.Habitat: Rocky coasts, harbors, and fishing ports of eastern Asia. Very rare vagrant to Pacific and Atlantic coasts of North America.
Black-tailed_Gull.Similar Looking Birds: Mew Gull and Ring-billed Gull similar. Black-tailed Gull's black tail band and yellow eyes distinctive.
Black-tailed_Gull.Best Ways to Identify: Black tail band contrasting with white rump distinctive. Yellow eyes, black-and-red bill tip. Asian vagrant to North America.

Black-throated_Blue_Warbler.Description: Male is deep blue above with black face, throat, and sides; clean white belly; small white wing spot. Female is olive-brown with subtle pale eyebrow.
Black-throated_Blue_Warbler.Behavior: Forages methodically in dense understory shrubs; males sing a buzzy rising "I am la-zy" song; male and female look so different they were once considered separate species.
Black-throated_Blue_Warbler.Habitat: Dense forest understory of eastern North America; prefers mountain forests in Appalachians and Adirondacks; winters in the Caribbean.
Black-throated_Blue_Warbler.Similar Looking Birds: Indigo Bunting male is all blue; female Black-throated Blue resembles Orange-crowned Warbler but has small white wing spot.
Black-throated_Blue_Warbler.Best Ways to Identify: Male's deep blue and black with white belly and tiny white wing spot are diagnostic; female's plain olive-brown with white wing spot is subtle.

Black-throated_Gray_Warbler.Description: Black-and-white patterned warbler with gray back; black throat, cheeks, and crown; white eyebrow and white sides; tiny yellow dot near bill.
Black-throated_Gray_Warbler.Behavior: Forages in oaks and other trees for insects; males sing a buzzy song with rising or falling quality; monochrome appearance is distinctive in the West.
Black-throated_Gray_Warbler.Habitat: Dry woodlands, shrubby hillsides, pinyon-juniper, and chaparral of the western United States; winters in Mexico and Central America.
Black-throated_Gray_Warbler.Similar Looking Birds: Black-and-white Warbler creeps on bark and has striped crown; Townsend's Warbler has yellow face and breast; Hermit Warbler has yellow face.
Black-throated_Gray_Warbler.Best Ways to Identify: Black-and-gray pattern with white eyebrow, tiny yellow dot near bill, and western range; buzzy song in dry western woodlands.

Black-throated_Green_Warbler.Description: Bright yellow face with olive-green crown; black throat and breast sides; white wing bars; male has solid black throat, female has partial black throat.
Black-throated_Green_Warbler.Behavior: Forages in tree canopy for insects; males sing persistent buzzy "zee-zee-zee- zoo-zee" song; a common spring migrant through the eastern U.S.
Black-throated_Green_Warbler.Habitat: Coniferous and mixed forests of the northeast and Appalachians; migrates through eastern North America; winters from Mexico to Colombia.
Black-throated_Green_Warbler.Similar Looking Birds: Townsend's Warbler (western) has black cap and cheek patch; Hermit Warbler has yellow face but white underparts and less black; Yellow-rumped Warbler lacks yellow face.
Black-throated_Green_Warbler.Best Ways to Identify: Bright yellow face, black throat, and buzzy "zee-zee-zee-zoo-zee" song; conifer forests; one of the most reliably heard spring warblers.

Black-throated_Sparrow.Description: Striking sparrow with gray back, black throat and breast, white facial stripes above and below eye, and white underparts. Bold head pattern. About 5.5 inches. Immatures lack black throat, show streaked breast.
Black-throated_Sparrow.Behavior: Forages on ground for seeds and insects. Highly adapted to desert heat and can survive without free water. Pairs or small groups. Melodic, complex song.
Black-throated_Sparrow.Habitat: Desert scrub, rocky slopes, and arid grasslands of the Sonoran and Chihuahuan deserts. Common in creosote and cholla cactus habitat. Year-round resident.
Black-throated_Sparrow.Similar Looking Birds: Lark Sparrow has complex head pattern but no black throat. Black-chinned Sparrow has gray head without white facial stripes. Unique pattern in range.
Black-throated_Sparrow.Best Ways to Identify: Bold black throat and white facial stripes are unmistakable in any plumage. Desert habitat. Melodic, bell-like song heard at dawn. Perches on cactus.

Black-vented_Oriole.Description: Medium oriole, black hood, black back and wings, orange-yellow below, black undertail coverts. About 8.5 inches.
Black-vented_Oriole.Behavior: Forages in flowering trees for nectar and insects. Rare vagrant to Texas and New Mexico from Mexico.
Black-vented_Oriole.Habitat: Open woodland and forest edge of Mexico and Central America. Rare vagrant to southwestern United States.
Black-vented_Oriole.Similar Looking Birds: Hooded Oriole has orange back and white wing bars. Scott's Oriole has yellow-black pattern.
Black-vented_Oriole.Best Ways to Identify: Black back and hood with orange-yellow body. Black undertail coverts. Rare Mexico vagrant to Texas.

Black-vented_Shearwater.Description: Small shearwater, dark brown above, white below with dark undertail coverts (vent). Dark sides of breast. About 12 inches.
Black-vented_Shearwater.Behavior: Common offshore California especially in winter. Breeds on islands off Baja California. Often in large flocks offshore.
Black-vented_Shearwater.Habitat: California coast offshore; breeds on Baja California islands. Very common California winter shearwater.
Black-vented_Shearwater.Similar Looking Birds: Manx Shearwater has white undertail. Black-vented's dark undertail coverts diagnostic.
Black-vented_Shearwater.Best Ways to Identify: Dark undertail coverts on otherwise white-bellied shearwater. Common off California in winter.

Black-whiskered_Vireo.Description: Medium vireo similar to Red-eyed but with black malar stripe (whisker). Olive-green above, white below. About 6 inches.
Black-whiskered_Vireo.Behavior: Sings a monotonous repeated phrase from mangroves and coastal trees. Florida's most common summer vireo in that habitat.
Black-whiskered_Vireo.Habitat: Mangroves, coastal hammocks, and tropical forests. Breeds in Florida Keys and south Florida, winters in South America.
Black-whiskered_Vireo.Similar Looking Birds: Red-eyed Vireo lacks the black malar stripe. Yucatan Vireo similar but occurs in different region.
Black-whiskered_Vireo.Best Ways to Identify: Black whisker mark below eye unique among vireos. Florida mangrove habitat. Olive above, white below, red eye.

Black-winged_Petrel.Description: Small gadfly petrel, pale gray above, bold black M-pattern on wings, white below. About 11 inches.
Black-winged_Petrel.Behavior: Breeds on Lord Howe and Kermadec Islands. Forages in tropical Pacific; very rare vagrant to North American Pacific coast.
Black-winged_Petrel.Habitat: Tropical Pacific Ocean. Very rare vagrant to North American Pacific coast.
Black-winged_Petrel.Similar Looking Birds: Cook's Petrel similar but has different underwing pattern. Black-winged has bolder upper wing pattern.
Black-winged_Petrel.Best Ways to Identify: Bold black M-pattern on pale gray wings. Small gadfly petrel in tropical Pacific. Very rare vagrant.

Black-winged_Stilt.Description: Elegant wader with extremely long pink legs, black back and wings, white underparts and head, long straight black bill. About 14 inches.
Black-winged_Stilt.Behavior: Wades in shallow water picking invertebrates from surface. Very noisy when disturbed. Rare vagrant to North America from Eurasia and Africa.
Black-winged_Stilt.Habitat: Shallow freshwater and coastal wetlands. Breeds across Eurasia and Africa. Rare vagrant to Atlantic coast of North America.
Black-winged_Stilt.Similar Looking Birds: Black-necked Stilt nearly identical; replaces it in North America. Black-winged has white head.
Black-winged_Stilt.Best Ways to Identify: Extremely long pink legs, black and white plumage. Black-winged has all-white head vs. black nape of Black-necked Stilt.

Black_Catbird.Description: Small mimic thrush, entirely glossy black with dark bill, red iris. Slim build. About 8 inches.
Black_Catbird.Behavior: Skulks in dense vegetation. Catbird-like behavior. Rare vagrant to Texas from Yucatan Peninsula of Mexico.
Black_Catbird.Habitat: Dense coastal scrub and second growth of the Yucatan Peninsula. Rare vagrant to Texas.
Black_Catbird.Similar Looking Birds: No other all-black catbird or mimic thrush in range. Gray Catbird gray not black.
Black_Catbird.Best Ways to Identify: Entirely glossy black, slim catbird shape. Red iris. Rare Texas vagrant from Yucatan Peninsula.

Black_Francolin.Description: Medium partridge. Male has black breast and face, chestnut collar, white cheek patch, spotted flanks. Female brown and streaked. About 13 inches.
Black_Francolin.Behavior: Skulks in dense grass. Loud distinctive call in early morning. Forages for seeds and insects. Introduced to Hawaiian islands and Louisiana.
Black_Francolin.Habitat: Tall grasslands, agricultural fields, and dense scrub. In Hawaii found on Kauai, Maui, and other islands; also feral in Louisiana.
Black_Francolin.Similar Looking Birds: Gray Francolin paler. Male Black Francolin's bold coloring unique in Hawaii.
Black_Francolin.Best Ways to Identify: Male's black chest with distinctive white ear patch and chestnut collar. Loud territorial call in early morning.

Black_Guillemot.Description: Medium seabird, all black in summer with bold white wing patch. Bright red feet and red mouth lining. Winter plumage is white with black back and wings. About 13 inches. Strong, whirring wingbeats.
Black_Guillemot.Behavior: Dives from surface to catch fish and invertebrates near rocky shores. Nests in rock crevices, often in small colonies. Stays near coast year-round.
Black_Guillemot.Habitat: Rocky coasts and fjords of the Arctic and northern Atlantic. Less pelagic than other auks, rarely far from shore. Common in Maine and Canadian Maritimes.
Black_Guillemot.Similar Looking Birds: Pigeon Guillemot (Pacific) is nearly identical but separated by range. Dovekie is much smaller. Razorbill and Common Murre are larger, more black.
Black_Guillemot.Best Ways to Identify: All-black body with striking white wing patch. Bright red feet visible when swimming or landing. Rocky coastal habitat. Often seen close to shore.

Black_Kite.Description: Medium brown raptor with slightly forked tail. Dark brown overall with pale head. About 22 inches.
Black_Kite.Behavior: Scavenger and opportunist. Extremely common in Africa, Europe, and Asia. Rare vagrant to Alaska and Atlantic coast.
Black_Kite.Habitat: Open areas, coasts, and urban areas of Old World. Rare vagrant to Alaska and Atlantic coast.
Black_Kite.Similar Looking Birds: Red Kite has deeper forked tail and reddish plumage. Black Kite brown with slight fork.
Black_Kite.Best Ways to Identify: Brown overall with shallow forked tail. Highly variable plumage. Common Old World raptor, rare North American vagrant.

Black_Mamo.Description: Large Hawaiian honeycreeper, entirely black with very long deeply curved bill. About 8 inches.
Black_Mamo.Behavior: Fed on flowers of native plants with very long bill. Extinct since approximately 1907 on Molokai.
Black_Mamo.Habitat: Native forests of Molokai. Extinct due to habitat destruction and introduced diseases.
Black_Mamo.Similar Looking Birds: Hawaii Mamo had yellow patches. No other all-black honeycreeper with extremely long curved bill.
Black_Mamo.Best Ways to Identify: Extinct. All-black with very long curved bill. From Molokai only. No longer exists in any forest.

Black_Noddy.Description: Small tern-like seabird. Entirely black with small white cap on forehead. Slender bill. Smaller and blacker than Brown Noddy. About 13 inches.
Black_Noddy.Behavior: Picks prey from water surface. Nests in trees on tropical islands. Uncommon visitor to Florida from Caribbean.
Black_Noddy.Habitat: Tropical oceanic islands. Occasional visitor to Dry Tortugas, Florida, from Caribbean. Nests on tropical Pacific and Atlantic islands.
Black_Noddy.Similar Looking Birds: Brown Noddy larger and browner with more extensive pale cap.
Black_Noddy.Best Ways to Identify: All-black plumage with small white cap on forehead. Smaller than Brown Noddy. Slender black bill.

Black_Oystercatcher.Description: Large all-black shorebird with a vivid long red-orange bill, yellow eyes with red orbital ring, and pale pinkish legs; stocky and crow-sized.
Black_Oystercatcher.Behavior: Pries open mussels and limpets from rocks with its strong laterally flattened bill; loud "kleep" calls; nests in a simple scrape on rocky shorelines.
Black_Oystercatcher.Habitat: Rocky Pacific Coast shores from Alaska to Baja California; closely tied to wave-washed rocky intertidal zones; rarely found on sandy beaches.
Black_Oystercatcher.Similar Looking Birds: American Oystercatcher has white on wings and belly; American Crow and Common Raven are all dark but lack the red bill and are found inland.
Black_Oystercatcher.Best Ways to Identify: All-black body with bright red-orange bill; yellow eye; found exclusively on rocky Pacific Coast shoreline; loud piping call.

Black_Phoebe.Description: Small flycatcher with entirely sooty black head, breast, back, and wings; white belly and lower flanks; no wing bars; faint white wing edging.
Black_Phoebe.Behavior: Perches upright on low rocks or branches near water, wagging tail; sallies out to catch flying insects; builds mud-and-grass cup nest on bridges and walls.
Black_Phoebe.Habitat: Near water in the western U.S. — streams, rivers, ponds, and coastal areas; year-round resident from California through Central America.
Black_Phoebe.Similar Looking Birds: Eastern Phoebe is brownish-gray (not black) with white belly; Dark-eyed Junco has white outer tail feathers and a conical seed-eating bill.
Black_Phoebe.Best Ways to Identify: Black-and-white pattern (clean black above, white below), tail-wagging habit, and association with water in the western U.S.

Black_Rail.Description: Tiny, secretive rail barely larger than a sparrow. Males are dark slate gray with chestnut nape and white spots on back. Red eye. Very small at 6 inches. Females similar but browner. Extremely hard to see.
Black_Rail.Behavior: Moves through dense marsh vegetation like a mouse. Mostly nocturnal and crepuscular. Distinctive kee-kee-kerr call heard at night. Rarely flies.
Black_Rail.Habitat: Dense saltmarshes and freshwater marshes along Atlantic and Gulf coasts, and in California. Severely threatened by habitat loss and sea level rise. Rare.
Black_Rail.Similar Looking Birds: Other rails are much larger. Sora has yellow bill. Virginia Rail has longer red bill. Black Rail's tiny size and dark plumage are unique.
Black_Rail.Best Ways to Identify: Tiny size and all-dark plumage in saltmarsh. Listen for kee-kee-kerr call at night. Almost never seen well; usually only heard. Critically imperiled.

Black_Rosy-Finch.Description: Medium finch, black body with pink wing patches and rump, gray crown. About 6 inches.
Black_Rosy-Finch.Behavior: Forages at snowfields and talus slopes. Breeds at highest elevations in central Rocky Mountains.
Black_Rosy-Finch.Habitat: Alpine tundra and rocky slopes above treeline in central Rockies. Winters lower in flocks.
Black_Rosy-Finch.Similar Looking Birds: Brown and Gray-crowned Rosy-Finches similar structure. Black body distinguishes from brownish relatives.
Black_Rosy-Finch.Best Ways to Identify: Black body with pink wing patches and rump. Gray crown. High Rocky Mountain alpine specialist.

Black_Scoter.Description: Medium sea duck, males entirely black with bright orange-yellow knob at base of bill. Females are dark brown with pale cheeks contrasting with dark cap. About 19 inches. Compact, heavy-bodied duck.
Black_Scoter.Behavior: Dives for mollusks, crustaceans, and aquatic insects. Migrates in large flocks along coasts. Rarely seen inland. Winters at sea in nearshore waters.
Black_Scoter.Habitat: Breeds on boreal lakes and tundra ponds. Winters along both coasts in nearshore ocean waters. Less common than Surf or White-winged Scoter on Pacific coast.
Black_Scoter.Similar Looking Birds: Surf Scoter male has orange and white bill pattern. White-winged Scoter has white wing patch. Ruddy Duck is smaller. Female Black Scoter has cleaner pale cheeks.
Black_Scoter.Best Ways to Identify: Male: all black with orange knob on bill. Female: two-toned head, pale cheeks. Coastal ocean habitat in winter. Often in flocks with other scoters.

Black_Skimmer.Description: Striking black-and-white bird with extraordinary bill — lower mandible much longer than upper; black above, white below; red-orange bill with dark tip.
Black_Skimmer.Behavior: Flies low over calm water with lower bill slicing the surface to catch fish; nests in colonies on sandy beaches; loud barking calls at colonies.
Black_Skimmer.Habitat: Coastal beaches, bays, estuaries, and tidal rivers; nests on sand spits and barrier beaches; found along both U.S. coasts and Gulf of Mexico.
Black_Skimmer.Similar Looking Birds: No other North American bird has the distinctive knife-blade bill shape; terns and gulls have symmetrical bills; the skimming flight is unique.
Black_Skimmer.Best Ways to Identify: Unique elongated lower mandible skimming the water surface; black back and white underparts; red-orange bill with black tip; coastal habitat.

Black_Storm-Petrel.Description: Large all-dark storm-petrel with slow languid wingbeats, pale upperwing bar, forked tail. About 9 inches.
Black_Storm-Petrel.Behavior: Breeds on islands off Baja California. Largest dark storm-petrel in eastern Pacific. Slow deep wingbeats distinctive.
Black_Storm-Petrel.Habitat: Eastern Pacific off California and Baja California. Forages over warm Pacific waters; breeds on Baja islands.
Black_Storm-Petrel.Similar Looking Birds: Ashy Storm-Petrel smaller and grayer. Black Storm-Petrel largest dark Pacific storm-petrel.
Black_Storm-Petrel.Best Ways to Identify: Largest all-dark storm-petrel in eastern Pacific. Slow languid wingbeats. Forked tail, pale upperwing bar.

Black_Swift.Description: Large, all-black swift with forked tail (appearing square when not spread). Long, scythe-shaped wings. About 7 inches. Noticeably larger than other swifts. Slow, deep wingbeats compared to Vaux's Swift.
Black_Swift.Behavior: Feeds on aerial insects high in the sky. Nests on wet cliff faces near waterfalls in small colonies. Highly aerial; rarely lands except at nest.
Black_Swift.Habitat: Mountain cliffs near waterfalls and sea cliffs in western North America. Forages widely over mountains and valleys. Rare and poorly known species. Winters in South America.
Black_Swift.Similar Looking Birds: Vaux's Swift is much smaller with pale throat and rump. White-throated Swift has white throat and sides. Chimney Swift is smaller. Purple Martin is a swallow with different flight profile.
Black_Swift.Best Ways to Identify: Large all-black swift with slow, rowing wingbeats. Look near mountain waterfalls. Much larger than Vaux's Swift. Rare; finding nest waterfall locations helps.

Black_Tern.Description: Small tern with black head and body in breeding plumage. Gray wings and tail. White undertail. In fall, white replaces black on head and underparts. Short bill, shallowly forked tail. About 9.5 inches long.
Black_Tern.Behavior: Dips to water surface to snatch insects and small fish. Feeds over freshwater marshes. Loose colonies for nesting on floating vegetation. Gregarious migrant.
Black_Tern.Habitat: Freshwater marshes and lakes in interior North America for breeding. Migrates along coasts and inland. Winters at sea off Central and South America.
Black_Tern.Similar Looking Birds: Sooty Tern is larger, ocean-going, with white forehead. Bridled Tern similar but with white forehead. Other terns have white bodies. Distinctive in breeding.
Black_Tern.Best Ways to Identify: Black body with gray wings in summer — unmistakable. In fall, dark cap with white forehead. Dipping, buoyant flight over freshwater marshes. Small size.

Black_Turnstone.Description: Stocky shorebird with black head, breast, and back in breeding plumage. White belly and white markings on face. Bill slightly upturned. Orange-red legs. About 9.5 inches. Winter birds lose white face markings.
Black_Turnstone.Behavior: Flips rocks, shells, and seaweed to find invertebrates, as name suggests. Highly territorial on wintering grounds. Loud, rattling calls in flight.
Black_Turnstone.Habitat: Rocky Pacific coastline — breeds on Alaska tidal marshes, winters on rocky shores south to Baja California. Almost exclusively coastal in winter.
Black_Turnstone.Similar Looking Birds: Ruddy Turnstone has orange-rufous back pattern and is found on sandy beaches. Surfbird is larger with yellow legs. Both species flip debris for food.
Black_Turnstone.Best Ways to Identify: All-black upperparts with white belly on Pacific rocky shores. Distinctive wing stripe pattern in flight. Flipping behavior with strong bill. Loud rattle.

Black_Vulture.Description: Large all-black bird with bald, wrinkled gray-black head; short hooked bill; short square tail; white wing patches at wingtips visible in flight.
Black_Vulture.Behavior: Soars on flat wings, interspersed with frequent flapping; roosts communally; often follows Turkey Vultures to carrion; aggressive and social at food.
Black_Vulture.Habitat: Open country, roadsides, farms, and urban areas; common in the southeastern U.S. and spreading northward; also found throughout Central and South America.
Black_Vulture.Similar Looking Birds: Turkey Vulture is larger with red head, two-toned wings, and soars in a strong dihedral (V-shape); Zone-tailed Hawk mimics vultures in flight.
Black_Vulture.Best Ways to Identify: All-black with white wingtip patches, gray bald head, short square tail, flap-flap-glide flight style, and flat (not V-shaped) soaring posture.

Blackburnian_Warbler.Description: Male has brilliant flame-orange throat and face, black back with white streaking, black cheeks, and white wing patch. Female is dull yellow-orange.
Blackburnian_Warbler.Behavior: Forages high in the crowns of tall conifers, difficult to see; males sing a very high thin ascending "zee-zee-zee-zeeeeee" song.
Blackburnian_Warbler.Habitat: Mature conifer forests of the Northeast and Appalachians in summer; a common fall migrant; winters in Andean forests of South America.
Blackburnian_Warbler.Similar Looking Birds: American Redstart male has orange on wings and tail; no other warbler has the fiery-orange throat; female resembles other streaked warblers.
Blackburnian_Warbler.Best Ways to Identify: Unmistakable fiery-orange throat on males; look high in spruce and hemlock canopy; very thin ascending song; most brilliantly colored warbler.

Blackpoll_Warbler.Description: Breeding male has black cap, white cheeks, black streaking on white underparts; white wing bars. Fall birds are olive-green with streaking and orange legs.
Blackpoll_Warbler.Behavior: Performs one of the longest migrations of any songbird — nonstop over the Atlantic Ocean to South America in fall; thin high "tseet" song.
Blackpoll_Warbler.Habitat: Boreal spruce forests in summer; migrates through eastern North America; fall migrants make a trans-oceanic flight to South America.
Blackpoll_Warbler.Similar Looking Birds: Fall Blackpoll is very similar to fall Bay-breasted Warbler — look for orange-yellow (not dark) feet; Black-and-white Warbler has striped crown.
Blackpoll_Warbler.Best Ways to Identify: Breeding male's black cap and white cheeks are diagnostic; fall birds have orange-yellow feet; look for heavy streaking; common fall migrant.

Blue-and-white_Swallow.Description: Small swallow, deep blue-black above, white below with black undertail coverts. Small bill. About 4.5 inches.
Blue-and-white_Swallow.Behavior: Forages over open areas and forest. Rare vagrant to North America. Highly migratory in South America.
Blue-and-white_Swallow.Habitat: Open areas, forest edges, and urban environments in Central and South America. Very rare vagrant to North America.
Blue-and-white_Swallow.Similar Looking Birds: Tree Swallow larger with green gloss above, white undertail coverts. Barn Swallow has rusty throat.
Blue-and-white_Swallow.Best Ways to Identify: Dark black undertail coverts contrast with white belly. Deep blue-black above. Very small swallow.

Blue-and-yellow_Macaw.Description: Large macaw, brilliant blue above, bright yellow below, green forehead, white face. About 33 inches.
Blue-and-yellow_Macaw.Behavior: Highly intelligent. Loud and conspicuous. Escaped birds occasionally seen; no established feral population.
Blue-and-yellow_Macaw.Habitat: Tropical forests. Occasional escaped individuals in United States. Native to South America.
Blue-and-yellow_Macaw.Similar Looking Birds: No other large blue-and-yellow bird in North America. Unmistakable combination of colors.
Blue-and-yellow_Macaw.Best Ways to Identify: Brilliant blue above and yellow below. Large size. Unmistakable. Occasional escaped birds in United States.

Blue-billed_White-Tern.Description: Small pure white tern. All white with blue-based black-tipped bill, large dark eye. Delicate and fairy-like appearance. About 10 inches.
Blue-billed_White-Tern.Behavior: Lays single egg on bare branch without nest. Picks fish from surface. Found on Pacific atolls and Hawaiian islands.
Blue-billed_White-Tern.Habitat: Low tropical Pacific atolls and islands. Found in Hawaiian Northwestern Islands and other Pacific atolls.
Blue-billed_White-Tern.Similar Looking Birds: Fairy Tern similar. Blue-billed has blue bill base.
Blue-billed_White-Tern.Best Ways to Identify: All-white plumage with blue-based bill. Large dark eye. Fairy-like flight over tropical Pacific islands.

Blue-black_Grassquit.Description: Tiny finch. Male brilliant blue-black throughout. Female streaked brown. About 4 inches.
Blue-black_Grassquit.Behavior: Male displays by leaping vertically singing. Forages for grass seeds. Rare vagrant to southern Texas from Mexico.
Blue-black_Grassquit.Habitat: Open grasslands, weedy fields, and roadsides from Mexico to South America. Rare vagrant to Texas.
Blue-black_Grassquit.Similar Looking Birds: Indigo Bunting male brighter blue. No other tiny all-blue-black finch in range.
Blue-black_Grassquit.Best Ways to Identify: Male tiny and all blue-black. Vertical leaping display. Rare Texas vagrant. Female streaked brown.

Blue-crowned_Parakeet.Description: Large parakeet, green with blue crown and face, long pointed tail, reddish bill. About 15 inches.
Blue-crowned_Parakeet.Behavior: Gregarious in flocks. Noisy. Feral populations in southern Florida and Miami area.
Blue-crowned_Parakeet.Habitat: Dry woodland and savanna. Feral populations in Florida. Native to South America.
Blue-crowned_Parakeet.Similar Looking Birds: Mitred Parakeet has red face. White-eyed Parakeet has white eye ring. Blue crown distinctive.
Blue-crowned_Parakeet.Best Ways to Identify: Blue crown and face on green parakeet. Long tail. Florida feral population.

Blue-footed_Booby.Description: Large seabird with unmistakable bright blue feet. Brown and white plumage, long pointed wings, pointed tail. Males have smaller pupil than females. About 32 inches. Bill is bluish-gray, pointed.
Blue-footed_Booby.Behavior: Plunge-dives from height for fish, hitting water like a missile. Males display their blue feet in courtship dances. Nests on ground on oceanic islands.
Blue-footed_Booby.Habitat: Tropical Pacific Ocean. Rare visitor to California coast, especially in warm water years. Breeds primarily on Galapagos and Mexican Pacific islands.
Blue-footed_Booby.Similar Looking Birds: Brown Booby has brown hood and yellow feet. Northern Gannet is all white with black wingtips and yellow head. Masked Booby has cleaner white body.
Blue-footed_Booby.Best Ways to Identify: Bright blue feet are unmistakable — nothing else looks like this. Brown and white plumage. Plunge-diving behavior. Rare vagrant to California coast.

Blue-gray_Gnatcatcher.Description: Tiny blue-gray bird with white eye ring, white underparts, long black tail with white outer feathers; male has black eyebrow in breeding season.
Blue-gray_Gnatcatcher.Behavior: Constantly active, flitting and flicking its long tail; gives a thin squeaky "spee" call; builds a lichen-covered cup nest; forages in canopy.
Blue-gray_Gnatcatcher.Habitat: Deciduous forests, woodlands, and thickets across much of North America in summer; winters in southern U.S., Caribbean, and Central America.
Blue-gray_Gnatcatcher.Similar Looking Birds: Other gnatcatchers have different head patterns; Gray Vireo is larger and lacks the tail-flicking; female Cerulean Warbler is larger and stockier.
Blue-gray_Gnatcatcher.Best Ways to Identify: Tiny blue-gray bird constantly flicking white-sided tail; thin squeaky call; white eye ring; abundant in open woods across much of North America.

Blue-gray_Noddy.Description: Small delicate seabird. Pale blue-gray plumage with darker wingtips, white eye ring, black bill and legs. About 11 inches.
Blue-gray_Noddy.Behavior: Picks small fish and invertebrates from water surface. Breeds on Hawaiian and Pacific atolls. Gentle and delicate in flight.
Blue-gray_Noddy.Habitat: Low-lying tropical Pacific islands and atolls. Breeds on Hawaiian Northwestern Islands and other Pacific atolls.
Blue-gray_Noddy.Similar Looking Birds: White Terns similar habitat. Blue-gray Noddy's pale blue-gray color distinctive.
Blue-gray_Noddy.Best Ways to Identify: Pale blue-gray plumage distinctive among tropical seabirds. Delicate flight. Found on Hawaiian Northwestern atolls.

Blue-gray_Tanager.Description: Medium tanager, pale blue-gray throughout with brighter blue wings and tail. About 6.5 inches.
Blue-gray_Tanager.Behavior: Bold and conspicuous in gardens and parks. Forages for fruit and insects. Introduced to Miami, Florida.
Blue-gray_Tanager.Habitat: Gardens, parks, forest edges, and suburban areas. Introduced to Miami, Florida. Native to Central and South America.
Blue-gray_Tanager.Similar Looking Birds: Blue-gray Gnatcatcher much smaller and slender. No similar pale blue tanager in its Florida range.
Blue-gray_Tanager.Best Ways to Identify: Pale blue-gray throughout with brighter blue wings. Introduced to Miami, Florida. Bold garden bird.

Blue-headed_Vireo.Description: Olive-green back, blue-gray head, bold white spectacles (eye ring + loral stripe), white throat and belly, yellowish sides, and two white wing bars.
Blue-headed_Vireo.Behavior: Sings persistently with rich slurred phrases; deliberately forages for caterpillars and insects in foliage; hangs nest from a forked branch.
Blue-headed_Vireo.Habitat: Mature mixed and coniferous forests of northeastern North America and Appalachians; winters in the Southeast, Caribbean, and Central America.
Blue-headed_Vireo.Similar Looking Birds: Cassin's and Plumbeous Vireos (formerly grouped as "Solitary Vireo"); Blue-headed has brightest white spectacles and most contrasting head pattern.
Blue-headed_Vireo.Best Ways to Identify: Bright white spectacles on blue-gray head; olive back; persistent rich melodious song; deliberate foraging in mixed forest canopy.

Blue-throated_Mountain-gem.Description: Largest hummingbird in the United States. Males have bright blue throat (gorget), green back, gray underparts, and bold white facial stripes. Large white tail spots. Female has gray throat, white stripes. About 5 inches.
Blue-throated_Mountain-gem.Behavior: Feeds on flower nectar and insects in mountain canyons. Males defend feeding territories aggressively. Loud, squeaky call. Moves seasonally with flowers.
Blue-throated_Mountain-gem.Habitat: Mountain stream canyons with sycamores and maples in southeastern Arizona and southwestern New Mexico. Found at middle elevations in pine-oak zones.
Blue-throated_Mountain-gem.Similar Looking Birds: Rivoli's Hummingbird is larger with purple crown. Black-chinned Hummingbird is smaller with purple-black throat. Female mountain-gem has white facial stripes.
Blue-throated_Mountain-gem.Best Ways to Identify: Largest U.S. hummingbird. Bold white facial stripes on both sexes. Blue throat on male. White tail spots. Found in southern Arizona mountain stream canyons.

Blue-winged_Teal.Description: Small duck; male has blue-gray head with white crescent in front of eye, brown-spotted body, and iridescent green speculum; female is mottled brown.
Blue-winged_Teal.Behavior: Early fall migrant; one of the first ducks to head south; flies in tight swift flocks; feeds on aquatic plants and invertebrates in shallow water.
Blue-winged_Teal.Habitat: Shallow freshwater marshes, prairie potholes, and flooded fields across North America; winters from the southern U.S. to South America.
Blue-winged_Teal.Similar Looking Birds: Cinnamon Teal male is deep reddish-brown; female Blue-winged resembles other female dabblers — look for the blue forewing patch in flight.
Blue-winged_Teal.Best Ways to Identify: Blue forewing patch visible in flight; male's white facial crescent; small size; early fall departure; prairie marsh habitat.

Blue-winged_Warbler.Description: Yellow head and underparts with black eye line; blue-gray wings with two white wing bars; white undertail; slim body; fairly long thin bill.
Blue-winged_Warbler.Behavior: Forages in shrubby second growth; song is a buzzy inhaled-exhaled "bee-bzzz"; hybridizes with Golden-winged Warbler to produce "Brewster's" and "Lawrence's" hybrids.
Blue-winged_Warbler.Habitat: Shrubby forest edges, overgrown fields, and brushy hillsides of the eastern U.S.; winters in Central America; declining in areas of Golden-winged contact.
Blue-winged_Warbler.Similar Looking Birds: Golden-winged Warbler has black throat and cheek patch; hybrids show intermediate characters; Yellow Warbler lacks black eye line and wing bars.
Blue-winged_Warbler.Best Ways to Identify: Yellow face and underparts with black eye line, blue-gray wings, two white wing bars, and distinctive buzzy "bee-bzzz" song.

Blue_Bunting.Description: Medium bunting. Male deep blue throughout with brighter blue supercilium and rump. Female plain brown. About 5.5 inches.
Blue_Bunting.Behavior: Forages in dense scrub. Rare vagrant to Texas from northeastern Mexico.
Blue_Bunting.Habitat: Dense thorn scrub and brushy woodland of northeastern Mexico. Rare vagrant to Texas.
Blue_Bunting.Similar Looking Birds: Indigo Bunting smaller and lighter blue. Blue Grosbeak larger with wing bars. Deep blue color distinctive.
Blue_Bunting.Best Ways to Identify: Deep rich blue male throughout. Brighter blue on brow and rump. Female plain brown. Rare Texas vagrant.

Blue_Grosbeak.Description: Male is deep rich blue with two chestnut wing bars and a large silver bill; female is warm brown with buffy wing bars and a large bill.
Blue_Grosbeak.Behavior: Forages on seeds in weedy fields; males sing a long rich warbled song from elevated perches; flicks and spreads tail; often in brushy edge habitats.
Blue_Grosbeak.Habitat: Shrubby grasslands, weedy fields, hedgerows, and woodland edges of the southern U.S.; winters in Central America; expanding range northward.
Blue_Grosbeak.Similar Looking Birds: Indigo Bunting is smaller and lacks chestnut wing bars; Eastern Bluebird has rusty breast and is not deep blue overall; female resembles female Indigo.
Blue_Grosbeak.Best Ways to Identify: Male's rich deep blue with chestnut wing bars and large silver bill; tail- flicking habit; brushy edge habitat in southern and central U.S.

Blue_Jay.Description: Bright blue above with white underparts; bold black necklace; blue crest; black bar on wing and tail; white wing bars and tail corners; blue, black, and white.
Blue_Jay.Behavior: Loud and bold; mimics hawk calls; caches thousands of acorns annually, helping forest regeneration; intelligent; aggressive at feeders.
Blue_Jay.Habitat: Deciduous and mixed forests, parks, suburbs, and backyards throughout the eastern and central U.S.; year-round resident; some migrate.
Blue_Jay.Similar Looking Birds: Steller's Jay (western) has dark sooty head and body; scrub-jays lack the crest; Western Scrub-Jay is blue and gray without a crest.
Blue_Jay.Best Ways to Identify: Bright blue crest, blue-and-white pattern, bold black necklace, and loud "jay-jay" screaming call; extremely common in eastern North America.

Blue_Mockingbird.Description: Medium bird, all deep blue with black mask and red eye. Long tail, curved bill. About 10 inches.
Blue_Mockingbird.Behavior: Forages on ground in dense scrub. Mimics other species. Rare vagrant to Arizona and New Mexico from Mexico.
Blue_Mockingbird.Habitat: Dense scrub, forest undergrowth, and brushy hillsides of Mexico. Rare vagrant to Arizona and New Mexico.
Blue_Mockingbird.Similar Looking Birds: Blue-gray Gnatcatcher much smaller. No other all-blue bird with these proportions in North America.
Blue_Mockingbird.Best Ways to Identify: All-blue plumage with black mask and red eye. Long tail. Rare Mexican vagrant to Arizona scrub.

Blue_Rock-Thrush.Description: Medium thrush. Male deep blue throughout with darker wings. Female brown with scaled pattern. About 8 inches.
Blue_Rock-Thrush.Behavior: Perches on rocky outcrops and buildings. Sings melodiously from exposed perch. Rare vagrant to North America.
Blue_Rock-Thrush.Habitat: Rocky cliffs, coastal bluffs, and buildings in Europe, Asia, and Africa. Rare vagrant to North America.
Blue_Rock-Thrush.Similar Looking Birds: Rufous-tailed Rock-Thrush male has orange underparts. Blue Grosbeak smaller with wing bars.
Blue_Rock-Thrush.Best Ways to Identify: Male uniformly deep blue on rocky habitat. Female scaled brown. Very rare vagrant from Europe/Asia.

Bluethroat.Description: Small robin-like bird. Male has brilliant blue throat with red or white central spot. Breeds in western Alaska.
Bluethroat.Behavior: Hops through dense willow scrub. Males sing complex song from exposed perch. Cocks and fans rufous-based tail.
Bluethroat.Habitat: Dense willow and alder scrub along rivers in western and northern Alaska. Winters in Asia.
Bluethroat.Similar Looking Birds: European Robin has orange-red face, different range. No other blue-throated bird in Alaska willow scrub.
Bluethroat.Best Ways to Identify: Brilliant blue throat with central spot on male. Rufous tail base. Western Alaska breeder. Bobs and fans tail.

Blyths_Reed_Warbler.Description: Plain brown warbler, olive-brown above, buff below with slightly darker breast sides. Pale supercilium. About 5 inches.
Blyths_Reed_Warbler.Behavior: Skulks in dense scrub and hedges. Slow deliberate movements. Rare vagrant to western Alaska from Asia.
Blyths_Reed_Warbler.Habitat: Dense scrub, hedgerows, and garden vegetation in Asia. Rare vagrant to western Alaska.
Blyths_Reed_Warbler.Similar Looking Birds: Marsh Warbler and Reed Warbler very similar. Differences in primary projection and song.
Blyths_Reed_Warbler.Best Ways to Identify: Plain brown warbler with short primary projection. Alaska vagrant. Indistinct supercilium. Very difficult identification.

Boat-tailed_Grackle.Description: Large grackle. Male iridescent blue-black with huge keel-shaped tail. Female brown. About 16 inches (male).
Boat-tailed_Grackle.Behavior: Highly gregarious, noisy. Forages on beaches and marshes. Male displays with wings drooped and tail cocked.
Boat-tailed_Grackle.Habitat: Coastal marshes, beaches, and adjacent areas along Atlantic and Gulf coasts.
Boat-tailed_Grackle.Similar Looking Birds: Great-tailed Grackle very similar. Boat-tailed has dark eye (in most of range) vs yellow eye.
Boat-tailed_Grackle.Best Ways to Identify: Huge keel-shaped tail. Eye color: dark in most of range. Coastal saltmarsh habitat specialist.

Bobolink.Description: Breeding male is unique — black below with white back and rump, creamy-yellow nape; female and fall male are streaked buffy-brown with striped crown.
Bobolink.Behavior: Males perform display flight over meadows giving bubbling metallic song; long-distance migrant to South America; flocks in rice fields in fall.
Bobolink.Habitat: Grasslands, hayfields, and meadows of northern North America in summer; migrates to South America via the eastern U.S. coast.
Bobolink.Similar Looking Birds: No other bird has the male's inverted black-below, white-above pattern; females resemble sparrows — look for wide buffy eyebrow.
Bobolink.Best Ways to Identify: Unique male with black underparts and white back; bubbling metallic flight song over meadows; large flocks in grasslands during migration.

Bohemian_Waxwing.Description: Sleek crested gray-brown bird with black mask and throat; yellow tail tip; red waxy wing tips; rusty undertail coverts; yellow and white wing markings.
Bohemian_Waxwing.Behavior: Nomadic flocks roam in search of berries; irrupts into the U.S. in winter when northern berry crops fail; trills constantly; gorges on mountain ash and crabapples.
Bohemian_Waxwing.Habitat: Boreal forests of northern North America and Eurasia; irruptive winter visitor to northern U.S. cities and towns when berry crops are scarce.
Bohemian_Waxwing.Similar Looking Birds: Cedar Waxwing is smaller and browner with yellow belly and lacks rusty undertail; both species sometimes flock together in winter.
Bohemian_Waxwing.Best Ways to Identify: Rusty undertail coverts (Cedar Waxwing has white), gray body, crest, red wax wing tips; nomadic winter flocks stripping berry trees.

Bonapartes_Gull.Description: Small graceful gull with black bill, pale gray back, white underparts, and black hood in summer; black bill and ear spot in winter; flashing white wing wedges.
Bonapartes_Gull.Behavior: Buoyant tern-like flight; dips and plunges to catch small fish; migrates in large flocks; nests in spruce trees near boreal lakes — unusual for a gull.
Bonapartes_Gull.Habitat: Boreal forest lakes in summer; migrates along both coasts and interior rivers and lakes; winters on coasts, bays, and large lakes.
Bonapartes_Gull.Similar Looking Birds: Laughing Gull is much larger; Little Gull is smaller with dark underwings; Black-headed Gull has a red bill; Franklin's Gull has half-hood pattern.
Bonapartes_Gull.Best Ways to Identify: Tiny gull with white triangular wing flash in flight, black bill, buoyant flight style, and large migrating flocks; common on fall coasts.

Bonin_Petrel.Description: Small gadfly petrel, pale gray above with dark M-pattern, white underparts, grayish sides of breast. About 12 inches.
Bonin_Petrel.Behavior: Breeds on Hawaiian Northwestern Islands. Common in Hawaiian offshore waters; occasional off mainland Pacific coast.
Bonin_Petrel.Habitat: North central Pacific Ocean. Breeds on Hawaiian Northwestern Islands; forages in Hawaiian offshore waters.
Bonin_Petrel.Similar Looking Birds: Cook's Petrel similar. Bonin Petrel has more extensive gray on sides of breast.
Bonin_Petrel.Best Ways to Identify: Small pale gadfly petrel with gray breast sides. Dark M-pattern above. Hawaiian Northwestern Islands breeder.

Boreal_Chickadee.Description: Small chickadee with brown cap (not black), brown back, black bib, gray cheeks, and rich rusty-brown flanks; dull overall compared to Black-capped.
Boreal_Chickadee.Behavior: Tame and curious; often found in small flocks; caches food; moves south in irruption years; nasal "tch-day-day" call distinct from Black-capped.
Boreal_Chickadee.Habitat: Boreal spruce-fir forests of Canada and the northern United States; rarely strays south except in winter irruptions; closely tied to conifers.
Boreal_Chickadee.Similar Looking Birds: Black-capped Chickadee has black (not brown) cap and back, whiter cheeks, and different call; Chestnut-backed Chickadee has richer chestnut back.
Boreal_Chickadee.Best Ways to Identify: Brown cap instead of black, rusty flanks, nasal "tch-day" call, and boreal conifer forest habitat; less contrasting than Black-capped.

Boreal_Owl.Description: Small owl with large square head, chocolate brown spotted with white above, white face disk with dark border, yellow eyes, and white-streaked brown breast.
Boreal_Owl.Behavior: Strictly nocturnal; hunts small mammals in dense boreal forest; irrupts southward in winter; male's prolonged tooting call carries far.
Boreal_Owl.Habitat: Dense boreal spruce-fir forests of Canada and high-elevation mountains in the West; difficult to find; roosts in cavities during the day.
Boreal_Owl.Similar Looking Birds: Northern Saw-whet Owl is smaller with unspotted forehead; flammulated Owl is tiny; Tengmalm's Owl is the Eurasian equivalent.
Boreal_Owl.Best Ways to Identify: Square head with dark-bordered white face disk, spotted crown, yellow eyes; dense northern conifer forest; nocturnal; tooting advertising call in spring.

Botteris_Sparrow.Description: Medium sparrow, streaked brown above, plain buff below, flat head, long rounded tail. About 6 inches.
Botteris_Sparrow.Behavior: Sings from grass clumps or low shrubs. Very difficult to see on ground. Restricted to specific grass habitats.
Botteris_Sparrow.Habitat: Native sacaton grass flats and coastal grass fields of southern Arizona and southern Texas.
Botteris_Sparrow.Similar Looking Birds: Cassin's Sparrow sings elaborate display flight. Bachman's Sparrow has rusty back. Grasshopper Sparrow has flat head.
Botteris_Sparrow.Best Ways to Identify: Plain buff below, streaked back, flat head. Specific sacaton grass habitat in Arizona. Bouncing ball song.

Brambling.Description: Medium finch, black head and back in breeding, orange shoulder and breast, white rump. About 6 inches.
Brambling.Behavior: Forages on ground in beech woodland and fields. Rare vagrant to western Alaska and occasionally farther east.
Brambling.Habitat: Birch and mixed forest of Eurasia. Rare vagrant to western Alaska; occasional further into North America.
Brambling.Similar Looking Birds: Common Chaffinch has no orange shoulder and different rump pattern. Different body pattern overall.
Brambling.Best Ways to Identify: Orange shoulder and white rump distinctive. Black head in breeding. Rare Alaska vagrant from Siberia.

Brandts_Cormorant.Description: Large dark seabird with black plumage and buffy throat pouch; breeding adults show bright blue throat pouch and tan-buff chin; white filoplume feathers.
Brandts_Cormorant.Behavior: Dives from the surface to pursue fish underwater; roosts communally on offshore rocks; breeds in large coastal colonies; silent except at nest.
Brandts_Cormorant.Habitat: Pacific Coast of North America from Alaska to Baja California; feeds offshore in cold upwelling waters; nests on rocky islands and sea stacks.
Brandts_Cormorant.Similar Looking Birds: Pelagic Cormorant is smaller with iridescent green gloss and red face skin; Double-crested Cormorant has orange-yellow face skin and often found inland.
Brandts_Cormorant.Best Ways to Identify: All-dark body with blue throat pouch (breeding), buffy chin, and Pacific Coast ocean habitat; often in large flocks on sea rocks.

Brant.Description: Small dark goose with black head, neck, and breast; white neck patch; dark brown back; pale gray-white belly; short bill; stubby appearance.
Brant.Behavior: Highly dependent on eelgrass; coastal; migrates in low flocks over water; rarely found inland; gives low rolling "r-r-r-ruk" calls in flocks.
Brant.Habitat: Breeds on high Arctic tundra; winters on coastal bays, estuaries, and tidal flats where eelgrass grows; Pacific and Atlantic populations differ slightly.
Brant.Similar Looking Birds: Canada Goose is much larger with white chin strap; Cackling Goose is smaller but has white cheek patch; Black Brant (Pacific) has darker belly.
Brant.Best Ways to Identify: Small dark goose with black head and neck, white neck patch, found in coastal salt bays in winter; low rolling calls; never far from saltwater.

Brants_Goose.Description: Small, dark goose with black head, neck, and breast. White neck patch (not complete collar). Dark brown back, pale flanks, white undertail. About 25 inches. Stubby bill. Two subspecies differ in belly color.
Brants_Goose.Behavior: Highly specialized on eelgrass and sea lettuce. Forms large flocks in coastal bays. Strong migrant between Arctic breeding grounds and coastal wintering areas.
Brants_Goose.Habitat: Arctic tundra for breeding; coastal bays, estuaries, and tidal flats in winter. Pacific coast birds winter in Baja California lagoons. Atlantic birds winter on mid-Atlantic coast.
Brants_Goose.Similar Looking Birds: Canada Goose is much larger with white cheek patch. Cackling Goose has white cheek patch. Barnacle Goose has white face. Brant has all-dark head.
Brants_Goose.Best Ways to Identify: Small, dark-headed goose in coastal saltwater. Black head, neck and breast. White neck patch (not complete). Flocks fly in irregular bunches. Coastal winter.

Brewers_Blackbird.Description: Male is glossy purplish-black on head and greenish-black on body with yellow eyes; female is plain brown-gray with dark eyes.
Brewers_Blackbird.Behavior: Walks on ground probing for food near livestock and in parking lots; forms large flocks; bold and approachable; common in open country.
Brewers_Blackbird.Habitat: Open areas, farmland, parking lots, parks, and urban areas of western North America; winters across the South and sometimes northward.
Brewers_Blackbird.Similar Looking Birds: Common Grackle has longer keel-shaped tail; Rusty Blackbird is similar but has fall rusty edges and brown eye; Brown-headed Cowbird has brown head.
Brewers_Blackbird.Best Ways to Identify: Male's glossy purple head and yellow eye walking confidently on the ground; female's plain brownish-gray with dark eye; western range; flocks.

Brewers_Sparrow.Description: Small plain sparrow with fine brown streaking on crown and back, thin white eye ring, light brown face, and white wing bars; very nondescript.
Brewers_Sparrow.Behavior: Forages on the ground in sagebrush; male sings long buzzy trilling canary-like song; often difficult to find despite the lengthy song.
Brewers_Sparrow.Habitat: Sagebrush steppes of the Great Basin and western mountains; one of the most sagebrush-dependent birds in North America; winters in desert shrublands.
Brewers_Sparrow.Similar Looking Birds: Clay-colored Sparrow has stronger face pattern; Chipping Sparrow has rusty cap; Field Sparrow has pink bill and plain face; all are more patterned.
Brewers_Sparrow.Best Ways to Identify: Plain fine-streaked sparrow in sagebrush; thin white eye ring; long trilling canary-like song; the plainest sparrow in sagebrush country.

Bridled_Tern.Description: Medium tern. Dark gray-brown back and wings, black cap with white forehead extending to eye, white underparts. About 15 inches.
Bridled_Tern.Behavior: Picks fish from surface; rarely dives. Breeds on tropical islands. Regular in Gulf Stream waters off southeastern US.
Bridled_Tern.Habitat: Tropical and subtropical oceanic waters. Regular in Gulf Stream off Atlantic coast. Breeds on Dry Tortugas and Caribbean islands.
Bridled_Tern.Similar Looking Birds: Gray-backed Tern paler. Sooty Tern darker overall.
Bridled_Tern.Best Ways to Identify: Dark brown-gray back with black cap and white forehead. White extends past eye to nape. Regular in Gulf Stream.

Bridled_Titmouse.Description: Small crested titmouse with distinctive black and white bridled face pattern. Gray above, white below. About 5 inches.
Bridled_Titmouse.Behavior: Active forager in oak and pine-oak woodlands. Often joins mixed-species flocks. Chickadee-like behavior but with crest.
Bridled_Titmouse.Habitat: Oak and pine-oak woodlands of the Madrean sky islands in Arizona and New Mexico south into Mexico.
Bridled_Titmouse.Similar Looking Birds: Other titmice lack bold black-and-white face pattern. No other titmouse in its sky island range.
