Bridled_Titmouse.Best Ways to Identify: Distinctive black-and-white bridle face pattern with pointed crest. Small size. Sky island oak woodland habitat.

Bristle-thighed_Curlew.Description: Large curlew. Brown streaked plumage with buff-orange rump and tail, downcurved bill. Named for bristle-like thigh feathers. About 17 inches.
Bristle-thighed_Curlew.Behavior: Only shorebird known to use tools; rolls eggs with stones. Breeds in Alaska; winters on Pacific islands. Rare vagrant on Pacific coast.
Bristle-thighed_Curlew.Habitat: Breeds on Alaskan tundra. Migrates across open Pacific Ocean. Winters on Pacific islands including Hawaii and Fiji.
Bristle-thighed_Curlew.Similar Looking Birds: Whimbrel similar but lacks orange rump. Bristle-thighed has buffy rump visible in flight.
Bristle-thighed_Curlew.Best Ways to Identify: Warm buff-orange rump patch visible in flight. Larger than Whimbrel with warmer overall tones. Breeds only in Alaska.

Broad-billed_Hummingbird.Description: Male has brilliant blue-green gorget and underparts, green back, red bill with black tip. Female is greenish above, gray below with white eye stripe and red- based bill. About 4 inches. Notched tail.
Broad-billed_Hummingbird.Behavior: Feeds on flower nectar from a variety of blooms. Hovers and also perch-feeds. Males chase intruders with chattering calls. Visible tail pumping while feeding.
Broad-billed_Hummingbird.Habitat: Desert canyons with streams, sycamores, and flowering plants in southeastern Arizona. Also suburban gardens. Extends into Mexico. Some year-round residents.
Broad-billed_Hummingbird.Similar Looking Birds: Blue-throated Mountain-gem is much larger. Magnificent Hummingbird has purple crown. Berylline Hummingbird has rufous wings. Female similar to other female hummers.
Broad-billed_Hummingbird.Best Ways to Identify: Red bill with black tip (both sexes) is key. Male's brilliant blue-green color. Female has distinctive red-based bill and clean gray underparts. Canyon habitat.

Broad-billed_Sandpiper.Description: Small sandpiper with distinctive broad kinked bill. Dark brown streaked upperparts with double white supercilium, streaked breast. About 7 inches.
Broad-billed_Sandpiper.Behavior: Forages on mudflats picking invertebrates. Rare vagrant to North America from Eurasian breeding grounds.
Broad-billed_Sandpiper.Habitat: Breeds in Scandinavian and Siberian bogs. Winters on Asian and African coasts. Rare vagrant to Pacific coast of North America.
Broad-billed_Sandpiper.Similar Looking Birds: Dunlin similar size. Broad-billed has distinctive double supercilium and bent bill tip.
Broad-billed_Sandpiper.Best Ways to Identify: Kinked bill tip (bent downward at end) distinctive. Double white supercilium. Dark upperparts. Rare vagrant.

Broad-tailed_Hummingbird.Description: Medium hummingbird with iridescent rose-magenta gorget on male; green back; white breast; broad tail; female is green above with buffy-white below.
Broad-tailed_Hummingbird.Behavior: Males produce a distinctive loud metallic cricket-like wing trill in flight; breeds in mountain meadows; visits red tubular flowers and sugar-water feeders.
Broad-tailed_Hummingbird.Habitat: Mountain meadows, pine-oak forests, and riparian zones of the Rocky Mountains and Great Basin; winters in Mexico; common at mountain feeders.
Broad-tailed_Hummingbird.Similar Looking Birds: Rufous Hummingbird male has orange-rufous sides; Calliope is smaller; Anna's Hummingbird is a West Coast resident with different habitat.
Broad-tailed_Hummingbird.Best Ways to Identify: Male's loud metallic wing trill is unique and diagnostic; rose gorget; common at mountain feeders in the West; green-and-white female in mountains.

Broad-winged_Hawk.Description: Small crow-sized hawk with brown back, reddish-brown barring on breast, bold black-and-white tail bands, and broad wings with pointed tips.
Broad-winged_Hawk.Behavior: Migrates in spectacular "kettles" of thousands at hawk watch sites; summers quietly in forests; calls with a thin high-pitched whistle.
Broad-winged_Hawk.Habitat: Deciduous forests of eastern North America in summer; migrates in enormous concentrations; winters in Central and South America.
Broad-winged_Hawk.Similar Looking Birds: Red-tailed Hawk is much larger; Red-shouldered Hawk has orange barring and longer tail; Cooper's Hawk has rounded tail and accipiter shape.
Broad-winged_Hawk.Best Ways to Identify: Broad black-and-white tail bands; spectacular fall migration kettles; small buteo size; thin whistle call; deciduous forest in summer.

Bronzed_Cowbird.Description: Medium cowbird, male all glossy bronze-black with red eye and neck ruff. Female gray-brown. About 8.5 inches.
Bronzed_Cowbird.Behavior: Brood parasite. Male displays with distinctive hunchback posture and inflated neck ruff. Expanding range.
Bronzed_Cowbird.Habitat: Open areas, farmland, and woodland edges in southwestern United States, Texas, and Mexico.
Bronzed_Cowbird.Similar Looking Birds: Brown-headed Cowbird male has brown head. Shiny Cowbird lacks neck ruff. Red eye distinctive.
Bronzed_Cowbird.Best Ways to Identify: Red eye on all-black male. Neck ruff inflated in display. Hunchback posture. Southwestern United States.

Brown-backed_Solitaire.Description: Medium thrush-like bird, brown above, gray below, white eye ring, orange-based bill. About 8 inches.
Brown-backed_Solitaire.Behavior: Beautiful, haunting song from forest understory. Rare vagrant to Arizona and Texas from Mexico.
Brown-backed_Solitaire.Habitat: Mountain forests of Mexico and Central America. Very rare vagrant to Arizona sky islands and Texas.
Brown-backed_Solitaire.Similar Looking Birds: Townsend's Solitaire has white outer tail feathers and buff wing patches. Different family relationship.
Brown-backed_Solitaire.Best Ways to Identify: White eye ring, brown above, gray below. Haunting beautiful song. Rare Mexican vagrant to mountain forests.

Brown-capped_Rosy-Finch.Description: Medium finch endemic to Colorado mountains. Brown cap (not black or gray). Rose-pink wash on wings, rump, and belly. Males brighter; females duller. About 6 inches. Pale bill in winter, dark in summer.
Brown-capped_Rosy-Finch.Behavior: Forages on snowfields and talus for seeds and insects blown onto snow. Forms flocks in winter moving to lower elevations. Nests in cliff crevices.
Brown-capped_Rosy-Finch.Habitat: Alpine tundra and rocky mountaintops in Colorado and southern Wyoming. Found above treeline. In winter, descends to foothill feeders and towns.
Brown-capped_Rosy-Finch.Similar Looking Birds: Black Rosy-Finch has black cap. Gray-crowned Rosy-Finch has gray crown and brown body. Brown-capped has brown cap with no gray, endemic to Colorado.
Brown-capped_Rosy-Finch.Best Ways to Identify: Brown cap (no gray or black). Rose-pink on wings and rump. Alpine Colorado habitat. In winter, visits feeders in mountain towns with other rosy-finches.

Brown-chested_Martin.Description: Medium martin, brown above, white below with brown breast band and brown streaks on sides. About 6.5 inches.
Brown-chested_Martin.Behavior: Aerial insect forager over open areas. Very rare vagrant to eastern North America from South America.
Brown-chested_Martin.Habitat: Open areas, farmland, and forest edges in South America. Very rare vagrant to northeastern North America.
Brown-chested_Martin.Similar Looking Birds: Bank Swallow smaller with narrower breast band. Purple Martin male all-dark, female has scaled throat.
Brown-chested_Martin.Best Ways to Identify: Brown breast band, brown streaks on flanks. Brown above. Larger than Bank Swallow. Very rare vagrant from South America.

Brown-crested_Flycatcher.Description: Large Myiarchus flycatcher, brown above with rufous tail, pale gray throat, yellow belly, prominent crest. About 9 inches.
Brown-crested_Flycatcher.Behavior: Gleans insects; nests in large tree cavities. Summer resident in saguaro desert and riparian forest of Southwest.
Brown-crested_Flycatcher.Habitat: Saguaro desert, cottonwood riparian forest. Southwestern US summer resident; winters in Mexico.
Brown-crested_Flycatcher.Similar Looking Birds: Ash-throated Flycatcher smaller. Brown-crested larger with heavier bill and brighter yellow belly.
Brown-crested_Flycatcher.Best Ways to Identify: Largest Myiarchus flycatcher in range. Heavy bill, bright yellow belly, rufous tail. Saguaro desert specialist.

Brown-headed_Cowbird.Description: Male has glossy black body with brown head; female is plain gray-brown with faint streaking; short conical bill; stubby tail; walks with head bobbing.
Brown-headed_Cowbird.Behavior: Brood parasite — lays eggs in other birds' nests, abandoning eggs for hosts to raise; follows cattle to catch disturbed insects; forms large flocks.
Brown-headed_Cowbird.Habitat: Open country, farmland, forest edges, and suburbs throughout North America; followed bison historically; now hugely expanded with forest fragmentation.
Brown-headed_Cowbird.Similar Looking Birds: European Starling is similar at a distance but has longer bill and no brown head; Rusty Blackbird and Brewer's Blackbird have yellow eyes.
Brown-headed_Cowbird.Best Ways to Identify: Male's brown head on glossy black body; female's plain gray-brown; following cattle or horses; short bill; common brood parasite everywhere.

Brown-headed_Nuthatch.Description: Tiny nuthatch with brown cap, white cheeks and throat, blue-gray back and wings, and buff underparts. Tiny white nape spot. About 4.5 inches. Uses pine bark scales as tools — one of few U.S. tool-using birds.
Brown-headed_Nuthatch.Behavior: Creeps headfirst down tree trunks. Uses bark flakes to pry up other bark. Highly social, often in mixed flocks. High-pitched squeaky calls. Roosts in cavities. Pairs cooperative breeders.
Brown-headed_Nuthatch.Habitat: Mature longleaf and loblolly pine forests of the southeastern United States. Requires open, park-like pine stands. Year-round resident; does not migrate.
Brown-headed_Nuthatch.Similar Looking Birds: Red-breasted Nuthatch has rust-orange underparts and black eyeline. White- breasted Nuthatch is larger with white face. Pygmy Nuthatch of West similar.
Brown-headed_Nuthatch.Best Ways to Identify: Brown cap and tiny size in southeastern pine forests. High squeaky rubber-duck call. Tool use with bark flakes. Pines of southeastern coastal plain.

Brown_Booby.Description: Large seabird with chocolate-brown hood, neck, and upperparts contrasting sharply with clean white belly and underwings. Yellow feet, blue-gray bill in adults. About 30 inches. Pointed wings and tail.
Brown_Booby.Behavior: Plunge-dives from height for flying fish and squid. Rests on buoys, boats, and rocky outcroppings. Breeds on tropical islands in ground colonies.
Brown_Booby.Habitat: Tropical and subtropical oceans worldwide. Rare but regular in Gulf of Mexico and off California. Wanders north after tropical storms. Nests on Caribbean islands.
Brown_Booby.Similar Looking Birds: Blue-footed Booby has blue feet and brown-and-white wings (not clean contrast). Masked Booby has white body with black mask and wingtips. Northern Gannet is white.
Brown_Booby.Best Ways to Identify: Sharp brown-white contrast between hood and belly. Yellow feet. Plunge-diving behavior. Tropical oceans and Gulf waters. Often perches on boats or buoys.

Brown_Creeper.Description: Tiny brown bird with heavily streaked brown-and-buff plumage above; white underparts; long curved bill; stiff pointed tail used for support.
Brown_Creeper.Behavior: Spirals upward on tree trunks probing bark crevices for insects; flies to base of next tree; extremely well camouflaged; thin high "seeee" call.
Brown_Creeper.Habitat: Mature forests with large trees throughout North America; more common in winter when joins mixed flocks; nests behind bark plates of dead trees.
Brown_Creeper.Similar Looking Birds: No other North American bird creeps up tree bark in quite this way; nuthatches go down tree trunks; wrens are brighter and shorter-tailed.
Brown_Creeper.Best Ways to Identify: Spiraling up tree trunks with curved bill; heavily streaked brown camouflage; thin high "seeee" call; stiff tail pressed against bark.

Brown_Jay.Description: Large, noisy jay, dark brown above and below with white belly. Yellow bill, blue eye ring. About 15 inches.
Brown_Jay.Behavior: Highly gregarious, travels in noisy flocks. Cooperative breeder with helpers at nest. Very loud and raucous calls.
Brown_Jay.Habitat: Tropical forests, woodlands, and forest edges from Mexico to Panama. Small population resident in extreme southern Texas.
Brown_Jay.Similar Looking Birds: No similar species in its range. Much larger than other jays. Dark brown color distinctive.
Brown_Jay.Best Ways to Identify: Large dark brown jay with white belly. Very noisy and gregarious. Yellow bill. South Texas resident.

Brown_Noddy.Description: Medium tern-like seabird. All dark brown with pale white cap and white crescent below eye. Long graduated tail. About 15 inches.
Brown_Noddy.Behavior: Picks fish from surface; rarely dives. Nests in colonies on tropical islands. Breeds on Dry Tortugas, Florida.
Brown_Noddy.Habitat: Tropical oceanic islands. Breeds on Dry Tortugas in Florida and Caribbean islands. Forages offshore in warm tropical waters.
Brown_Noddy.Similar Looking Birds: Black Noddy smaller with all-black plumage. Brown Noddy browner with more extensive pale cap.
Brown_Noddy.Best Ways to Identify: All brown except pale cap. Long graduated tail. Breeds on Dry Tortugas, Florida. Tropical seabird.

Brown_Pelican.Description: Large seabird with dark brown body, pale yellowish-white head, and enormous pouched bill; breeding adults have chestnut nape; wingspan up to 7 feet.
Brown_Pelican.Behavior: Plunge-dives from height into ocean for fish, filling pouch then draining it; flies in formation just above waves; colonies nest on coastal islands.
Brown_Pelican.Habitat: Coastal ocean, bays, estuaries, and fishing piers along both coasts and Gulf; once nearly wiped out by DDT, now fully recovered and common.
Brown_Pelican.Similar Looking Birds: American White Pelican is all white and doesn't plunge-dive; Double-crested Cormorant is smaller, darker, and has an orange face.
Brown_Pelican.Best Ways to Identify: Brown body with huge pouched bill; spectacular plunge-dives into the ocean; formation flight over waves; ubiquitous along warm coastal waters.

Brown_Shrike.Description: Medium shrike, warm brown above, buff below with fine barring. Black mask through eye, white supercilium. About 8 inches.
Brown_Shrike.Behavior: Perches on exposed branches watching for prey. Impales insects and small vertebrates on thorns. Rare vagrant to Alaska.
Brown_Shrike.Habitat: Open country, forest edges, and scrubland in Asia. Rare but regular vagrant to western Alaska and occasionally farther east.
Brown_Shrike.Similar Looking Birds: Red-backed Shrike similar but male has gray head. Loggerhead Shrike gray above with heavy bill.
Brown_Shrike.Best Ways to Identify: Warm brown tones throughout with buff underparts. Black mask, white brow. Perches upright on exposed branches.

Brown_Thrasher.Description: Large thrush-like bird with rich rufous-brown upperparts, bold dark brown streaking on white underparts, long tail, curved bill, and yellow eyes.
Brown_Thrasher.Behavior: Forages by tossing leaf litter with its bill; males sing one of the largest songbird repertoires — over 1,000 song types; secretive in thickets.
Brown_Thrasher.Habitat: Dense shrubby thickets, forest edges, and hedgerows of eastern North America; uncommon in the open; state bird of Georgia.
Brown_Thrasher.Similar Looking Birds: Wood Thrush has round spots (not streaks) and shorter tail; Hermit Thrush is smaller with spotted breast; Long-billed Thrasher is found in Texas.
Brown_Thrasher.Best Ways to Identify: Rich rufous-brown above, heavily streaked below, long tail, curved bill, yellow eyes; thickets in the East; sings in doubled phrases.

Bryans_Shearwater.Description: Tiny shearwater, black above, white below. Smallest shearwater in Pacific. Newly described species. About 10 inches.
Bryans_Shearwater.Behavior: One of world's rarest birds; fewer than 10 known specimens. Breeds on small Pacific island; very poorly known.
Bryans_Shearwater.Habitat: Central North Pacific. Extremely rare; only known from small islands in Pacific. Among least-known birds.
Bryans_Shearwater.Similar Looking Birds: Other small black-and-white shearwaters larger. Bryan's Shearwater smallest Pacific shearwater.
Bryans_Shearwater.Best Ways to Identify: Tiny size, black above with white below. Extremely rare; one of world's least-known bird species.

Budgerigar.Description: Small parrot, wild type green and yellow with black barring, blue cheek patches. Captive birds vary. About 7 inches.
Budgerigar.Behavior: Nomadic flocking parrot of Australian grasslands. Established feral population in southwestern Florida (now declining).
Budgerigar.Habitat: Australian grassland and scrub. Former feral population in southwestern Florida; very few remain.
Budgerigar.Similar Looking Birds: No wild parakeet has the same barred pattern with blue cheek patches.
Budgerigar.Best Ways to Identify: Wild-type green and yellow with black barring, blue cheeks. Very small parrot. Former Florida feral population.

Buff-bellied_Hummingbird.Description: Medium hummingbird. Iridescent green throat and upperparts, buffy-cinnamon belly, red bill with dark tip, rufous tail. About 4 inches.
Buff-bellied_Hummingbird.Behavior: Feeds on nectar; aggressive at feeders. Nests in southern Texas. Moves north along Gulf Coast after breeding in some years.
Buff-bellied_Hummingbird.Habitat: Woodland edges, riparian areas, and gardens in Lower Rio Grande Valley, Texas, and south along Gulf Coast of Mexico.
Buff-bellied_Hummingbird.Similar Looking Birds: Berylline Hummingbird. Buff-bellied has rufous tail and clean separation of green and buff colors.
Buff-bellied_Hummingbird.Best Ways to Identify: Green throat contrasting with buff-cinnamon belly. Rufous tail visible in flight. Red bill. Found in Texas near Mexican border.

Buff-breasted_Flycatcher.Description: Tiny Empidonax flycatcher with distinctive pale buff- orange wash on breast. Small size, two wing bars. About 5 inches.
Buff-breasted_Flycatcher.Behavior: Nests in open pine woodland. Regular rare summer resident in Chiricahua and Huachuca mountain ranges of southeastern Arizona.
Buff-breasted_Flycatcher.Habitat: Open pine woodland in mountains of southeastern Arizona. Rare but regular summer resident.
Buff-breasted_Flycatcher.Similar Looking Birds: Other Empidonax lack strong buff wash on breast. Buff-breasted has distinctive warm buff tone.
Buff-breasted_Flycatcher.Best Ways to Identify: Warm buff wash on breast and belly unique among Empidonax. Small size. Southeastern Arizona mountain pine forest.

Buff-breasted_Sandpiper.Description: Medium sandpiper with buffy face, neck and underparts, scaly brown back, yellow legs. Short bill. About 8 inches.
Buff-breasted_Sandpiper.Behavior: Forages in dry grasslands and short grass fields, not mudflats. Males display at leks. Migrates through Great Plains.
Buff-breasted_Sandpiper.Habitat: Breeds on Arctic tundra. Migrates through Great Plains grasslands. Winters on South American pampas.
Buff-breasted_Sandpiper.Similar Looking Birds: Ruff (non-breeding) similar buffy tones. Buff-breasted uniform buff with scaly brown back.
Buff-breasted_Sandpiper.Best Ways to Identify: Entirely buffy face and underparts with scaly brown back. Grassland habitat. Yellow legs. Elegant long-necked appearance.

Buff-collared_Nightjar.Description: Medium nightjar. Brown, gray, and black cryptic plumage with pale buff collar around hindneck. About 9 inches.
Buff-collared_Nightjar.Behavior: Nocturnal insect catcher. Roosts on ground by day. Rare in US; found in dry rocky canyons of southern Arizona and New Mexico.
Buff-collared_Nightjar.Habitat: Dry rocky canyon slopes with sparse scrub in southern Arizona, New Mexico, and adjacent Mexico. Uncommon and local.
Buff-collared_Nightjar.Similar Looking Birds: Whip-poor-will similar patterning. Buff-collared has distinctive pale buff collar on hindneck.
Buff-collared_Nightjar.Best Ways to Identify: Pale buff hindneck collar distinctive among nightjars. Dry rocky canyon habitat in Arizona. Loud repeated nocturnal call.

Bufflehead.Description: A tiny diving duck. Males show bold black-and-white plumage with a large iridescent green and purple head patch. Females are brown with a small white cheek spot.
Bufflehead.Behavior: Dives frequently for aquatic invertebrates. Takes flight easily from water. Often seen in small flocks. Monogamous and returns to same nest sites yearly.
Bufflehead.Habitat: Breeds near forested lakes and ponds in Canada. Winters along coasts, bays, and large inland lakes across the United States.
Bufflehead.Similar Looking Birds: Common Goldeneye is larger with a rounder head. Hooded Merganser has a fan-shaped crest. Male Ruddy Duck is reddish with a white cheek.
Bufflehead.Best Ways to Identify: Smallest North American diving duck. Males unmistakable with large white head patch. Fast wingbeats create a buzzing sound in flight.

Bullers_Shearwater.Description: Elegant shearwater, pale gray above with bold dark M-pattern, clean white below, dark gray cap. About 16 inches.
Bullers_Shearwater.Behavior: Breeds on Poor Knights Islands, New Zealand. Migrates north into Pacific; uncommon offshore California in fall.
Bullers_Shearwater.Habitat: North Pacific in non-breeding season. Offshore California and Oregon coast in fall. Breeds on New Zealand islands.
Bullers_Shearwater.Similar Looking Birds: Cook's Petrel smaller. Buller's Shearwater larger with bold M-pattern and clean white below.
Bullers_Shearwater.Best Ways to Identify: Bold dark M-pattern on pale gray upperwings. Clean white below, dark cap. Elegant Pacific shearwater offshore California.

Bullocks_Oriole.Description: Male has brilliant orange body with black back, wings, and crown. Large white wing patch, black eyeline and throat. Female is yellowish-olive with whitish belly. About 8.5 inches. Long tail.
Bullocks_Oriole.Behavior: Forages in tree canopy for insects, nectar, and fruit. Builds long, pendulous woven nest hanging from branch tips. Males sing a rich, whistling song.
Bullocks_Oriole.Habitat: Open woodlands, riparian corridors, orchards, and parks in western North America. Winters in Mexico and Central America. Common backyard visitor.
Bullocks_Oriole.Similar Looking Birds: Baltimore Oriole (eastern) male has all-orange head. Hooded Oriole is thinner with more orange and less black. Scott's Oriole has black hood in male.
Bullocks_Oriole.Best Ways to Identify: Large white wing patch with black eyeline on orange male. Western range. Female's yellowish tones with whitish belly. Hanging nest. Loud whistles.

Bulwers_Petrel.Description: All-dark petrel with long wedge-shaped tail. Brown-black overall with pale diagonal wing bar. About 10 inches.
Bulwers_Petrel.Behavior: Erratic bat-like flight low over water. Breeds on Atlantic and Pacific tropical islands; disperses widely.
Bulwers_Petrel.Habitat: Tropical Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. Offshore Hawaiian waters; rare vagrant to North American Pacific coast.
Bulwers_Petrel.Similar Looking Birds: Dark storm-petrels smaller. Bulwer's distinctive long wedge tail unlike all storm-petrels.
Bulwers_Petrel.Best Ways to Identify: Long wedge-shaped tail unique. All-dark with pale diagonal wing bar. Bat-like erratic flight near ocean surface.

Bumblebee_Hummingbird.Description: Tiny hummingbird, one of world's smallest birds. Male has rose-purple gorget, green back, white below with green spots. About 3 inches.
Bumblebee_Hummingbird.Behavior: Feeds on nectar from small flowers. Extremely rare vagrant to Arizona from Mexico. Easily overlooked due to tiny size.
Bumblebee_Hummingbird.Habitat: Pine-oak mountain forests of Mexico. Extremely rare vagrant to mountain canyons of southeastern Arizona.
Bumblebee_Hummingbird.Similar Looking Birds: Calliope Hummingbird similar tiny size. Bumblebee male's round gorget vs. streaked in Calliope.
Bumblebee_Hummingbird.Best Ways to Identify: Extremely small size. Male's round rose-purple gorget and short bill. Very rare vagrant in Arizona mountains.

Burrowing_Owl.Description: A small, long-legged owl standing about 9 inches tall. Brown and white spotted plumage. Bright yellow eyes and white eyebrows give it a perpetually surprised look.
Burrowing_Owl.Behavior: Active day and night; often seen standing at burrow entrance. Bobs head when alarmed. Nests underground in old prairie dog or ground squirrel burrows.
Burrowing_Owl.Habitat: Open grasslands, deserts, agricultural fields, and golf courses. Found from western Canada through Florida and throughout Central and South America.
Burrowing_Owl.Similar Looking Birds: Short-eared Owl is larger and rarely stands on ground. Ferruginous Pygmy-Owl lacks long legs. Burrowing Owl's ground habitat is distinctive.
Burrowing_Owl.Best Ways to Identify: Long legs, round head without ear tufts, and ground- dwelling habit are key. Often perches on fence posts near burrow entrances in open terrain.

Burrowing_Parakeet.Description: Large parakeet, olive-brown above, yellow and red belly patch, white breast patches. About 18 inches.
Burrowing_Parakeet.Behavior: Nests in burrows in cliffs and embankments. Gregarious. Very small feral population in California.
Burrowing_Parakeet.Habitat: Open grasslands and cliffs. Tiny feral population in California. Native to Argentina and Chile.
Burrowing_Parakeet.Similar Looking Birds: Monk Parakeet all green. Conures more uniformly colored. Olive-brown color distinctive.
Burrowing_Parakeet.Best Ways to Identify: Olive-brown with yellow and red belly. Burrow-nesting habit. Very rare feral bird in California.

Bushtit.Description: Tiny gray bird, about 4.5 inches long with a long tail. Plain gray-brown overall. Males have dark eyes; females have pale yellow eyes. No bold markings.
Bushtit.Behavior: Highly social; travels in noisy flocks of 10-40 birds. Gleans insects from leaves and branches. Builds an intricate hanging sock-shaped nest.
Bushtit.Habitat: Open woodlands, chaparral, parks, and suburban gardens from southern British Columbia through Central America. Avoids dense forests and open grasslands.
Bushtit.Similar Looking Birds: Plain gray color can suggest gnatcatchers, but Bushtit lacks the blue-gray tone and white eye ring. Its tiny size and long tail distinguish it from most wrens.
Bushtit.Best Ways to Identify: Tiny size, plain gray plumage, and long tail are distinctive. Almost always found in active, chattering flocks moving through shrubs.

Cackling_Goose.Description: Formerly considered a small Canada Goose race, now a separate species. Black head and neck, white cheek patch, brown body, white undertail. Very small — about 24 inches (much smaller than Canada Goose). Short, stubby bill.
Cackling_Goose.Behavior: Grazes on grasses and grains in flocks. Migrates in large flocks, often with Canada Geese. High-pitched, cackling call (higher than Canada Goose honk).
Cackling_Goose.Habitat: Breeds on Arctic tundra. Winters in Pacific lowlands, fields, and wetlands. Common in California's Central Valley and Pacific Northwest in winter.
Cackling_Goose.Similar Looking Birds: Canada Goose is larger with longer neck and bill. Brant has all-dark head. Distinguishing from small Canada Goose subspecies can be very difficult.
Cackling_Goose.Best Ways to Identify: Much smaller size and stubby bill compared to Canada Goose. Cackling, high- pitched call. Short neck. Often mixed in flocks with Canada Geese in winter.

Cactus_Wren.Description: Largest wren in North America, about 8 inches long. Brown back with white streaks. Bold white eyebrow stripe. Heavily spotted breast and barred wings and tail.
Cactus_Wren.Behavior: Loud and bold; calls frequently with a harsh, repetitive churr. Builds bulky grass nests in cholla or saguaro cacti. Defends territory year-round.
Cactus_Wren.Habitat: Desert scrub and arid lowlands of the southwestern United States and Mexico. Closely associated with cacti, especially cholla and saguaro.
Cactus_Wren.Similar Looking Birds: Sage Thrasher is slimmer with a shorter bill and less bold spotting. Curve-billed Thrasher has a longer curved bill. Other wrens are much smaller.
Cactus_Wren.Best Ways to Identify: Very large for a wren, with bold white supercilium and heavily spotted underparts. Its loud raspy call and cactus habitat make it easy to find.

California_Condor.Description: Enormous black vulture with 9.5-foot wingspan. Bald orange-red head on adults. Large white triangular patches on underwings.
California_Condor.Behavior: Soars on thermals for hours without flapping. Feeds on large carrion. Highly social; nests in cliff caves and large trees.
California_Condor.Habitat: Rocky shrublands, coniferous forests, and oak savannas of California, Arizona, Utah, and Baja California.
California_Condor.Similar Looking Birds: Turkey Vulture is much smaller with a red head and two-toned flight feathers. Black Vulture is smaller with white wingtips.
California_Condor.Best Ways to Identify: Massive size and wingspan are unmistakable. White underwing triangles and bare orange head on soaring adults are definitive.

California_Gnatcatcher.Description: Tiny gnatcatcher, blue-gray above, gray below without white. Black cap on male. Mostly black tail. About 4.5 inches.
California_Gnatcatcher.Behavior: Extremely restricted to coastal sage scrub habitat. Endangered. Pairs defend territory year-round with cat-like calls.
California_Gnatcatcher.Habitat: Coastal sage scrub of southern California and Baja California. Threatened by development and invasive grasses.
California_Gnatcatcher.Similar Looking Birds: Blue-gray Gnatcatcher lighter below with white tail edges. Black-tailed in desert. Range and habitat important.
California_Gnatcatcher.Best Ways to Identify: Coastal sage scrub of southern California. Darker gray below than Blue-gray Gnatcatcher. Cat-like mewing call.

California_Gull.Description: Medium-large gull with white head and body, gray back, and yellow bill with red and black spots near tip.
California_Gull.Behavior: Omnivorous scavenger; follows plows and forages at landfills, lakes, and coasts. Nests colonially on islands in inland lakes.
California_Gull.Habitat: Breeds at inland lakes and marshes in the western U.S. Winters along the Pacific Coast from British Columbia to Mexico.
California_Gull.Similar Looking Birds: Herring Gull is larger with a pinkish bill. Ring-billed Gull is smaller with a complete black ring on the bill.
California_Gull.Best Ways to Identify: Medium size with yellow bill showing both red and black spots. Dark eye gives a gentle expression compared to pale-eyed gulls.

California_Quail.Description: Plump, gray-brown quail with a teardrop-shaped black plume. Males have a black face with white stripe; females are plain.
California_Quail.Behavior: Travels in coveys of 10-200 birds. Scratches ground for seeds. Runs rather than flies when threatened. Roosts in dense shrubs.
California_Quail.Habitat: Chaparral, open woodlands, and scrubby parks from southern British Columbia through Baja California. Common in suburbs.
California_Quail.Similar Looking Birds: Gambel's Quail has a chestnut crown and rusty flanks. Mountain Quail has a straight vertical plume and bold white side stripes.
California_Quail.Best Ways to Identify: Teardrop topknot is distinctive. Males show black-and-white face pattern. Often seen in large, noisy groups on the ground.

California_Scrub-Jay.Description: Long-tailed jay with blue head, back, and tail. Gray-brown back patch. White throat outlined by a blue necklace band.
California_Scrub-Jay.Behavior: Bold and inquisitive; visits feeders regularly. Caches acorns for winter. Loud, raspy calls. Hops on ground to forage.
California_Scrub-Jay.Habitat: Coastal scrub, chaparral, oak woodlands, and suburban gardens in the western United States and Pacific Coast.
California_Scrub-Jay.Similar Looking Birds: Steller's Jay has a crest and entirely dark head. Woodhouse's Scrub-Jay is paler and limited to interior regions.
California_Scrub-Jay.Best Ways to Identify: Bright blue with gray-brown back patch and no crest. White supercilium and blue necklace are distinctive field marks.

California_Thrasher.Description: Large, long-tailed brown bird with a very long, downcurved bill. Pale buff underparts with a darker brown back.
California_Thrasher.Behavior: Uses bill to dig and toss leaf litter for insects. Stays low in dense shrubs. Loud, melodious, mimicking song.
California_Thrasher.Habitat: Dense chaparral and coastal scrub of California and northern Baja California. Rarely found outside its core range.
California_Thrasher.Similar Looking Birds: Curve-billed Thrasher has spotted breast and spotted orange eyes. Crissal Thrasher has rusty undertail. Both are inland.
California_Thrasher.Best Ways to Identify: Extremely long, sharply curved bill and long tail are key. Plain brown above with buff belly. Found only in California.

California_Towhee.Description: Large, plain brown sparrow with a long tail. Buffy-orange throat patch outlined with dark streaks. Rusty undertail.
California_Towhee.Behavior: Forages on the ground by scratching in leaf litter. Stays near dense cover. Often seen in pairs year-round.
California_Towhee.Habitat: Chaparral, brushy gardens, and oak woodlands of California and Oregon. A common backyard bird in much of its range.
California_Towhee.Similar Looking Birds: Canyon Towhee is very similar but grayer with a rusty crown patch and found inland. Abert's Towhee has a black mask.
California_Towhee.Best Ways to Identify: Plain brown overall with a buffy-orange throat and rusty undertail. Long tail and ground-foraging habits are useful.

Calliope_Hummingbird.Description: Smallest bird in North America. Males have magenta-streaked gorget. Females are greenish above with peachy-buff underparts.
Calliope_Hummingbird.Behavior: Migrates to high mountain meadows to breed. Hovers at flowers and feeders. Males perform steep U-shaped display dives.
Calliope_Hummingbird.Habitat: Mountain meadows, willow thickets, and shrubby forest edges from 4,000 to 11,000 feet in the western United States.
Calliope_Hummingbird.Similar Looking Birds: Broad-tailed Hummingbird is larger and males have a solid rosy-red gorget. Rufous Hummingbird has rufous sides and tail.
Calliope_Hummingbird.Best Ways to Identify: Tiny size is distinctive. Male's streaked magenta gorget is unique. Short bill and tail barely extends beyond wingtips.

Canada_Goose.Description: Large goose with black head and neck and a distinctive white chinstrap. Brown body, pale chest, and white undertail.
Canada_Goose.Behavior: Grazes on grass; highly adaptable to urban parks and golf courses. Honks loudly in flight. Flies in V-formation.
Canada_Goose.Habitat: Lakes, ponds, rivers, golf courses, and parks across most of North America. Many populations are now year-round residents.
Canada_Goose.Similar Looking Birds: Cackling Goose is much smaller with a stubbier bill. Brant is smaller with no white chinstrap and darker underparts.
Canada_Goose.Best Ways to Identify: Black head and neck with bold white chinstrap are unmistakable. Large size and loud honking call. Common in urban parks.

Canada_Jay.Description: Fluffy, medium-sized gray bird with a darker gray back and white forehead. Dark nape and short bill. No crest.
Canada_Jay.Behavior: Bold camp robber; pilfers food from campsites. Caches food in bark crevices for winter. Tame and curious around humans.
Canada_Jay.Habitat: Boreal and subalpine coniferous forests across Canada and the northern United States, especially spruce-fir forests.
Canada_Jay.Similar Looking Birds: Clark's Nutcracker is larger with white wing patches and black-and-white wings. Gray Jay (old name) refers to same bird.
Canada_Jay.Best Ways to Identify: Fluffy gray plumage with white face and dark nape cap. Found in boreal forests and often approaches humans without fear.

Canada_Warbler.Description: Yellow underparts with a bold black necklace of streaks. Blue-gray upperparts. Yellow spectacles around the dark eye.
Canada_Warbler.Behavior: Active forager in dense understory; often fans tail. Migrates long distances to South America. Males sing complex songs.
Canada_Warbler.Habitat: Breeds in moist forest understory with ferns near streams in Canada and northeastern U.S. Winters in South America.
Canada_Warbler.Similar Looking Birds: Magnolia Warbler has yellow rump and white tail spots. Wilson's Warbler has a black cap but no necklace. Lacks wing bars.
Canada_Warbler.Best Ways to Identify: Bold black necklace on bright yellow breast is distinctive. Yellow spectacles and blue-gray back complete the field marks.

Canvasback.Description: Large diving duck. Males have a chestnut-red head and neck, black breast, and white body. Females are brown with pale flanks.
Canvasback.Behavior: Dives for aquatic plants, especially wild celery. Fast flier with rapid wingbeats. Forms large flocks on open water.
Canvasback.Habitat: Breeds in prairie potholes and marshes. Winters on large bays, lakes, and estuaries across the United States.
Canvasback.Similar Looking Birds: Redhead has a rounder red head and gray back. Ring-necked Duck is smaller and darker. Male Canvasback has a distinctive profile.
Canvasback.Best Ways to Identify: Long sloping forehead creates a distinctive wedge-shaped profile. Male's red head and white back are unmistakable at a distance.

Canyon_Towhee.Description: Large, gray-brown sparrow with a rusty-orange crown patch and buffy throat outlined by a necklace of dark spots.
Canyon_Towhee.Behavior: Forages on the ground in rocky terrain. Often seen in pairs year-round. Scratches in leaf litter; sings from low perches.
Canyon_Towhee.Habitat: Rocky desert canyons, brushy hillsides, and arid scrublands of the southwestern U.S. and Mexico.
Canyon_Towhee.Similar Looking Birds: California Towhee is nearly identical but browner and found along the coast. Abert's Towhee has a black mask and bill base.
Canyon_Towhee.Best Ways to Identify: Rusty crown patch, buffy throat, and dark necklace spots are key. Found in rocky desert areas, not coastal chaparral.

Canyon_Wren.Description: Rich rufous body with a bright white throat and breast. Dark brown barring on back and tail. Long, slightly curved bill.
Canyon_Wren.Behavior: Creeps along rocky cliff faces probing crevices for insects. Loud, descending cascade of whistled notes echoes in canyons.
Canyon_Wren.Habitat: Rocky canyons, cliff faces, and boulder fields from southern British Columbia to Mexico in the western United States.
Canyon_Wren.Similar Looking Birds: Rock Wren is paler and grayer with a buffy rump. Bewick's Wren lacks the white throat and rufous body. Both prefer rocks.
Canyon_Wren.Best Ways to Identify: White bib contrasting with rufous body is unmistakable. Its cascading, descending song is one of the most distinctive.

Cape_May_Warbler.Description: Breeding male has chestnut cheek patch, yellow neck, and heavily streaked breast. Female is duller with yellow-green tones.
Cape_May_Warbler.Behavior: Feeds heavily on spruce budworms during irruption years. Has a unique tubular tongue for sipping nectar in winter.
Cape_May_Warbler.Habitat: Breeds in boreal spruce-fir forests. Winters in Caribbean forests and gardens. Migrates through eastern North America.
Cape_May_Warbler.Similar Looking Birds: Yellow-rumped Warbler has a yellow rump patch. Palm Warbler has yellow undertail. Breeding male Cape May is unmistakable.
Cape_May_Warbler.Best Ways to Identify: Chestnut cheek patch and yellow neck stripe on breeding male are unique. Yellow rump and streaked breast visible year-round.

Cape_Verde_Shearwater.Description: Large shearwater, brown above, white below. Darker than Scopoli's/Cory's with more prominent dark bill. About 19 inches.
Cape_Verde_Shearwater.Behavior: Breeds on Cape Verde Islands; migrates into Atlantic. Rare vagrant to North American Atlantic coast.
Cape_Verde_Shearwater.Habitat: Atlantic Ocean. Rare vagrant to North American Atlantic coast. Breeds on Cape Verde Islands off Africa.
Cape_Verde_Shearwater.Similar Looking Birds: Scopoli's and Cory's Shearwaters very similar but slightly larger and paler.
Cape_Verde_Shearwater.Best Ways to Identify: Similar to Cory's/Scopoli's but smaller and darker with more prominent bill markings. Cape Verde endemic, rare Atlantic vagrant.

Carolina_Chickadee.Description: Tiny bird with black cap and bib, white cheeks, gray back, and pale buff flanks. Nearly identical to Black-capped Chickadee.
Carolina_Chickadee.Behavior: Active and acrobatic; clings upside down to search for insects. Forms mixed flocks in winter. Visits feeders for sunflower seeds.
Carolina_Chickadee.Habitat: Deciduous and mixed forests, parks, and suburbs of the southeastern United States from New Jersey to Texas.
Carolina_Chickadee.Similar Looking Birds: Black-capped Chickadee is nearly identical but has wider white wing edging and a slower, lower-pitched chick-a-dee call.
Carolina_Chickadee.Best Ways to Identify: In range, the only chickadee in the Southeast. Contact zone with Black-capped Chickadee in mid-Atlantic; call note is key.

Carolina_Parakeet.Description: EXTINCT. Green parrot with yellow and orange head. North America's only native parrot. About 12 inches.
Carolina_Parakeet.Behavior: Extinct since 1918; last wild birds collected 1904. Flocked in deciduous forest. Hunted for feathers and as crop pests.
Carolina_Parakeet.Habitat: Bottomland forest of eastern North America. Extinct since 1918; last captive bird died Cincinnati Zoo 1918.
Carolina_Parakeet.Similar Looking Birds: Green parakeets established as escapes. Carolina Parakeet was North America's only native parrot.
Carolina_Parakeet.Best Ways to Identify: Extinct since 1918. Green with orange-yellow head. Only known from museum specimens and historical accounts.

Carolina_Wren.Description: Rich rufous-brown above, warm buff below. Bold white supercilium eyebrow stripe. Short, slightly curved bill.
Carolina_Wren.Behavior: Loud singer year-round; sings teakettle-teakettle repeatedly. Forages low in dense cover. Often cocks tail upward while moving.
Carolina_Wren.Habitat: Dense shrubby undergrowth, brushy forest edges, and suburban thickets of the eastern United States and Central America.
Carolina_Wren.Similar Looking Birds: Bewick's Wren has a longer tail with white spots and is more gray-brown. House Wren is smaller and plainer with no eyebrow.
Carolina_Wren.Best Ways to Identify: Bold white eyebrow, rufous tones, and loud repetitive song are distinctive. Tail often cocked upright while perching.

Caspian_Tern.Description: Largest tern in the world. Heavy red-orange bill with dark tip. Black cap in breeding plumage (streaked in winter). Gray back and wings. White body. About 21 inches with 50-inch wingspan. Crow-sized.
Caspian_Tern.Behavior: Plunge-dives for fish. Raucous, harsh calls — sounds like a large crow or heron. Aggressive to other birds at colonies. Kleptoparasitizes other terns.
Caspian_Tern.Habitat: Large lakes, reservoirs, rivers, estuaries, and coasts. Breeds colonially on islands and sandbars. Present on all coasts and Great Lakes. Widespread migrant.
Caspian_Tern.Similar Looking Birds: Royal Tern is similar but smaller with orange (not red) bill and often crested. Elegant Tern is slimmer, more orange. Caspian is the largest and heaviest tern.
Caspian_Tern.Best Ways to Identify: Massive red bill, large size. Harsh, croaking calls unlike any other tern. Black cap streaked in winter. Widespread on large water bodies year-round.

Cassia_Crossbill.Description: Medium finch nearly identical to Red Crossbill. Male brick-red, female olive-green, crossed bill tips. About 6 inches.
Cassia_Crossbill.Behavior: Restricted to South Hills and Albion Mountains where lodgepole pine lacks squirrel seed predators. Non-migratory.
Cassia_Crossbill.Habitat: Lodgepole pine forests of Cassia County, Idaho. Resident, non-migratory, unlike other crossbills.
Cassia_Crossbill.Similar Looking Birds: Red Crossbill nearly identical. Best identified by call type, range, and non-migratory behavior.
Cassia_Crossbill.Best Ways to Identify: Cassia County Idaho lodgepole pine only. Nearly identical to Red Crossbill. Non-migratory resident.

Cassins_Auklet.Description: Small gray alcid. Uniform dark gray above and below, white spot above eye, white crescent below eye. Short thick bill. About 9 inches.
Cassins_Auklet.Behavior: Highly pelagic; rarely seen from shore. Dives for krill and small fish. Nests in burrows on Pacific coast islands.
Cassins_Auklet.Habitat: Offshore Pacific waters. Nests on islands from Alaska to Baja California. Rarely seen from shore except near colonies.
Cassins_Auklet.Similar Looking Birds: Other small auklets. Cassin's distinctive uniform gray color with white eye marks.
Cassins_Auklet.Best Ways to Identify: Uniform dark gray color with white spot above eye. Rarely seen from shore. Pelagic Pacific species.

Cassins_Finch.Description: Male has bright crimson crown, rosy-pink breast, and streaked brown back. Female is heavily streaked brown and white.
Cassins_Finch.Behavior: Forages in conifer treetops for seeds and buds. Forms flocks in winter. Male sings a rich, varied warbling song.
Cassins_Finch.Habitat: Mountain conifer forests of the western United States, from the Rockies to the Sierra Nevada. Winters at lower elevations.
Cassins_Finch.Similar Looking Birds: Purple Finch is similar but smaller with a less peaked crown. House Finch male has brown streaking on flanks.
Cassins_Finch.Best Ways to Identify: Peaked head profile and bright crimson (not rosy) crown on male are key. Larger and longer-billed than House Finch.

Cassins_Kingbird.Description: Gray head and breast, olive-green back, bright yellow belly. White chin contrasts with gray chest. No white tail edges.
Cassins_Kingbird.Behavior: Perches conspicuously to hawk flying insects. Aggressive defender of territory. Loud chi-bew call is distinctive.
Cassins_Kingbird.Habitat: Open woodlands, pinyon-juniper scrub, and riparian areas in the southwestern United States and Mexico.
Cassins_Kingbird.Similar Looking Birds: Western Kingbird has white outer tail feathers and a paler gray breast. Tropical Kingbird is very similar but larger.
Cassins_Kingbird.Best Ways to Identify: Dark gray breast contrasting with bright yellow belly and white chin. Dark tail without white edges distinguishes it.

Cassins_Sparrow.Description: Streaked brown and gray, pale below with faint streaking on breast. Flat crown, long rounded tail with white tips.
Cassins_Sparrow.Behavior: Males skylarks in flight song, rising and parachuting while singing. Secretive on ground; flushes reluctantly.
Cassins_Sparrow.Habitat: Arid grasslands with scattered shrubs in the southern Great Plains and Chihuahuan Desert of the United States and Mexico.
Cassins_Sparrow.Similar Looking Birds: Botteri's Sparrow is very similar but has plain brown tail. Grasshopper Sparrow is smaller with flat head and stubby tail.
Cassins_Sparrow.Best Ways to Identify: Skylark display flight and sweet trilled song are distinctive. White tips on rounded tail visible in flight.

Cassins_Vireo.Description: Gray head, white spectacles, olive-green back, white wingbars, and yellow-washed flanks. White throat and underparts.
Cassins_Vireo.Behavior: Forages slowly through foliage for insects and berries. Sings a slow, burry series of phrases with pauses between.
Cassins_Vireo.Habitat: Mixed and coniferous forests of the Pacific Coast mountains and western slopes from British Columbia to Baja California.
Cassins_Vireo.Similar Looking Birds: Blue-headed Vireo is nearly identical but has a blue-gray head. Plumbeous Vireo is grayer with less olive tones on back.
Cassins_Vireo.Best Ways to Identify: Bold white spectacles and wingbars, olive-green back, and yellow flanks. Found in western mountains, not east.

Cattle_Tyrant.Description: Medium flycatcher, brown above, bright yellow below with rusty crown patch. Walks on ground near cattle. About 8 inches.
Cattle_Tyrant.Behavior: Forages on ground near cattle for insects disturbed by hooves. Very rare vagrant to North America from South America.
Cattle_Tyrant.Habitat: Open grasslands and ranchland near livestock in South America. Extremely rare vagrant to North America.
Cattle_Tyrant.Similar Looking Birds: Great Kiskadee larger with black-and-white head. Western Kingbird lacks brown back and ground foraging.
Cattle_Tyrant.Best Ways to Identify: Yellow below, brown above, ground forager near cattle. Extremely rare South American vagrant.

Cave_Swallow.Description: Square tail, dark blue back, rusty-orange rump, pale orange throat and forehead. Buffy underparts with chestnut cheek.
Cave_Swallow.Behavior: Colonial nester in caves, culverts, and bridges. Hawking insects in flight over open terrain. Fast, agile flier.
Cave_Swallow.Habitat: Open country near cliffs, caves, and bridges in Texas, New Mexico, Florida, and Caribbean. Expanding range northward.
Cave_Swallow.Similar Looking Birds: Cliff Swallow has a dark throat and white forehead. Barn Swallow has deeply forked tail and blue-black breast band.
Cave_Swallow.Best Ways to Identify: Pale orange forehead and throat (not dark like Cliff Swallow) combined with rusty rump and square tail are key.

Cedar_Waxwing.Description: Sleek brown-gray bird with silky plumage, black mask, yellow tail tip, and waxy red wing tips. Crested head.
Cedar_Waxwing.Behavior: Highly social; travels in flocks. Feeds heavily on berries. Passes berries along a perched flock. High-pitched trilled call.
Cedar_Waxwing.Habitat: Woodland edges, orchards, and berry-producing shrubs across North America. Nomadic; follows fruit crops.
Cedar_Waxwing.Similar Looking Birds: Bohemian Waxwing is grayer with rusty undertail and yellow and white wing markings. Larger and only in the north.
Cedar_Waxwing.Best Ways to Identify: Sleek crested silhouette, black mask, yellow tail tip, and waxy red wing spots make this species unmistakable.

Cerulean_Warbler.Description: Male is sky blue above with white underparts and black streaks. Female is blue-green above with yellowish eyebrow.
Cerulean_Warbler.Behavior: Forages high in forest canopy, hard to see. Male sings a buzzy ascending trill with a final upward slur.
Cerulean_Warbler.Habitat: Mature deciduous forests with tall trees, especially in the Appalachians and Midwest. Winters in Andean cloud forests.
Cerulean_Warbler.Similar Looking Birds: Black-throated Blue Warbler male has black throat and face. Blackburnian Warbler has orange throat. Female resembles female Black-throated Blue but bluer.
Cerulean_Warbler.Best Ways to Identify: Male's sky-blue back and narrow black breast band are unique. Look and listen high in forest canopy in breeding season.

Chatham_Albatross.Description: Medium mollymawk albatross. White head with gray cheek, dark back, distinctive yellow bill with dark culmen. About 35 inches.
Chatham_Albatross.Behavior: Breeds only on Pyramid Rock, Chatham Islands. Very rare vagrant to North American Pacific coast.
Chatham_Albatross.Habitat: Southern Pacific Ocean, Chatham Islands. Very rare vagrant to North American Pacific coast.
Chatham_Albatross.Similar Looking Birds: Other mollymawk albatrosses similar. Chatham has distinctive dark-tipped yellow bill.
Chatham_Albatross.Best Ways to Identify: Bright yellow bill with dark tip. Gray wash on head sides. Very rare Pacific vagrant. Critically endangered species.

Chestnut-backed_Chickadee.Description: Black cap and bib, white cheeks, rich chestnut back and sides. Small and compact with gray wings and tail.
Chestnut-backed_Chickadee.Behavior: Active and acrobatic in conifers. Joins mixed flocks in winter. Responds to pishing. High-pitched chick-a-dee call.
Chestnut-backed_Chickadee.Habitat: Moist conifer and mixed forests of the Pacific Coast from Alaska to central California. Common in coastal redwoods.
Chestnut-backed_Chickadee.Similar Looking Birds: Black-capped Chickadee lacks chestnut on back and sides. Mountain Chickadee has white eyebrow. Both lack chestnut back.
Chestnut-backed_Chickadee.Best Ways to Identify: Unmistakable rich chestnut back and flanks set against black cap and white cheeks. Only chickadee with chestnut back.

Chestnut-bellied_Sandgrouse.Description: Pigeon-sized bird with cryptic sandy-brown plumage, chestnut belly, long pointed tail. Male has thin black breast band. About 12 inches.
Chestnut-bellied_Sandgrouse.Behavior: Flies long distances to water at dawn. Male soaks breast feathers to carry water to chicks. Introduced to Hawaii from Africa and Asia.
Chestnut-bellied_Sandgrouse.Habitat: Arid grasslands and scrubland. Introduced to Hawaii, found on dry leeward slopes of several islands. Native to African and Asian drylands.
Chestnut-bellied_Sandgrouse.Similar Looking Birds: No similar sandgrouse in Hawaii. Dove-like in shape but flight pattern very different.
Chestnut-bellied_Sandgrouse.Best Ways to Identify: Sandy-brown cryptic plumage with chestnut belly. Long pointed tail. Fast direct flight. Found in Hawaii on dry grassy slopes.

Chestnut-collared_Longspur.Description: Breeding male has black and white face, chestnut nape, black belly. Female is streaked brown. White tail with black triangle.
Chestnut-collared_Longspur.Behavior: Forages on ground in flocks. Male displays in hovering song flight. Runs rather than hops across grassland.
Chestnut-collared_Longspur.Habitat: Short-grass prairies and mixed-grass plains of the Great Plains. Winters in southwestern grasslands and Mexico.
Chestnut-collared_Longspur.Similar Looking Birds: McCown's Longspur has more white in tail. Lapland Longspur female is similar but has heavier streaking.
Chestnut-collared_Longspur.Best Ways to Identify: Breeding male's black belly and chestnut collar unmistakable. White tail with black triangle visible in all plumages in flight.

Chestnut-fronted_Macaw.Description: Medium macaw, green with chestnut forehead and chin, red under wings and tail. About 18 inches.
Chestnut-fronted_Macaw.Behavior: Gregarious in flocks. Loud calls. Small feral population in Florida.
Chestnut-fronted_Macaw.Habitat: Tropical forest and savanna. Small feral population in southern Florida. Native to South America.
Chestnut-fronted_Macaw.Similar Looking Birds: Severe Macaw is same species. Military Macaw larger. Smaller macaw with chestnut forehead.
Chestnut-fronted_Macaw.Best Ways to Identify: Green with chestnut forehead and red under wings. Medium-sized macaw. Florida feral population.

Chestnut-sided_Warbler.Description: Breeding male has yellow crown, black eye stripe, white face, and chestnut sides. Fall birds are lime-green with white eye ring.
Chestnut-sided_Warbler.Behavior: Forages at mid-level in shrubby forest edges. Cocks tail upward. Sings a distinctive please-please-pleased to MEET you.
Chestnut-sided_Warbler.Habitat: Shrubby second-growth forests and woodland edges in the eastern United States and southern Canada.
Chestnut-sided_Warbler.Similar Looking Birds: Bay-breasted Warbler has chestnut on breast not just sides. Fall birds unique with lime-green back and white eye ring.
Chestnut-sided_Warbler.Best Ways to Identify: Chestnut sides and yellow crown in breeding plumage unique. Fall birds' lime-green back and clean white eye ring are key.

Chestnut_Munia.Description: Small finch, black head, deep chestnut body, whitish lower belly. Heavy gray bill. About 4.5 inches.
Chestnut_Munia.Behavior: Highly gregarious in large flocks. Forages for grass seeds. Introduced to Hawaii; very common on several islands.
Chestnut_Munia.Habitat: Grasslands, open areas, and gardens. Common introduced species in Hawaii.
Chestnut_Munia.Similar Looking Birds: Tricolored Munia has black belly, white sides. Scaly-breasted Munia has pale scaly breast.
Chestnut_Munia.Best Ways to Identify: Black head with uniform deep chestnut body. Heavy bill. Gregarious flocks in Hawaiian grasslands.

Chihuahuan_Meadowlark.Description: Medium bird, streaked brown above, bright yellow below with black V on breast. About 9 inches.
Chihuahuan_Meadowlark.Behavior: Sings from fence posts and shrubs in grassland. Recently split from Eastern Meadowlark. Song different from relatives.
Chihuahuan_Meadowlark.Habitat: Chihuahuan Desert grasslands of southwestern Texas and New Mexico, and adjacent Mexico.
Chihuahuan_Meadowlark.Similar Looking Birds: Eastern Meadowlark very similar. Western Meadowlark has different song pattern. Range important for identification.
Chihuahuan_Meadowlark.Best Ways to Identify: Nearly identical to Eastern Meadowlark. Chihuahuan Desert grassland range. Song and genetic differences key.

Chihuahuan_Raven.Description: Medium-large raven, smaller than Common Raven but larger than American Crow. All black with white feather bases (usually hidden). Wedge-shaped tail. About 19.5 inches. Rounded head, strong bill.
Chihuahuan_Raven.Behavior: Highly omnivorous and opportunistic. Forms large winter flocks, sometimes thousands. Follows livestock and agricultural operations for food scraps.
Chihuahuan_Raven.Habitat: Arid grasslands, deserts, and scrublands of the Chihuahuan desert region — Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, and northern Mexico. Avoids forests and mountains.
Chihuahuan_Raven.Similar Looking Birds: Common Raven is larger with deeper voice and more prominent bill. American Crow is smaller with fan-shaped tail. Fish Crow is smaller and coastal.
Chihuahuan_Raven.Best Ways to Identify: Smaller than Common Raven, larger than crow. Chihuahuan desert grasslands. Forms large winter flocks. White feather bases sometimes visible on neck.

Chimney_Swift.Description: All dark sooty-brown, tiny feet, very short tail. Wings long and swept back. Cigar-shaped body in flight.
Chimney_Swift.Behavior: Almost never lands except to nest and roost. Feeds entirely on the wing. Loud chattering calls in flight.
Chimney_Swift.Habitat: Urban and suburban areas with chimneys and hollow trees across the eastern United States. Winters in the Amazon basin.
Chimney_Swift.Similar Looking Birds: Vaux's Swift is smaller and found in the West. Swallows have longer tails and perch on wires. Purple Martin is bigger.
Chimney_Swift.Best Ways to Identify: Twinkling flight on stiff bowed wings with rapid shallow beats. Chittering calls and cigar body shape are distinctive.

Chinese_Egret.Description: Medium white egret, yellow bill with dark tip, blue-gray facial skin in breeding, yellow feet. About 26 inches.
Chinese_Egret.Behavior: Forages in coastal wetlands and tidal flats. Endangered in Asia. Very rare vagrant to western Alaska.
Chinese_Egret.Habitat: Coastal East Asia. Very rare vagrant to western Alaska, particularly Aleutian Islands. Endangered Asian species.
Chinese_Egret.Similar Looking Birds: Snowy Egret has black bill and yellow feet. Chinese Egret has yellow bill with dark tip.
Chinese_Egret.Best Ways to Identify: Yellow bill with dark tip, blue-gray facial skin in breeding. Yellow feet. Endangered Asian vagrant to western Alaska.

Chinese_Hwamei.Description: Medium brown bird with streaked pattern, white eye ring with streak extending back (spectacles). About 9 inches.
Chinese_Hwamei.Behavior: Highly vocal with beautiful varied song. Skulks in dense vegetation. Introduced to Hawaii, especially Oahu.
Chinese_Hwamei.Habitat: Dense forest undergrowth and scrub. Introduced to Hawaiian Islands, particularly common on Oahu and Kauai.
Chinese_Hwamei.Similar Looking Birds: No similar bird in Hawaii. White spectacle markings make it distinctive.
Chinese_Hwamei.Best Ways to Identify: White spectacle stripe from eye distinctive. Brown streaked plumage. Loud musical song. Hawaiian forest.

Chinese_Pond-Heron.Description: Small compact heron, brown and white streaked body, brilliant white wings in flight, chestnut and black breeding plumage. About 18 inches.
Chinese_Pond-Heron.Behavior: Stands motionless then strikes for fish. Very rare vagrant to Alaska from East Asia. Distinctive white wings in flight.
Chinese_Pond-Heron.Habitat: Ponds and rice paddies of East Asia. Very rare vagrant to western Alaska from East Asia.
Chinese_Pond-Heron.Similar Looking Birds: Other small herons lack the brilliant white wings. Chinese Pond-Heron's white wings unique.
Chinese_Pond-Heron.Best Ways to Identify: Brilliant white wings contrasting with brown body in flight. Compact pond heron. Rare Alaska vagrant from Asia.

Chinese_Sparrowhawk.Description: Small accipiter. Male blue-gray above, pale below with unmarked white underparts. Red eyes. About 11 inches.
Chinese_Sparrowhawk.Behavior: Migratory raptor of East Asia. Rare vagrant to Alaska from East Asia.
Chinese_Sparrowhawk.Habitat: Forest and woodland of East and Southeast Asia. Very rare vagrant to western Alaska.
Chinese_Sparrowhawk.Similar Looking Birds: Sharp-shinned Hawk similar size. Chinese Sparrowhawk has all-white unmarked underparts.
Chinese_Sparrowhawk.Best Ways to Identify: Pale unmarked underparts, blue-gray above. Red iris. Small accipiter. Rare vagrant to western Alaska from Asia.

Chipping_Sparrow.Description: Rufous cap, white eyebrow, black eye line, and clean gray breast. Small and slim with notched tail.
Chipping_Sparrow.Behavior: Forages on the ground near trees. Sings a long dry trill. Common in lawns and parks. Forms flocks in winter.
Chipping_Sparrow.Habitat: Open woodlands, parks, gardens, and forest edges across North America. One of the most widespread sparrows.
Chipping_Sparrow.Similar Looking Birds: American Tree Sparrow has rufous cap but also a central breast spot. Clay-colored Sparrow has brown cheek patch.
Chipping_Sparrow.Best Ways to Identify: Clean gray breast, bright rufous cap, and white eyebrow bordered by black are distinctive. Very common in suburbs.

Christmas_Shearwater.Description: Small all-dark brown shearwater with rounded wings and relatively short tail. Dark bill and feet. About 14 inches.
Christmas_Shearwater.Behavior: Breeds on Hawaiian Northwestern Islands. Forages in central Pacific; occasional in Hawaiian waters.
Christmas_Shearwater.Habitat: Central North Pacific Ocean. Breeds on Hawaiian Northwestern Islands including Midway and Laysan.
Christmas_Shearwater.Similar Looking Birds: Other all-dark shearwaters larger. Christmas Shearwater small, rounded wings.
Christmas_Shearwater.Best Ways to Identify: Small all-dark shearwater with rounded wings. Central Pacific; Hawaiian Northwestern Islands breeder.

Chuck-wills-widow.Description: Large nightjar with cryptic brown mottled plumage. Buffy collar, large flat head, and very wide gape.
Chuck-wills-widow.Behavior: Strictly nocturnal. Calls its name chuck-will's-widow loudly at night. Sits on ground or low branches in daytime.
Chuck-wills-widow.Habitat: Open pine and mixed forests, woodland edges in the southeastern United States. Winters in the Caribbean and Central America.
Chuck-wills-widow.Similar Looking Birds: Whip-poor-will is smaller with less buff coloring and a white tail tip on males. Eastern Whip-poor-will has similar call.
Chuck-wills-widow.Best Ways to Identify: Very loud repeated chuck-will's-widow call at dusk and night. Larger than Whip-poor-will with more buffy-brown tones.

Chukar.Description: Medium partridge. Gray-brown body with bold black and white barred flanks, black necklace on white face and throat, red bill and legs. About 14 inches.
Chukar.Behavior: Runs quickly over rocky terrain. Calls loudly "chuk-chuk-chukar." Gregarious; found in coveys. Widely introduced for upland game hunting.
Chukar.Habitat: Rocky, steep, arid hillsides with sparse vegetation. Introduced across western US including Nevada, Idaho, Oregon, and other western states.
Chukar.Similar Looking Birds: Himalayan Snowcock much larger. Hungarian Partridge lacks bold flank barring.
Chukar.Best Ways to Identify: Bold black-and-white flank bars, black necklace on white face, red bill and legs. Rocky arid habitat in western US.

Cinnamon_Hummingbird.Description: Medium hummingbird. Entirely cinnamon-rufous underparts, iridescent green upperparts, red bill with dark tip. Vivid cinnamon coloring. About 4.5 inches.
Cinnamon_Hummingbird.Behavior: Feeds on nectar from various flowers. Rare vagrant to southern Arizona from Mexico and Central America. Active and conspicuous.
Cinnamon_Hummingbird.Habitat: Dry coastal scrub, woodland, and forest edges of Mexico and Central America. Very rare vagrant to southern Arizona.
Cinnamon_Hummingbird.Similar Looking Birds: Buff-bellied Hummingbird has similar reddish tones but greener breast. Cinnamon brighter overall.
Cinnamon_Hummingbird.Best Ways to Identify: Entirely vivid cinnamon underparts with metallic green back unique among hummingbirds. Red bill. Very rare vagrant in Arizona.

Cinnamon_Teal.Description: Male is rich cinnamon-red with blue wing patches and red eye. Female is mottled brown. Spatula-shaped bill.
Cinnamon_Teal.Behavior: Feeds by dabbling and tipping in shallow wetlands. Often in pairs or small groups. Somewhat secretive.
Cinnamon_Teal.Habitat: Shallow marshes, ponds, and wetlands in the western United States. Winters in Mexico and Central America.
Cinnamon_Teal.Similar Looking Birds: Blue-winged Teal female is almost identical to female Cinnamon. Ruddy Duck male is also cinnamon but has stiff upright tail.
Cinnamon_Teal.Best Ways to Identify: Male's deep cinnamon-red head and body with blue wing patch are unmistakable. Female best told by range and bill shape.

Citrine_Wagtail.Description: Small wagtail, gray back, bright yellow head and underparts, white wing bars. About 6.5 inches.
Citrine_Wagtail.Behavior: Wagtail behavior: bobs tail constantly, runs on ground. Very rare vagrant to western Alaska from Asia.
Citrine_Wagtail.Habitat: Wet meadows and marshes in Asia and Siberia. Very rare vagrant to western Alaska.
Citrine_Wagtail.Similar Looking Birds: Eastern Yellow Wagtail less yellow on head. White Wagtail has black and white pattern.
Citrine_Wagtail.Best Ways to Identify: Bright yellow head contrasting with gray back. Rare Alaska vagrant from Asia. Constant tail wagging.

Clapper_Rail.Description: Large, secretive rail with gray-brown streaked upperparts, rusty-orange breast, and gray cheeks. Long, slightly decurved bill. Barred flanks. About 14.5 inches. Laterally compressed body for moving through marsh grass.
Clapper_Rail.Behavior: Wades and runs through dense saltmarsh grasses. Rarely flies. Gives loud, cackling clapper call, especially at dawn and dusk. Difficult to observe.
Clapper_Rail.Habitat: Atlantic and Gulf coast saltmarshes from New England to Texas. Locally in California marshes. Threatened by habitat loss and sea level rise.
Clapper_Rail.Similar Looking Birds: King Rail inhabits freshwater and has brighter rufous breast and barred flanks. Virginia Rail is smaller with reddish bill. California Clapper Rail is a subspecies.
Clapper_Rail.Best Ways to Identify: Large rail in saltmarsh. Grating, accelerating cackle call is diagnostic. Gray cheeks separate from King Rail. Saltwater marsh habitat. Rarely seen well.

Clarks_Grebe.Description: Black and white with long thin neck, orange-yellow bill, and red eye. White face with black cap above the eye.
Clarks_Grebe.Behavior: Dives for fish. Famous for rushing courtship display with mate. Forms large flocks on open water in winter.
Clarks_Grebe.Habitat: Large western lakes and reservoirs for nesting; coastal bays and open ocean in winter along the Pacific Coast.
Clarks_Grebe.Similar Looking Birds: Western Grebe is nearly identical but has a black face that extends below the eye and a duller olive-yellow bill.
Clarks_Grebe.Best Ways to Identify: White face extends above eye and bright orange-yellow bill distinguish Clark's from Western Grebe. Best told at close range.

Clarks_Nutcracker.Description: Gray body with black wings, white wing patches, and black tail with white outer feathers. Long sharp bill.
Clarks_Nutcracker.Behavior: Caches thousands of pine seeds per year. Remarkable spatial memory. Loud harsh kraaa call in mountain forests.
Clarks_Nutcracker.Habitat: High-elevation conifer forests of the Rocky Mountains and Pacific ranges, particularly near whitebark and limber pines.
Clarks_Nutcracker.Similar Looking Birds: Gray Jay is softer gray without black wings. Nuthatches are much smaller. Unmistakable in its mountain habitat.
Clarks_Nutcracker.Best Ways to Identify: Bold black-and-white wing pattern on gray body, with long bill and white outer tail feathers in flight.

Clay-colored_Sparrow.Description: Striped crown, brown cheek patch outlined in white, whitish median crown stripe, and pale unstreaked breast.
Clay-colored_Sparrow.Behavior: Forages in low shrubs and on ground. Sings a flat mechanical buzz. Males perch conspicuously to sing.
Clay-colored_Sparrow.Habitat: Brushy fields, prairie edges, and shrubby areas of the Great Plains and north-central Canada. Winters in Mexico.
Clay-colored_Sparrow.Similar Looking Birds: Chipping Sparrow has rufous cap and lacks brown cheek patch. Brewer's Sparrow is grayer and lacks the facial pattern.
Clay-colored_Sparrow.Best Ways to Identify: Brown cheek patch with white border, striped crown, and buzzy insect-like song are key identification features.

Clay-colored_Thrush.Description: Medium thrush, plain warm brown throughout above and below. Yellow-green bill, dull orange-yellow legs. About 9.5 inches.
Clay-colored_Thrush.Behavior: Forages on ground for fruit and invertebrates. Bold and conspicuous in gardens and parks. Beautiful melodious song.
Clay-colored_Thrush.Habitat: Forest edges, gardens, parks, and second growth from Mexico through Central America. Established in southern Texas.
Clay-colored_Thrush.Similar Looking Birds: American Robin much brighter with red-orange breast. White-throated Thrush has white throat. Veery has spotted breast.
Clay-colored_Thrush.Best Ways to Identify: Plain dull brown throughout with yellow-green bill. South Texas resident. No bold markings. Very plain thrush.

Cliff_Swallow.Description: Square tail, blue-black back, orange-buff rump, dark throat, and white forehead patch. Pale underparts.
Cliff_Swallow.Behavior: Highly colonial nester on cliff faces and bridges. Builds gourd-shaped mud nests. Gregarious in large flocks.
Cliff_Swallow.Habitat: Open country near cliffs, bridges, and buildings across North America. Winters in South America.
Cliff_Swallow.Similar Looking Birds: Cave Swallow has pale orange throat instead of dark. Barn Swallow has forked tail and chestnut throat.
Cliff_Swallow.Best Ways to Identify: Bright rusty-orange rump, square tail, and white forehead on dark head identify this colonial nesting swallow.

Cocos_Booby.Description: Medium booby. Dark brown above and on head and neck, white belly, pale yellowish bill. About 28 inches.
Cocos_Booby.Behavior: Pacific subspecies/species of Brown Booby. Plunge-dives for fish. Rare vagrant to Pacific coast of North America.
Cocos_Booby.Habitat: Eastern tropical Pacific, Cocos Island and adjacent waters. Rare vagrant to Pacific coast.
Cocos_Booby.Similar Looking Birds: Brown Booby nearly identical. Cocos Booby paler overall with lighter head.
Cocos_Booby.Best Ways to Identify: Brown and white booby, similar to Brown Booby. Paler head than typical Brown Booby. Eastern Pacific species.

Colima_Warbler.Description: Medium warbler, gray above, yellow undertail coverts, rusty crown patch, plain grayish- white below. About 5 inches.
Colima_Warbler.Behavior: Forages in oak and pinyon-juniper scrub. Breeds only in Chisos Mountains of Big Bend National Park.
Colima_Warbler.Habitat: Oak woodland in the Chisos Mountains of Big Bend National Park, Texas. Breeds nowhere else in United States.
Colima_Warbler.Similar Looking Birds: Virginia's Warbler similar but white not yellow undertail. Nashville Warbler has yellow below.
Colima_Warbler.Best Ways to Identify: Yellow undertail coverts, rusty crown, gray body. Chisos Mountains only in U.S. Big Bend National Park specialist.

Collared_Forest-Falcon.Description: Large forest falcon, black above with white collar and underparts. Long tail, small rounded wings. About 20 inches.
Collared_Forest-Falcon.Behavior: Pursues prey through dense forest. Heard more often than seen. Rare vagrant from Mexico to southern Texas.
Collared_Forest-Falcon.Habitat: Dense tropical forest of Mexico and Central America. Rare vagrant to southern Texas.
Collared_Forest-Falcon.Similar Looking Birds: Other falcons in open habitat. Collared Forest-Falcon a dense forest specialist.
Collared_Forest-Falcon.Best Ways to Identify: Black above with white collar and underparts. Forest interior, often heard not seen. Very rare vagrant from Mexico.

Collared_Plover.Description: Small plover. Brown above with rufous tones, white underparts with black breast band, white forehead, rufous crown. About 6 inches.
Collared_Plover.Behavior: Forages on bare ground and river margins for invertebrates. Rare vagrant to southern US and Caribbean from Central and South America.
Collared_Plover.Habitat: Sandy riverbanks, gravel bars, and beaches in Central and South America. Rare vagrant to southern US.
Collared_Plover.Similar Looking Birds: Semipalmated and other small plovers. Rufous tones and facial pattern distinctive.
Collared_Plover.Best Ways to Identify: Rufous forecrown and neck sides with black breast band. Small size. Rare vagrant from Central America.

Common_Black_Hawk.Description: Large, stocky hawk, nearly all black with single broad white tail band. Short, broad wings. Yellow-orange cere and legs. About 21 inches with wide wingspan. Immatures are brown with streaked underparts.
Common_Black_Hawk.Behavior: Wades into streams and pools to catch fish, crayfish, and frogs. Perches low near water. Slow-flying. Nest in large riparian trees near permanent water.
Common_Black_Hawk.Habitat: Riparian corridors with large cottonwoods and sycamores along permanent streams in Arizona, New Mexico, Utah, and Texas. Very limited U.S. range.
Common_Black_Hawk.Similar Looking Birds: Zone-tailed Hawk mimics Turkey Vulture in flight but has banded tail. Black-and-white Hawk-Eagle is tropical. Harris's Hawk has chestnut shoulders.
Common_Black_Hawk.Best Ways to Identify: Large, all-black hawk near streams with single broad white tail band. Yellow legs. Southwest riparian canyons. Wading behavior in water is distinctive.

Common_Chaffinch.Description: Medium finch. Male has blue-gray head, pinkish breast, chestnut back, white wing bars. About 6 inches.
Common_Chaffinch.Behavior: Forages on ground for seeds. Common garden bird in Europe. Very rare vagrant to northeastern North America.
Common_Chaffinch.Habitat: Woodland, gardens, and farmland across Europe. Very rare vagrant to northeastern North America.
Common_Chaffinch.Similar Looking Birds: Brambling has white rump and orange shoulder. No similar brightly patterned finch in North America range.
Common_Chaffinch.Best Ways to Identify: Male blue-gray head with pinkish breast and chestnut back. White wing bars. Very rare European vagrant.

Common_Chiffchaff.Description: Small leaf warbler, olive-brown above, off-white below with yellow-buff tones. Dark legs. About 4.5 inches.
Common_Chiffchaff.Behavior: Active insect forager. Named for repetitive chiff-chaff song. Rare vagrant to eastern and western North America.
Common_Chiffchaff.Habitat: Woodland, scrub, and gardens across Europe and Asia. Rare vagrant to both coasts of North America.
Common_Chiffchaff.Similar Looking Birds: Willow Warbler has flesh-colored legs, more yellow below. Arctic Warbler larger with wing bar.
Common_Chiffchaff.Best Ways to Identify: Black legs distinctive versus Willow Warbler. Olive-brown above, dirty white below. Repetitive chiff-chaff song.

Common_Crane.Description: Very large gray crane. Gray body, black and white head with red crown patch, long neck and legs. About 45 inches with 7-foot wingspan.
Common_Crane.Behavior: Migratory; travels in large V-shaped flocks with loud bugling calls. Rare vagrant to North America from Eurasia; sometimes mixes with Sandhill Cranes.
Common_Crane.Habitat: Breeds in Eurasian wetlands and boreal forests. Winters on European farmland. Rare vagrant to North America, often with Sandhill Cranes.
Common_Crane.Similar Looking Birds: Sandhill Crane very similar but browner. Common Crane has black and white head pattern.
Common_Crane.Best Ways to Identify: All-gray body with distinctive black and white head pattern. Often mixes with Sandhill Crane flocks in migration.

Common_Cuckoo.Description: Medium slender bird. Male gray above, barred black and white below, yellow eye ring. Female can be reddish-brown. About 13 inches.
Common_Cuckoo.Behavior: Brood parasite; lays eggs in other birds' nests. Famous "cuckoo" call. Migrates to Africa for winter. Rare vagrant to western North America.
Common_Cuckoo.Habitat: Breeds in open woodland, moorland, and farmland across Eurasia. Winters in Africa. Rare vagrant to Alaska and Atlantic coast.
Common_Cuckoo.Similar Looking Birds: Accipiter hawks similar in silhouette. Oriental Cuckoo nearly identical; separated by call.
Common_Cuckoo.Best Ways to Identify: Hawk-like silhouette with drooping wingtips and long tail. Barred underparts. Distinctive "cuck-oo" call. Rare vagrant in North America.

Common_Eider.Description: Large, heavy sea duck. Males have white back and breast, black belly and cap, green nape, and distinctive sloping forehead with orange bill shield. Females brown with heavy barring. About 24 inches. Largest North American duck.
Common_Eider.Behavior: Dives for mussels and other mollusks in coastal waters. Highly social in large flocks. Females famous for soft down feathers used in duvets. Distinctive growling display calls.
Common_Eider.Habitat: Arctic and sub-Arctic coastal waters. Winters along rocky coastlines south to mid-Atlantic states on East Coast. Common off New England and Maritime coasts.
Common_Eider.Similar Looking Birds: King Eider male has round orange bill knob. Spectacled Eider has pale eye patch. Female eiders are similar brown ducks; bill shape and size help.
Common_Eider.Best Ways to Identify: Massive size and sloping forehead profile unique. Male's white-and-black pattern with green nape. Rocky coastal habitats. Large flocks offshore in winter.

Common_Gallinule.Description: Medium waterbird with slate-gray plumage, brown back, white flank stripe, and distinctive red frontal shield and bill with yellow tip. Green legs with red garter ring. About 14 inches. Formerly called Common Moorhen.
Common_Gallinule.Behavior: Swims on open water and walks on lily pads, pumping head with each step. Clucks and squawks from marshes. Builds floating nests in vegetation. Omnivore.
Common_Gallinule.Habitat: Freshwater marshes, ponds, lakes with emergent vegetation across much of the United States. Year-round in South; migratory in North. Common in wetlands.
Common_Gallinule.Similar Looking Birds: American Coot has white bill and no red shield. Purple Gallinule has purple plumage and yellow legs. Common Gallinule's red bill and shield are distinctive.
Common_Gallinule.Best Ways to Identify: Red frontal shield and bill with yellow tip. White flank stripe. Gray-brown plumage. Head-bobbing swimming behavior. Common in freshwater marshes.

Common_Goldeneye.Description: Male has iridescent green head, round white cheek spot, and yellow eye. Female has brown head and gray body.
Common_Goldeneye.Behavior: Dives for aquatic invertebrates. Wings produce loud whistling in flight. Nests in tree cavities near boreal lakes.
Common_Goldeneye.Habitat: Boreal lakes and forest ponds for breeding. Winters on coastal bays, lakes, and rivers across North America.
