Hawaii_Akepa.Best Ways to Identify: Male bright orange-red, crossed bill tips. Big Island ohia forest above 4,000 feet. Endangered endemic.

Hawaii_Amakihi.Description: Small Hawaiian honeycreeper, olive-green above, yellow-green below, slightly curved bill. About 4.5 inches.
Hawaii_Amakihi.Behavior: Active forager for nectar and insects. More disease-resistant than many Hawaiian birds. Most common surviving honeycreeper on Big Island.
Hawaii_Amakihi.Habitat: Native forests of the Big Island from near sea level to treeline. More tolerant of lower elevations than most species.
Hawaii_Amakihi.Similar Looking Birds: Oahu and Kauai Amakihi island-specific. Apapane red. Anianiau smaller and brighter yellow.
Hawaii_Amakihi.Best Ways to Identify: Olive-green with slightly curved bill on Big Island. One of most common native birds in Hawaii forests.

Hawaii_Creeper.Description: Small Hawaiian honeycreeper, olive-green above, pale below with short straight bill. Creeps along bark. About 4.5 inches.
Hawaii_Creeper.Behavior: Creeps along branches and bark searching for insects. Critically endangered; found in scattered forest remnants.
Hawaii_Creeper.Habitat: Native ohia and koa forests of the Big Island above 5,000 feet.
Hawaii_Creeper.Similar Looking Birds: Maui Alauahio similar behavior on Maui. Oahu Alauahio extinct. Bark-creeping behavior distinctive.
Hawaii_Creeper.Best Ways to Identify: Creeping bark behavior on Big Island. Small olive-green bird. Short straight bill. Critically endangered endemic.

Hawaii_Elepaio.Description: Small monarch flycatcher endemic to Big Island. Variable plumage with white, brown, and dark morphs. About 5 inches.
Hawaii_Elepaio.Behavior: Highly active and inquisitive, often follows hikers. Cocks tail frequently. Ancient Hawaiians considered it sacred.
Hawaii_Elepaio.Habitat: Native forests from sea level to treeline on Hawaii. Found in ohia, koa, and mixed forest habitats.
Hawaii_Elepaio.Similar Looking Birds: Other Elepaio species on Kauai and Oahu but island-specific. Variable plumage makes identification complex.
Hawaii_Elepaio.Best Ways to Identify: Upward-cocked tail on Big Island of Hawaii. Variable plumage. Curious and bold behavior near humans.

Hawaii_Mamo.Description: Large Hawaiian honeycreeper, mostly black with yellow rump, undertail, and thighs. Very long curved bill. About 8 inches.
Hawaii_Mamo.Behavior: Fed on nectar of lobelias. Hunted to extinction for its yellow feathers used in royal Hawaiian cloaks. Extinct ~1898.
Hawaii_Mamo.Habitat: Native forests of the Big Island of Hawaii. Extinct due to feather trade and habitat destruction.
Hawaii_Mamo.Similar Looking Birds: Black Mamo all black. Iiwi red. No other black-and-yellow nectar feeder survives in Hawaii.
Hawaii_Mamo.Best Ways to Identify: Extinct. Black with yellow rump and thighs. Very long curved bill. Big Island. No longer exists.

Hawaii_Oo.Description: Large Hawaiian honeyeater, glossy black with yellow thigh and wing patches. Long curved bill. About 12 inches.
Hawaii_Oo.Behavior: Foraged for nectar. Prized yellow feathers used in Hawaiian royal cloaks. Driven extinct by feather trade and habitat loss.
Hawaii_Oo.Habitat: Native forests of the Big Island of Hawaii. Extinct since approximately 1934.
Hawaii_Oo.Similar Looking Birds: Other Oo species on different islands. All Hawaiian Oo now extinct.
Hawaii_Oo.Best Ways to Identify: Extinct species from Big Island. Largest Oo species. Black with yellow patches. No longer exists.

Hawaiian_Coot.Description: Medium waterbird. Sooty black body with white bill and large white frontal shield. Some individuals have red frontal shield knob. About 15 inches.
Hawaiian_Coot.Behavior: Swims and dives for aquatic plants. Found year-round on Hawaiian ponds and wetlands. Endemic to Hawaiian Islands.
Hawaiian_Coot.Habitat: Freshwater ponds, wetlands, and coastal lagoons throughout Hawaiian Islands. Endemic; found nowhere else in the world.
Hawaiian_Coot.Similar Looking Birds: American Coot nearly identical but not found in Hawaii. Hawaiian Coot endemic to Hawaiian Islands.
Hawaiian_Coot.Best Ways to Identify: Black body with white bill and frontal shield. Found only in Hawaiian Islands. Some individuals show red knob on shield.

Hawaiian_Crow.Description: Medium crow endemic to Hawaii. All black with brownish tinge to body feathers. Stout bill. About 19 inches.
Hawaiian_Crow.Behavior: Extinct in wild since 2002; captive breeding program ongoing. Omnivorous forager in native forest. Uses tools.
Hawaiian_Crow.Habitat: Native forests of the Big Island of Hawaii. All remaining individuals in captive breeding program.
Hawaiian_Crow.Similar Looking Birds: No other crow in Hawaii. Uniquely Hawaiian species now extinct in the wild.
Hawaiian_Crow.Best Ways to Identify: Only crow in Hawaii. Larger than American Crow. Brownish-tinged black plumage. Currently only in captivity.

Hawaiian_Duck.Description: Small dabbling duck, Mallard relative. Male has greenish head, mottled brown body, less colorful than Mallard. Female mottled brown. About 20 inches.
Hawaiian_Duck.Behavior: Feeds in freshwater ponds, streams, and wetlands. Dabbles for aquatic insects, plants, and seeds. Endemic to Hawaiian Islands; endangered.
Hawaiian_Duck.Habitat: Found only in Hawaii. Lives in freshwater marshes, rivers, taro fields, and coastal ponds on Kauai and other islands.
Hawaiian_Duck.Similar Looking Birds: Mallard; hybridization is a major conservation concern. Koloa is darker with less colorful plumage than Mallard.
Hawaiian_Duck.Best Ways to Identify: Darker and smaller than Mallard with mottled brown plumage year-round. Orange-speckled bill. Found only in Hawaii.

Hawaiian_Goose.Description: A medium-sized goose with black face and crown, buff-colored cheeks, and heavily furrowed neck. Reduced webbing between toes for rocky terrain.
Hawaiian_Goose.Behavior: Grazes on native Hawaiian vegetation, grasses, and berries. Lives in pairs or small groups. Largely terrestrial adapted to lava fields.
Hawaiian_Goose.Habitat: Found only in Hawaii on volcanic slopes, grasslands, and shrublands on Maui, Kauai, and the Big Island. Hawaii's state bird.
Hawaiian_Goose.Similar Looking Birds: Distantly resembles Canada Goose due to black head, but the buff cheeks and furrowed neck are unique to the Nene.
Hawaiian_Goose.Best Ways to Identify: Distinctive cream-buff cheeks contrasting with black face, deeply furrowed neck, reduced toe webbing, and restricted Hawaiian habitat are definitive.

Hawaiian_Hawk.Description: Small to medium buteo, polymorphic. Dark morph all dark brown; light morph brown above and pale below. About 16 inches.
Hawaiian_Hawk.Behavior: Endemic Hawaiian hawk; only raptor breeding in Hawaii. Hunts birds, lizards, and insects. Common on Big Island.
Hawaiian_Hawk.Habitat: Big Island of Hawaii from sea level to tree line. Most common in forest and forested agricultural areas.
Hawaiian_Hawk.Similar Looking Birds: Only hawk breeding in Hawaii. Dark morph can suggest various buteos. Endemic species.
Hawaiian_Hawk.Best Ways to Identify: Only hawk on Big Island of Hawaii. Polymorphic but location is definitive. Crying call, soars over Big Island forest.

Hawaiian_Petrel.Description: Medium gadfly petrel, dark gray-brown back, black cap, white forehead, white underparts. About 17 inches.
Hawaiian_Petrel.Behavior: Breeds on Hawaiian mountain slopes; forages far offshore in Pacific. Endangered; declining due to predators and habitat loss.
Hawaiian_Petrel.Habitat: Breeds on Hawaiian high mountains (Haleakala, Mauna Loa). Forages over eastern North Pacific.
Hawaiian_Petrel.Similar Looking Birds: Black-capped Petrel similar. Hawaiian Petrel has narrower white collar and different face pattern.
Hawaiian_Petrel.Best Ways to Identify: Dark cap with white forehead, dark back and wings. White underparts. Hawaiian mountain breeder, offshore Pacific forager.

Hawaiian_Rail.Description: EXTINCT small flightless rail endemic to Hawaii. Brown with gray underparts, short bill, vestigial wings. Very small at about 6 inches.
Hawaiian_Rail.Behavior: Ran through dense grass on Laysan and other Hawaiian islands. Fed on insects and plant material. Extinct by 1884 due to introduced predators.
Hawaiian_Rail.Habitat: Dense lowland grasslands of Hawaiian Islands. Last recorded on Hawaii (Big Island) in 1884. Extinct due to rats, cats, and mongoose.
Hawaiian_Rail.Similar Looking Birds: Other small flightless rails of Pacific islands. Unique to Hawaiian Islands.
Hawaiian_Rail.Best Ways to Identify: Only known from museum specimens. Extinct since 1884. Small flightless brown rail of Hawaiian lowland grasslands.

Hawfinch.Description: Large finch with enormous powerful bill, orange-brown body, blue-black wings, white wing patches. About 7 inches.
Hawfinch.Behavior: Crushes cherry and olive pits with powerful bill. Shy and difficult to observe. Rare vagrant to western Alaska.
Hawfinch.Habitat: Deciduous woodland of Europe and Asia. Rare vagrant to western Alaska and Aleutian Islands.
Hawfinch.Similar Looking Birds: Evening Grosbeak has yellow and black pattern. No similar massive-billed finch in Alaska range.
Hawfinch.Best Ways to Identify: Massive bill, orange-brown body, white wing patches. Large size for a finch. Rare Alaska vagrant from Asia.

Heermanns_Gull.Description: Distinctive gull with dark gray body, red bill, and white head (in breeding). Black tail with white tip.
Heermanns_Gull.Behavior: Kleptoparasitizes Brown Pelicans, stealing fish as they surface. Nests in Baja California.
Heermanns_Gull.Habitat: Pacific coast from Alaska to Mexico; rarely inland.
Heermanns_Gull.Similar Looking Birds: No other Pacific gull has this dark gray body with red bill and white head combination.
Heermanns_Gull.Best Ways to Identify: Dark gray body, red bill, white head in breeding — reverse of most gull color patterns.

Hen_Harrier.Description: Medium harrier, white rump. Male pale gray; female brown streaked. Same species as North American Northern Harrier. About 19 inches.
Hen_Harrier.Behavior: Hunts small mammals and birds low over open fields. Breeds in Europe and Asia; Old World population of Northern Harrier.
Hen_Harrier.Habitat: Open moors, grasslands, and marshes of Europe and Asia. Considered same species as Northern Harrier by some authorities.
Hen_Harrier.Similar Looking Birds: Northern Harrier is the same species or very similar. Both have distinctive white rump.
Hen_Harrier.Best Ways to Identify: White rump, low quartering flight over open fields. Old World counterpart to North American Northern Harrier.

Henslows_Sparrow.Description: Small sparrow with large flat olive-green head, streaked chestnut back, streaked breast. About 5 inches.
Henslows_Sparrow.Behavior: Secretive and hard to flush. Gives insect-like hiccup song. Nest in wet grass fields.
Henslows_Sparrow.Habitat: Wet dense grasslands and old fields in eastern United States. Declining rapidly.
Henslows_Sparrow.Similar Looking Birds: Baird's Sparrow has orange head. Grasshopper Sparrow has flat head but plain belly. Olive head distinctive.
Henslows_Sparrow.Best Ways to Identify: Large flat olive-green head. Streaked chestnut back. Wet dense grass. Short insect-like hiccup song.

Hepatic_Tanager.Description: Medium tanager. Male brick-red with dark gray bill and cheek. Female olive-yellow with gray bill. About 8 inches.
Hepatic_Tanager.Behavior: Forages in pine and pine-oak canopy for insects. Mountain pine forest specialist. Less common than Summer Tanager.
Hepatic_Tanager.Habitat: Pine and pine-oak forests in mountains of southwestern United States.
Hepatic_Tanager.Similar Looking Birds: Summer Tanager male brighter red with lighter bill. Scarlet Tanager male has black wings. Gray bill helpful.
Hepatic_Tanager.Best Ways to Identify: Brick-red male with gray bill and gray cheek patch. Mountain pine forest. Darker than Summer Tanager.

Herald_Petrel.Description: Polymorphic gadfly petrel; light, intermediate, and dark morphs. White primary flash below. About 15 inches.
Herald_Petrel.Behavior: Tropical Pacific species. Rare visitor to North American Pacific coast and occasionally Atlantic via confused records.
Herald_Petrel.Habitat: Tropical South Pacific Ocean. Rare visitor to North American Pacific coast.
Herald_Petrel.Similar Looking Birds: Kermadec Petrel very similar. Herald has different underwing pattern.
Herald_Petrel.Best Ways to Identify: Polymorphic gadfly petrel with white primary flash. Difficult to distinguish from Kermadec Petrel. Tropical Pacific.

Hermit_Thrush.Description: Olive-brown thrush with rufous tail contrasting with brown back, spotted breast, and red-tinged tail.
Hermit_Thrush.Behavior: Raises and slowly lowers tail repeatedly. Song is the most musical of any North American bird.
Hermit_Thrush.Habitat: Coniferous and mixed forests; the only spotted thrush that regularly winters in the US.
Hermit_Thrush.Similar Looking Birds: Swainson's Thrush has buffy eye ring; Veery is rusty with faint spots; Hermit has rufous tail.
Hermit_Thrush.Best Ways to Identify: Reddish tail contrasting with brown back, and habit of slowly raising and lowering tail.

Hermit_Warbler.Description: Bright yellow head with gray nape, gray-streaked back, white underparts with no streaking on sides.
Hermit_Warbler.Behavior: Forages high in coniferous trees. Hybridizes with Townsend's Warbler.
Hermit_Warbler.Habitat: Coniferous forests of the Pacific Coast mountains, breeding in tall Douglas firs.
Hermit_Warbler.Similar Looking Birds: Townsend's Warbler has black cheek patch and streaked sides; Hermit Warbler has plain sides.
Hermit_Warbler.Best Ways to Identify: Brilliant yellow head with gray body and no streaking on sides — coniferous forest.

Herring_Gull.Description: Large familiar gull with gray mantle, white body, pink legs, and yellow bill with red spot.
Herring_Gull.Behavior: Omnivorous scavenger at landfills, fishing ports, and beaches. Drops shellfish to crack them.
Herring_Gull.Habitat: Coasts, large lakes, and landfills across North America.
Herring_Gull.Similar Looking Birds: Ring-billed Gull is smaller with black ring on bill; Glaucous has white wingtips.
Herring_Gull.Best Ways to Identify: Classic large gull with gray back, pink legs, and yellow bill with red spot.

Himalayan_Snowcock.Description: Very large partridge. Gray-brown with chestnut streaks, white face and throat with rust-colored stripes, white primary feathers visible in flight. About 28 inches.
Himalayan_Snowcock.Behavior: Feeds on roots, berries, and alpine plants. Difficult to approach; runs uphill when disturbed. Only introduced to Nevada's Ruby Mountains.
Himalayan_Snowcock.Habitat: Rocky alpine slopes above treeline. In US found only in Ruby Mountains, Nevada, at 10,000+ feet elevation.
Himalayan_Snowcock.Similar Looking Birds: Chukar at lower elevations. Snowcock much larger than other partridges.
Himalayan_Snowcock.Best Ways to Identify: Very large size and white wing patches visible in flight. Alpine habitat in Nevada's Ruby Mountains only.

Hoary_Redpoll.Description: Small finch with red forehead, pinkish breast on male, white rump, and frosty pale plumage overall.
Hoary_Redpoll.Behavior: Irruptive migrant that moves south in winter when birch and alder seed crops fail.
Hoary_Redpoll.Habitat: Arctic tundra; winters in open brushy areas and weedy fields.
Hoary_Redpoll.Similar Looking Birds: Common Redpoll is darker and more streaked; Hoary is frostier and paler with smaller bill.
Hoary_Redpoll.Best Ways to Identify: Frosty pale plumage, small bill, and unstreaked white rump distinguishing it from Common Redpoll.

Hooded_Crane.Description: Large crane. Mostly dark gray-black body with white head and neck contrasting sharply, red forehead. About 37 inches.
Hooded_Crane.Behavior: Migratory; breeds in Siberia, winters in East Asia. Extremely rare vagrant to North America; a few records from Pacific states.
Hooded_Crane.Habitat: Breeds in Siberian boreal wetlands. Winters in Japanese and Korean paddies and marshes. Extremely rare vagrant to western North America.
Hooded_Crane.Similar Looking Birds: Sandhill Crane much larger. White head and dark body combination unique among North American cranes.
Hooded_Crane.Best Ways to Identify: Dark gray-black body with contrasting white head and neck. Red forehead patch. Extremely rare vagrant from Asia.

Hooded_Crow.Description: Medium crow, gray body with black hood, wings, and tail. Two-toned gray-and-black pattern. About 19 inches.
Hooded_Crow.Behavior: Omnivorous scavenger and forager. Solves complex problems. Very rare vagrant to northeastern North America from Europe.
Hooded_Crow.Habitat: Open country, farmland, and coasts in Europe. Very rare vagrant to North America.
Hooded_Crow.Similar Looking Birds: American Crow all black. Eurasian Jackdaw smaller. No other crow has gray body with black hood.
Hooded_Crow.Best Ways to Identify: Gray body with black hood, wings, and tail. Two-tone pattern distinctive. Very rare European vagrant.

Hooded_Merganser.Description: Small diving duck with fan-shaped crest. Male has striking black-and-white crest, rufous sides.
Hooded_Merganser.Behavior: Dives for fish in clear shallow water. Raises and lowers its large fan-shaped crest.
Hooded_Merganser.Habitat: Wooded ponds, rivers, and swamps across North America.
Hooded_Merganser.Similar Looking Birds: Common and Red-breasted Mergansers are larger with red bills; Hooded has yellow-green bill.
Hooded_Merganser.Best Ways to Identify: Fan-shaped black-and-white crest on male is unmistakable among ducks.

Hooded_Oriole.Description: Medium oriole. Male is bright orange-yellow with black face and throat, black back and wings with white bars.
Hooded_Oriole.Behavior: Often nests in hanging fibers of palm fronds. Feeds on nectar and insects.
Hooded_Oriole.Habitat: Desert riparian areas, palms, and urban gardens of the southwestern United States.
Hooded_Oriole.Similar Looking Birds: Bullock's Oriole male has more orange on face; Hooded has black hood extending to back.
Hooded_Oriole.Best Ways to Identify: Orange-yellow with black hood, back, and wings — frequently nests in palm trees.

Hooded_Warbler.Description: Bright yellow face encircled by full black hood on male. Female has yellow-green with faint hood traces.
Hooded_Warbler.Behavior: Stays low in forest understory, frequently fanning tail to flash white outer feathers.
Hooded_Warbler.Habitat: Rich deciduous forest understory in eastern North America.
Hooded_Warbler.Similar Looking Birds: Wilson's Warbler has black cap but no full hood; Yellow Warbler lacks all dark on head.
Hooded_Warbler.Best Ways to Identify: Full black hood framing yellow face; tail-flashing behavior in forest understory.

Hook-billed_Kite.Description: Medium hawk with distinctive large hooked bill. Variable plumage: gray-barred below, or dark morph. About 18 inches.
Hook-billed_Kite.Behavior: Specializes in eating snails. Rare resident of Rio Grande Valley, Texas; casual along southern border.
Hook-billed_Kite.Habitat: Riparian woodland and tropical forest. Rare resident in extreme southern Texas, particularly Santa Ana NWR area.
Hook-billed_Kite.Similar Looking Birds: Other kites lack the distinctive large hooked bill. Hook-billed Kite's bill unmistakable.
Hook-billed_Kite.Best Ways to Identify: Enormously large hooked bill. Gray barring below. Rare resident southern Texas riparian forest near Mexican border.

Horned_Grebe.Description: Small grebe. Breeding adult has black head, golden-buff ear tufts, rufous neck, and red eye.
Horned_Grebe.Behavior: Dives for fish and aquatic invertebrates. Carries young on back after hatching.
Horned_Grebe.Habitat: Breeds on freshwater ponds; winters on coastal bays and open water.
Horned_Grebe.Similar Looking Birds: Eared Grebe has peaked head and black neck in breeding; Horned has flat head and rufous neck.
Horned_Grebe.Best Ways to Identify: Golden ear tufts, flat head profile, and rufous neck in breeding plumage.

Horned_Lark.Description: Sandy-brown lark with black breast band, yellow face, black mask, and tiny black horn feathers.
Horned_Lark.Behavior: Walks on the ground in open areas foraging for seeds. Often forms large winter flocks.
Horned_Lark.Habitat: Open habitats — beaches, fields, tundra, and deserts across North America.
Horned_Lark.Similar Looking Birds: The only true lark native to North America. No other bird has tiny horn feathers on head.
Horned_Lark.Best Ways to Identify: Tiny horn feathers, black mask and breast band, yellow face on open ground.

Horned_Puffin.Description: Seabird with large orange-red and yellow bill, white face, black back, and fleshy horn above eye.
Horned_Puffin.Behavior: Dives to catch fish, carrying multiple fish crosswise in bill back to burrow nest.
Horned_Puffin.Habitat: North Pacific Ocean; nests on rocky sea cliffs in Alaska.
Horned_Puffin.Similar Looking Birds: Atlantic Puffin has more colorful bill without the fleshy horn; Tufted Puffin has tufts.
Horned_Puffin.Best Ways to Identify: White face with fleshy horn above eye and massive colorful bill in the North Pacific.

House_Crow.Description: Medium crow, black with gray nape, breast, and belly. Glossy black crown, bill, wings, and tail. About 16 inches.
House_Crow.Behavior: Urban scavenger. Highly invasive where introduced. Extremely rare vagrant to North America; likely ship-assisted.
House_Crow.Habitat: Urban areas and ports. Rare vagrant to North America. Native to South Asia, invasive worldwide.
House_Crow.Similar Looking Birds: American Crow all black without gray areas. Eurasian Jackdaw similar pattern but smaller with pale eye.
House_Crow.Best Ways to Identify: Black crow with contrasting gray nape and breast. Rare ship-assisted vagrant. Very unusual occurrence in North America.

House_Finch.Description: Small finch with heavy bill. Male has red head, breast, and rump; female is brown with blurry streaks.
House_Finch.Behavior: Abundant at backyard feeders. Nests in a wide variety of structures including cacti and ornaments.
House_Finch.Habitat: Nearly every habitat including cities, suburbs, deserts, and forests across North America.
House_Finch.Similar Looking Birds: Purple Finch male is raspberry-colored overall; House Finch male has more orange-red.
House_Finch.Best Ways to Identify: Red restricted to head and breast on male; female is plain brown with blurry streaking.

House_Sparrow.Description: Introduced sparrow. Male has gray cap, chestnut nape, black bib, and white cheek. Female is plain buffy-brown.
House_Sparrow.Behavior: Lives in close association with humans. Nests in building cavities and nest boxes.
House_Sparrow.Habitat: Cities, suburbs, farms, and rural areas throughout North America.
House_Sparrow.Similar Looking Birds: Other sparrows are native; House Sparrow male has bold black bib and white cheek.
House_Sparrow.Best Ways to Identify: Bold black bib, chestnut nape, and white cheek on male; found everywhere humans live.

House_Wren.Description: Small brown wren with faintly barred wings and tail, thin bill, and cocked tail. No bold facial markings.
House_Wren.Behavior: Aggressively fills cavities with sticks, then chooses one nest. Very loud bubbly song.
House_Wren.Habitat: Forest edges, open woods, shrubby areas, and gardens across North America.
House_Wren.Similar Looking Birds: Winter Wren is smaller and darker with shorter tail; Bewick's Wren has white supercilium.
House_Wren.Best Ways to Identify: Plain brown with faint barring, no facial stripe, and exuberant bubbling song.

Hudsonian_Godwit.Description: Large godwit. Breeding adult has dark reddish-barred underparts, dark back, white wing stripe, black and white tail. About 15 inches.
Hudsonian_Godwit.Behavior: Migrates along narrow corridor through Great Plains. Winters in South America. Forages on mudflats and wet fields for invertebrates.
Hudsonian_Godwit.Habitat: Breeds in subarctic Alaska and Canada. Migrates through Great Plains. Winters on South American coasts.
Hudsonian_Godwit.Similar Looking Birds: Bar-tailed and Black-tailed Godwits similar. Hudsonian has distinctive black and white tail.
Hudsonian_Godwit.Best Ways to Identify: Black and white tail with white wing stripe visible in flight. Upturned bill. Migrates through central North America.

Huttons_Vireo.Description: Small stocky vireo, olive-gray above with two white wing bars and bold white eye ring. About 4.5 inches.
Huttons_Vireo.Behavior: Year-round resident in oak woodland. Sounds and looks like Ruby-crowned Kinglet but larger and heavier.
Huttons_Vireo.Habitat: Oak woodland in western foothills and mountains from British Columbia to Nicaragua. Year-round resident.
Huttons_Vireo.Similar Looking Birds: Ruby-crowned Kinglet very similar! Hutton's Vireo larger, heavier bill, different wing pattern.
Huttons_Vireo.Best Ways to Identify: Bold white eye ring, two wing bars. Looks like kinglet but larger. Oak woodland resident. Year-round western species.

Iceland_Gull.Description: Medium-large pale gull with white wingtips, no dark primary tips. Pale gray back, pink legs, small bill. About 22 inches.
Iceland_Gull.Behavior: Winter visitor from Arctic Canada. Frequents harbors, dumps, and beaches. Softer expression than Herring Gull.
Iceland_Gull.Habitat: Breeds on cliffs in Arctic Canada and Greenland. Winters on Atlantic coast; some reach Great Lakes region.
Iceland_Gull.Similar Looking Birds: Glaucous Gull larger with more robust bill. Iceland Gull smaller with rounder head.
Iceland_Gull.Best Ways to Identify: White wingtips with no dark markings. Small rounded head, small bill. Winter visitor to Atlantic coast harbors.

Icterine_Warbler.Description: Medium warbler, greenish-gray above, bright yellow below. Peaked crown, long bill, bluish-gray legs. About 5 inches.
Icterine_Warbler.Behavior: Active forager in tree canopy. Loud, varied song with mimicry. Very rare vagrant to northeastern North America.
Icterine_Warbler.Habitat: Deciduous forests, parks, and gardens in Europe and western Asia. Very rare vagrant to North America.
Icterine_Warbler.Similar Looking Birds: Yellow Warbler much smaller. Melodious Warbler very similar but different primary projection.
Icterine_Warbler.Best Ways to Identify: Yellow-green plumage, peaked crown, blue-gray legs. Pale panel on folded wing. Very rare European vagrant.

Iiwi.Description: Medium Hawaiian honeycreeper, brilliant scarlet-red with long decurved salmon-pink bill, black wings. About 6 inches.
Iiwi.Behavior: Feeds on tubular ohia and lobelia flowers. Long bill perfectly adapted. Declining due to avian malaria moving upslope.
Iiwi.Habitat: Native forests of main Hawaiian Islands above 4,000 feet where mosquitoes are less prevalent.
Iiwi.Similar Looking Birds: Apapane smaller without long curved bill. No other bird with long salmon-pink bill in Hawaii.
Iiwi.Best Ways to Identify: Long salmon-pink decurved bill, brilliant red body. Black wings and tail. One of most beautiful Hawaiian birds.

Inca_Dove.Description: Very small dove with scaly-looking plumage from dark feather edges, reddish-brown wings, and long tail.
Inca_Dove.Behavior: Common in urban and suburban areas, foraging on the ground for seeds.
Inca_Dove.Habitat: Urban and suburban areas of the southwestern United States and Mexico.
Inca_Dove.Similar Looking Birds: Common Ground-Dove is even smaller with spotted wings; Inca Dove has scaled pattern.
Inca_Dove.Best Ways to Identify: Scaly feather pattern, long tail with white edges, and reddish-brown wing flash in flight.

Inca_Tern.Description: Unmistakable tern. All dark gray with white mustache plumes, red bill and legs, white trailing wing edge. About 16 inches.
Inca_Tern.Behavior: Forages along South American Pacific coast. Rare vagrant to California. Catches fish near surface and follows fishing boats.
Inca_Tern.Habitat: Humboldt Current coastline of Peru and Chile. Rare vagrant to California. Associated with cold Pacific current waters.
Inca_Tern.Similar Looking Birds: No similar tern in range. Absolutely unmistakable.
Inca_Tern.Best Ways to Identify: All gray with white mustache plumes and red bill absolutely unmistakable. Rare vagrant on California coast.

Indian_Peafowl.Description: Enormous pheasant family bird. Male (peacock) has iridescent blue-green body, famous long ornamental train with eyespots. Female brown. Male up to 90 inches.
Indian_Peafowl.Behavior: Roosts in trees. Males fan out train in courtship display. Forages for seeds, insects, and small animals. Introduced feral populations in Florida.
Indian_Peafowl.Habitat: Native to South Asian forests and scrubland. Feral populations in Florida and other warm US states. Often seen near farms and parks.
Indian_Peafowl.Similar Looking Birds: No other bird approaches the peacock's size and ornamental tail train.
Indian_Peafowl.Best Ways to Identify: Unmistakable; male's iridescent blue neck and enormous fan train with eyespots. Female large brown bird with green neck.

Indigo_Bunting.Description: Male is entirely brilliant iridescent blue; female is plain brown with faint streaking and bluish tinge.
Indigo_Bunting.Behavior: Males sing persistently from exposed perches all summer. Migrates at night using stars.
Indigo_Bunting.Habitat: Brushy fields, forest edges, and roadsides across eastern North America.
Indigo_Bunting.Similar Looking Birds: Blue Grosbeak is larger with wing bars and rusty shoulder patch; Bunting is small.
Indigo_Bunting.Best Ways to Identify: All-over brilliant iridescent blue on male — no wing bars or other markings.

Island_Canary.Description: Small finch, olive-green with yellow-green underparts, streaked above. Wild-type ancestor of domestic canary. About 5 inches.
Island_Canary.Behavior: Forages for seeds and insects. Beautiful melodious song. Introduced to Hawaii and Puerto Rico.
Island_Canary.Habitat: Scrub and forest edges. Introduced populations in Hawaii and Puerto Rico. Native to Canary Islands.
Island_Canary.Similar Looking Birds: Yellow-fronted Canary brighter yellow below. American Goldfinch brighter yellow. Wild birds more olive than domestic.
Island_Canary.Best Ways to Identify: Olive-green finch with streaked back. Introduced to Hawaii. Wild ancestor of pet canary. Melodious song.

Island_Scrub-Jay.Description: Large scrub-jay endemic to Santa Cruz Island. Deep blue above, white below, blue breast band. About 12 inches.
Island_Scrub-Jay.Behavior: Bold and curious, largest scrub-jay species. Forages on ground and in oaks for acorns and invertebrates.
Island_Scrub-Jay.Habitat: Oak woodland and chaparral on Santa Cruz Island, California. Found nowhere else on Earth. Vulnerable species.
Island_Scrub-Jay.Similar Looking Birds: California Scrub-Jay on mainland similar but smaller. No other jay on Santa Cruz Island.
Island_Scrub-Jay.Best Ways to Identify: Location is definitive: Santa Cruz Island only. Larger and deeper blue than mainland California Scrub-Jay.

Ivory-billed_Woodpecker.Description: Largest North American woodpecker. Black and white with large ivory-white bill, red crest on male. About 20 inches.
Ivory-billed_Woodpecker.Behavior: Stripped bark from large dead trees for beetle larvae. Possibly extinct; last confirmed sighting debated (1944 or 1987).
Ivory-billed_Woodpecker.Habitat: Old-growth bottomland hardwood forest. Possibly extinct. Former range southeastern US; any recent sightings unconfirmed.
Ivory-billed_Woodpecker.Similar Looking Birds: Pileated Woodpecker similar but smaller with dark bill. Ivory-billed larger with white bill.
Ivory-billed_Woodpecker.Best Ways to Identify: Enormous size, ivory-white bill. Male has red crest. Possibly extinct; any sighting would be extraordinary.

Ivory_Gull.Description: Entirely pure white plumage with black eyes and legs; medium-sized gull with rounded wings and stout yellow-tipped bill.
Ivory_Gull.Behavior: Scavenges carrion near polar bears and seals; gives harsh, tern-like calls; follows ships in Arctic waters.
Ivory_Gull.Habitat: High Arctic sea ice, glaciers, and rocky coastal cliffs; rarely seen south of Arctic Circle outside winter.
Ivory_Gull.Similar Looking Birds: Snowy Owl lacks webbed feet; albino gulls may appear similar but show pink wingtips and skin tones.
Ivory_Gull.Best Ways to Identify: Completely white plumage at all ages; black legs; yellow bill tip; compact rounded body shape on sea ice.

Jabiru.Description: Enormous stork; tallest flying bird in Americas. Mostly white with bare black head and neck and red neck band. About 55 inches.
Jabiru.Behavior: Wades in marshes and wetlands for fish and frogs. Rare vagrant from Mexico and Central America to southern Texas.
Jabiru.Habitat: Tropical wetlands and marshes. Very rare vagrant to southern Texas from Mexico and Central America.
Jabiru.Similar Looking Birds: Wood Stork smaller with black flight feathers. Jabiru much larger and all-white with bare black head.
Jabiru.Best Ways to Identify: Enormous size; tallest flying North American bird. All-white with bare black head, red neck band. Unmistakable if seen.

Jack_Snipe.Description: Small snipe. Cryptically patterned brown with broad buff stripes on back, short bill, no white on tail. About 7.5 inches.
Jack_Snipe.Behavior: Extremely secretive; crouches rather than flushing. Bobs body while feeding. Rare vagrant to North America from Eurasia.
Jack_Snipe.Habitat: Breeds in northern Eurasian bogs. Winters in European and African wetlands. Rare vagrant to Atlantic coast of North America.
Jack_Snipe.Similar Looking Birds: Common Snipe similar but larger with long bill. Jack Snipe smaller with short bill.
Jack_Snipe.Best Ways to Identify: Smaller than Common Snipe with shorter bill. No white tail edge. Bouncing feeding motion. Rarely flushes.

Japanese_Bush_Warbler.Description: Medium warbler, olive-brown above, pale buff below with pale supercilium. Loud distinctive call. About 6 inches.
Japanese_Bush_Warbler.Behavior: Skulks in dense vegetation. Famous in Japan for its beautiful spring song. Introduced to Hawaii.
Japanese_Bush_Warbler.Habitat: Dense scrub, forest edges, and bamboo in Japan and East Asia. Introduced population throughout Hawaiian Islands.
Japanese_Bush_Warbler.Similar Looking Birds: No similar skulking brown warbler in Hawaii. Distinctive loud call helpful. Rarely seen in open.
Japanese_Bush_Warbler.Best Ways to Identify: Loud, distinctive song from dense vegetation in Hawaii. Plain olive-brown with pale buff underparts. Very skulking.

Japanese_Quail.Description: Small rotund quail, streaked brown, black-and-white face stripes, dark chestnut throat on male. About 7 inches.
Japanese_Quail.Behavior: Runs through dense grass. Rarely flies unless flushed. Escaped agricultural birds occur occasionally.
Japanese_Quail.Habitat: Grasslands and croplands. Occasionally escapes from farms and aviaries. Hypothetical record for North America.
Japanese_Quail.Similar Looking Birds: Stubble Quail similar. Northern Bobwhite has different facial pattern. Smaller than most quail.
Japanese_Quail.Best Ways to Identify: Very small quail, heavily streaked brown. Chestnut throat on male. Occasional escaped birds in North America.

Java_Sparrow.Description: Medium finch, gray body with black head, white cheek patch, red bill, pink legs. About 5.5 inches.
Java_Sparrow.Behavior: Highly gregarious, forms large flocks. Forages for seeds in open areas. Invasive in Hawaii.
Java_Sparrow.Habitat: Grasslands, rice fields, and urban areas. Introduced to Hawaii; now common in open areas.
Java_Sparrow.Similar Looking Birds: No other bird in Hawaii has combination of black head, white cheeks, and red bill.
Java_Sparrow.Best Ways to Identify: Black head with white cheek patch, red bill, gray body. Plump shape. Common Hawaiian introduced species.

Jouanins_Petrel.Description: Large all-dark petrel with long wedge tail. Larger than Bulwer's Petrel, very similar in appearance. About 12 inches.
Jouanins_Petrel.Behavior: Poorly known petrel breeding in western Indian Ocean. Very rare vagrant to North American Pacific coast.
Jouanins_Petrel.Habitat: Western Indian Ocean. Very rare vagrant to North American Pacific coast.
Jouanins_Petrel.Similar Looking Birds: Bulwer's Petrel very similar but smaller. Jouanin's distinguished mainly by larger size.
Jouanins_Petrel.Best Ways to Identify: Larger than Bulwer's Petrel but virtually identical. All-dark with long wedge tail. Extremely rare vagrant from Indian Ocean.

Juan_Fernandez_Petrel.Description: Large gadfly petrel, pale gray above, white underparts and face, dark cap and M-pattern on upperwing. About 17 inches.
Juan_Fernandez_Petrel.Behavior: Breeds on Juan Fernandez Islands, Chile. Migrates north into North Pacific; occasional vagrant off California.
Juan_Fernandez_Petrel.Habitat: Eastern North Pacific in non-breeding season. Rare vagrant off California coast. Breeds on Chilean islands.
Juan_Fernandez_Petrel.Similar Looking Birds: White-necked Petrel very similar. Juan Fernandez has more extensive dark cap.
Juan_Fernandez_Petrel.Best Ways to Identify: Large pale gadfly petrel with dark cap and M-pattern above. White underparts. Rare vagrant off California.

Juniper_Titmouse.Description: Plain gray titmouse with small crest, small dark bill, and no wing bars or facial markings.
Juniper_Titmouse.Behavior: Forages actively in junipers, caching seeds and insects under bark.
Juniper_Titmouse.Habitat: Pinyon-juniper woodlands of the Great Basin and southwestern plateaus.
Juniper_Titmouse.Similar Looking Birds: Oak Titmouse is nearly identical but found in oak woodland; ranges barely overlap.
Juniper_Titmouse.Best Ways to Identify: Plain gray titmouse with crest — nearly identical to Oak Titmouse but in juniper habitat.

Kakawahie.Description: Small Hawaiian creeper. Male brilliant scarlet-red. Female brown above, buff below. About 4.5 inches.
Kakawahie.Behavior: Crept along branches searching bark for insects. Extinct since approximately 1963. Last recorded on Molokai.
Kakawahie.Habitat: Native forests of Molokai. Extinct due to deforestation and introduced avian diseases.
Kakawahie.Similar Looking Birds: Iiwi larger and more curved bill. Apapane darker crimson. No creeper-like red bird survives in Hawaii.
Kakawahie.Best Ways to Identify: Extinct Hawaiian creeper from Molokai. Male brilliant red. No longer exists in the wild.

Kalij_Pheasant.Description: Large pheasant introduced to Hawaii. Male has blue-black plumage with red facial wattles, white rump. Female brown with scaly pattern. About 28 inches.
Kalij_Pheasant.Behavior: Forages on forest floor for seeds, berries, and insects. Introduced to Hawaii; now established on Big Island in forest understory.
Kalij_Pheasant.Habitat: Dense montane forest and woodland in Hawaii, particularly Big Island slopes. Native to South Asian Himalayan forests.
Kalij_Pheasant.Similar Looking Birds: Ring-necked Pheasant; male Kalij darker with different face pattern.
Kalij_Pheasant.Best Ways to Identify: Male's glossy blue-black plumage with red facial skin and white lower back. Long tail. Found only in Hawaii in dense forest.

Kamao.Description: Medium Hawaiian thrush, brown above, gray below with slight spotting on breast. Orange-based bill. About 8 inches.
Kamao.Behavior: Foraged for fruit in wet Hawaiian forest. Beautiful melodic song. Extinct since approximately 2002.
Kamao.Habitat: Wet native forests of Kauai. Extinct due to introduced avian diseases, rats, and habitat loss.
Kamao.Similar Looking Birds: Omao similar but on Big Island. All Hawaiian thrushes now rare or extinct.
Kamao.Best Ways to Identify: Extinct Hawaiian thrush from Kauai. Brown above, gray below. No longer exists in the wild.

Kamchatka_Leaf_Warbler.Description: Medium leaf warbler, olive-green above, whitish below with single weak wing bar. Very similar to Arctic Warbler.
Kamchatka_Leaf_Warbler.Behavior: Breeds in forests of Kamchatka. Occasional vagrant to western Alaska. Separated from Arctic Warbler by call.
Kamchatka_Leaf_Warbler.Habitat: Forests of Kamchatka and nearby regions of Russia. Occasional vagrant to western Alaska and Aleutians.
Kamchatka_Leaf_Warbler.Similar Looking Birds: Arctic Warbler nearly identical; best separated by call and genetic analysis. Willow Warbler lacks wing bar.
Kamchatka_Leaf_Warbler.Best Ways to Identify: Extremely similar to Arctic Warbler. Best identified by unique call. Western Alaska vagrant in fall migration.

Kauai_Akialoa.Description: Small Hawaiian honeycreeper, extremely long strongly decurved bill, yellow-olive body. Extinct since approximately 1969.
Kauai_Akialoa.Behavior: Probed flowers and bark with extremely long curved bill. Last seen in Kauai forest in 1969.
Kauai_Akialoa.Habitat: Native forests of Kauai. Extinct due to avian disease and habitat destruction.
Kauai_Akialoa.Similar Looking Birds: Other akialoa on different islands, all extinct. Kauai Nukupuu slightly shorter bill.
Kauai_Akialoa.Best Ways to Identify: Extinct. Extremely long decurved bill. From Kauai. No longer exists in any Hawaiian forest.

Kauai_Amakihi.Description: Small Hawaiian honeycreeper, olive-green above, yellow-green below, longer curved bill than other amakihi. About 4.5 inches.
Kauai_Amakihi.Behavior: Active forager for nectar and insects. Longer bill used to probe deeper flowers. Declining but still present.
Kauai_Amakihi.Habitat: Native forests of Kauai from sea level to higher elevations. Threatened by avian disease.
Kauai_Amakihi.Similar Looking Birds: Anianiau smaller and brighter. Other amakihi on different islands. Longer bill distinguishes from relatives.
Kauai_Amakihi.Best Ways to Identify: Longer curved bill compared to other amakihi. Kauai native forest. Olive-green with yellow-green underparts.

Kauai_Elepaio.Description: Small monarch flycatcher endemic to Kauai. Brown above with white wing bars, whitish below with streaked breast. About 5 inches.
Kauai_Elepaio.Behavior: Active and curious, often approaches observers. Cocks tail upward characteristically. Forages for insects in forest understory.
Kauai_Elepaio.Habitat: Native wet forests of Kauai, Hawaii. Found in ohia-lehua and koa forests from sea level to high elevations.
Kauai_Elepaio.Similar Looking Birds: Oahu and Hawaii Elepaio similar but on different islands. No other flycatcher in its Kauai forest habitat.
Kauai_Elepaio.Best Ways to Identify: Small flycatcher with upward-cocked tail on Kauai. Brown-streaked plumage, white wing bars. Curious behavior.

Kauai_Nukupuu.Description: Small Hawaiian honeycreeper with very long, strongly decurved upper bill. Male yellow, female greenish. About 5.5 inches.
Kauai_Nukupuu.Behavior: Used long bill to probe bark for insects. Possibly extinct; last confirmed record in 1996 on Kauai.
Kauai_Nukupuu.Habitat: Native wet forests of Kauai. Possibly extinct due to avian disease and habitat degradation.
Kauai_Nukupuu.Similar Looking Birds: Akiapolaau has different bill with shorter lower mandible. Kauai Amakihi smaller with shorter bill.
Kauai_Nukupuu.Best Ways to Identify: Very long decurved bill. Yellow male. Possibly extinct on Kauai. Last confirmed record 1996.

Kauai_Oo.Description: Small black Hawaiian honeyeater with yellow thighs, white-streaked breast, long bill. Last recorded 1987. About 8 inches.
Kauai_Oo.Behavior: Foraged for nectar in ohia flowers. Last confirmed recording was a lone male singing in 1987. Extinct.
Kauai_Oo.Habitat: Native ohia-lehua forests of Kauai. Extinct due to habitat destruction, introduced predators, and avian disease.
Kauai_Oo.Similar Looking Birds: Other Hawaiian Oo species similar but on different islands. No similar birds survive in Hawaiian forests.
Kauai_Oo.Best Ways to Identify: Extinct species. Last records from Kauai forest. Black with yellow thigh patches. Last Hawaii Oo to survive.

Kelp_Gull.Description: Large gull, jet black back, white body, yellow bill with red spot, yellow-green legs. About 23 inches.
Kelp_Gull.Behavior: Dominant gull of southern hemisphere. Rare vagrant to Gulf Coast of North America; occasional hybrid with Herring Gull at Chandeleur Islands.
Kelp_Gull.Habitat: Southern hemisphere coastlines. Rare vagrant to Gulf Coast; Louisiana coast records include possible hybrids.
Kelp_Gull.Similar Looking Birds: Great Black-backed Gull similar but has pink legs. Kelp Gull's yellow-green legs distinctive.
Kelp_Gull.Best Ways to Identify: Black back with yellow-green legs. Southern hemisphere species, rare Gulf Coast vagrant. Largest all-black-backed gull in range.

Kentish_Plover.Description: Small pale plover. Sandy-brown above, white below with incomplete breast band (dark side patches). Black or brown lateral breast patches. About 6.5 inches.
Kentish_Plover.Behavior: Forages on sandy beaches and mudflats for invertebrates. Rare vagrant to Atlantic and Pacific coasts from Eurasia.
Kentish_Plover.Habitat: Sandy beaches, salt marshes, and lakeshores across Eurasia and Africa. Rare vagrant to North America.
Kentish_Plover.Similar Looking Birds: Snowy Plover nearly identical and closely related. Kentish larger with different leg color.
Kentish_Plover.Best Ways to Identify: Incomplete breast band with side patches. Sandy- brown plumage. Very similar to Snowy Plover; identified by leg color and subtle size.

Kentucky_Warbler.Description: Olive-green warbler with bright yellow underparts, black sideburns extending below eye, and yellow eye ring.
Kentucky_Warbler.Behavior: Stays low in dense forest understory. Loud rolling churry-churry-churry song.
Kentucky_Warbler.Habitat: Rich deciduous forest floor and understory in the eastern United States.
Kentucky_Warbler.Similar Looking Birds: Common Yellowthroat has black mask; Kentucky Warbler has yellow spectacles and sideburns.
Kentucky_Warbler.Best Ways to Identify: Yellow spectacles, black sideburns on otherwise yellow-and-olive bird in forest understory.

Kermadec_Petrel.Description: Polymorphic gadfly petrel; light, intermediate, and dark morphs. White primary flash below. About 15 inches.
Kermadec_Petrel.Behavior: Breeds on Kermadec and Lord Howe Islands. Forages tropical Pacific; rare visitor to Hawaiian and Pacific coast waters.
Kermadec_Petrel.Habitat: Tropical Pacific Ocean. Rare visitor to Hawaiian waters and North American Pacific coast.
Kermadec_Petrel.Similar Looking Birds: Herald Petrel similar polymorphic species. Kermadec has larger white primary flash below.
Kermadec_Petrel.Best Ways to Identify: Large white primary flash visible in flight. Polymorphic plumage from white to dark. Tropical Pacific visitor.

Key_West_Quail-Dove.Description: Medium dove with iridescent reddish-purple back, bold white facial stripe, white belly, and green neck iridescence. About 12 inches.
Key_West_Quail-Dove.Behavior: Walks on forest floor foraging for seeds and fruit. Secretive. Historically bred in Florida Keys; now rare vagrant from Bahamas.
Key_West_Quail-Dove.Habitat: Dense dry forest and scrub of Caribbean islands, especially Bahamas and Cuba. Rare visitor to Florida Keys.
Key_West_Quail-Dove.Similar Looking Birds: Ruddy Quail-Dove smaller and darker without the bold white facial stripe.
Key_West_Quail-Dove.Best Ways to Identify: Bold white stripe from bill to behind eye on rusty-brown head. Iridescent neck patch. Walks on dense forest floor.

Killdeer.Description: Plover with two black breast bands, orange-red rump, and brown back. Long tail.
Killdeer.Behavior: Famous for broken-wing display to lure predators away from nest on open ground.
Killdeer.Habitat: Open areas including fields, parking lots, and gravel rooftops across North America.
Killdeer.Similar Looking Birds: Semipalmated and other plovers have only one breast band; Killdeer has two.
Killdeer.Best Ways to Identify: Two black breast bands and orange rump — broken-wing distraction display near nest.

King_Eider.Description: Sea duck. Male has orange frontal shield, blue-gray head, peach breast, and black-and-white body.
King_Eider.Behavior: Dives deeply in Arctic seas for mollusks and crustaceans.
King_Eider.Habitat: Arctic Ocean and coasts; rare winter visitor on Atlantic and Pacific coasts.
King_Eider.Similar Looking Birds: Common Eider male has white back; King Eider has black back with white chest patches.
King_Eider.Best Ways to Identify: Male's orange frontal shield and blue-gray head are unmistakable.

King_Rail.Description: Large rail with rich cinnamon-orange breast, brown streaked back, and long slightly downcurved reddish bill.
King_Rail.Behavior: Walks stealthily through marsh vegetation; grunts and cackles loudly; rarely flies; forages for invertebrates.
King_Rail.Habitat: Freshwater marshes, tidal wetlands, and rice fields of eastern North America; declining due to habitat loss.
King_Rail.Similar Looking Birds: Clapper Rail is very similar but lives in saltwater marshes; Virginia Rail is much smaller with gray cheeks.
King_Rail.Best Ways to Identify: Large size; bright rufous breast; long reddish bill; bold white barring on flanks; freshwater marsh habitat.

Kioea.Description: Large extinct Hawaiian bird, brown-streaked plumage with pale underparts, long decurved bill. About 13 inches.
Kioea.Behavior: Foraged for nectar and possibly fruit in native Hawaiian forest. Extinct by approximately 1859.
Kioea.Habitat: Native forests of the Big Island of Hawaii. Extinct due to deforestation following Western contact.
Kioea.Similar Looking Birds: Hawaiian honeyeaters similar in habits but Kioea was one of a kind. Related to Oo birds.
Kioea.Best Ways to Identify: Extinct species. No surviving individuals. Large streaked brown bird with long curved bill from Big Island.

Kirtlands_Warbler.Description: Blue-gray warbler with black streaks above, yellow underparts with black streaks on sides. Bobs tail.
Kirtlands_Warbler.Behavior: Nests only in young jack pines in Michigan; requires specific wildfire succession habitat.
Kirtlands_Warbler.Habitat: Jack pine barrens of Michigan for breeding; winters in Bahamas.
Kirtlands_Warbler.Similar Looking Birds: Prairie Warbler has facial markings; Kirtland's is plain-faced with tail-bobbing habit.
Kirtlands_Warbler.Best Ways to Identify: Tail-bobbing, yellow belly with black streaks, and restricted to Michigan jack pines.

Kittlitzs_Murrelet.Description: Small alcid. Breeding adult mottled brown-gold. Winter plumage has extensive white on face. Very short bill. About 9.5 inches.
Kittlitzs_Murrelet.Behavior: Found near glaciers and tidewater ice. Dives for fish. Endangered; population declining with glacier retreat in Alaska.
Kittlitzs_Murrelet.Habitat: Glacial fjords and inshore coastal waters of Alaska. Nests on rocky ground near glaciers. Declining with climate change.
Kittlitzs_Murrelet.Similar Looking Birds: Marbled Murrelet similar. Kittlitz's has shorter bill and more white on face in winter.
Kittlitzs_Murrelet.Best Ways to Identify: Extremely short stubby bill. Winter bird has extensive white face. Found near glaciers and sea ice.

Kona_Grosbeak.Description: Large Hawaiian honeycreeper, olive-green body with massive rounded grosbeak bill for seed-crushing. About 7 inches.
Kona_Grosbeak.Behavior: Foraged for seeds in native forests of Kona, Hawaii. Extinct since approximately 1894.
Kona_Grosbeak.Habitat: Native forests of Kona district, Big Island of Hawaii. Extinct due to deforestation and introduced species.
Kona_Grosbeak.Similar Looking Birds: Palila has yellow head. No other surviving bird has such a massive rounded bill in Hawaii.
Kona_Grosbeak.Best Ways to Identify: Extinct species. Massive rounded grosbeak bill, olive-green. Big Island Kona district. No longer exists.

La_Sagras_Flycatcher.Description: Medium Myiarchus flycatcher, brown above, whitish below, pale yellow belly. Cuban and Bahaman species. About 8 inches.
La_Sagras_Flycatcher.Behavior: Caribbean island Myiarchus. Rare vagrant to southern Florida from Cuba and Bahamas.
La_Sagras_Flycatcher.Habitat: Forest and woodland of Cuba and Bahamas. Rare vagrant to southern Florida.
La_Sagras_Flycatcher.Similar Looking Birds: Ash-throated Flycatcher similar but from different range. La Sagra's whiter below.
La_Sagras_Flycatcher.Best Ways to Identify: Whitish below with pale yellow belly. Caribbean Myiarchus. Rare vagrant to southern Florida.

Labrador_Duck.Description: EXTINCT sea duck, last seen 1878. Male was black and white; female brownish gray. Had unusual broad flat bill adapted for filter-feeding shellfish. About 22 inches.
Labrador_Duck.Behavior: Fed on mollusks and invertebrates along Atlantic shores. Apparently never very common. Went extinct before detailed study was possible.
Labrador_Duck.Habitat: Wintered along Atlantic coast from Nova Scotia to Chesapeake Bay. Breeding range unknown, possibly Labrador coast. Extinct since 1878.
Labrador_Duck.Similar Looking Birds: Common and White-winged Scoters have similar dark and white male plumage.
Labrador_Duck.Best Ways to Identify: Only known from museum specimens; extinct since 1878. Broad flat bill distinctive among North American sea ducks.

Ladder-backed_Woodpecker.Description: Small woodpecker with black-and-white barred back, spotted underparts, and red cap on males.
Ladder-backed_Woodpecker.Behavior: Forages on cacti, mesquite, and desert trees for insects and cactus fruit.
Ladder-backed_Woodpecker.Habitat: Desert scrub, cactus flats, and dry woodlands of the southwestern United States.
Ladder-backed_Woodpecker.Similar Looking Birds: Nuttall's Woodpecker is nearly identical but found only in California oaks.
Ladder-backed_Woodpecker.Best Ways to Identify: Barred back, spotted underparts in desert habitat — nearly identical to Nuttall's.

Lanai_Hookbill.Description: Small Hawaiian honeycreeper, olive-green with strongly hooked bill for extracting snails from shells. About 5.5 inches.
Lanai_Hookbill.Behavior: Specialized for extracting snails. Extinct since approximately 1918; known from only two museum specimens.
Lanai_Hookbill.Habitat: Native forests of Lanai. Extinct due to deforestation following pineapple plantation development.
Lanai_Hookbill.Similar Looking Birds: No similar snail-eating honeycreeper survives. Extremely unusual hooked bill unlike any other honeycreeper.
Lanai_Hookbill.Best Ways to Identify: Extinct species known from two specimens. Hooked bill for snail-eating. Lanai native forest. No longer exists.

Lanceolated_Warbler.Description: Very small warbler, heavily streaked above and below. Brown with dark streaks throughout. About 4.5 inches.
Lanceolated_Warbler.Behavior: Extremely secretive, creeps through dense grass. Rarely seen in open. Rare vagrant to western Alaska.
Lanceolated_Warbler.Habitat: Wet meadows, sedge, and tall grass in Asia. Very rare vagrant to western Alaska and Aleutian Islands.
Lanceolated_Warbler.Similar Looking Birds: Grasshopper Warbler larger with less streaking below. Pallas's Grasshopper Warbler larger with different pattern.
Lanceolated_Warbler.Best Ways to Identify: Tiny heavily streaked warbler throughout. Mouse-like creeping behavior. Very rare western Alaska vagrant.

Lapland_Longspur.Description: Arctic breeding ground bird. Breeding male has black face and breast, chestnut nape, and white belly.
Lapland_Longspur.Behavior: Migrates in enormous flocks over open fields and grasslands in winter.
Lapland_Longspur.Habitat: Breeds on Arctic tundra; winters in open fields and prairies of North America.
Lapland_Longspur.Similar Looking Birds: Chestnut-collared Longspur has chestnut collar; Smith's has yellowish face. Lapland has rufous nape.
Lapland_Longspur.Best Ways to Identify: Chestnut nape, black face and bib in breeding, and enormous winter flocks in fields.

Large-billed_Tern.Description: Large tern. Black cap, gray back, white underparts, very large yellow bill, bold black and white wing pattern in flight. About 15 inches.
Large-billed_Tern.Behavior: Forages on large rivers for fish. Occasional vagrant to North America from South America. Found in interior river habitats.
Large-billed_Tern.Habitat: Large rivers and lakes of South America. Rare vagrant to eastern North America from South America.
Large-billed_Tern.Similar Looking Birds: No other tern has similar large yellow bill and wing pattern.
Large-billed_Tern.Best Ways to Identify: Enormous yellow bill. Striking black and white wing pattern visible in flight. Rare vagrant from South America.

Lark_Bunting.Description: Breeding male is all-black with large white wing patch. Female is brown-streaked with white wing patch.
Lark_Bunting.Behavior: Males perform spiraling display flights over prairie grass singing a melodious song.
Lark_Bunting.Habitat: Shortgrass prairie and grasslands of the Great Plains.
Lark_Bunting.Similar Looking Birds: Bobolink male has yellow nape and white back patches; Lark Bunting male is all black.
Lark_Bunting.Best Ways to Identify: All-black breeding male with large white wing patch — gregarious in Great Plains prairies.

Lark_Sparrow.Description: Large sparrow with bold chestnut-and-white head pattern, white underparts with central breast spot.
Lark_Sparrow.Behavior: Often runs on the ground. Male courts female by strutting with spread tail.
Lark_Sparrow.Habitat: Open grasslands, roadsides, and fields with scattered trees across North America.
Lark_Sparrow.Similar Looking Birds: No other sparrow has the bold chestnut-and-white striped head pattern.
Lark_Sparrow.Best Ways to Identify: Bold chestnut, black, and white striped head with central black breast spot.

Laughing_Gull.Description: Medium gull with black hood, dark gray mantle, red bill, and dark wingtips. White eye crescents.
Laughing_Gull.Behavior: Common at beaches and fishing piers. Laughing ha-ha-ha call gives it its name.
Laughing_Gull.Habitat: Atlantic and Gulf coasts of North America.
Laughing_Gull.Similar Looking Birds: Franklin's Gull is smaller and has white band across wingtip; Laughing Gull is larger.
Laughing_Gull.Best Ways to Identify: Black hood, dark gray back, red bill, and laughing call at Atlantic beaches.

Lavender_Waxbill.Description: Tiny finch, pale lavender-gray body, crimson rump and tail, red bill. About 4 inches.
Lavender_Waxbill.Behavior: Gregarious in small flocks. Forages for small seeds. Introduced to Hawaii; present on several islands.
Lavender_Waxbill.Habitat: Dry grasslands and scrub. Introduced to Hawaii, found particularly on Big Island.
Lavender_Waxbill.Similar Looking Birds: Orange-cheeked Waxbill has orange cheek. Common Waxbill has red face mask. Lavender gray color distinctive.
Lavender_Waxbill.Best Ways to Identify: Pale lavender-gray with crimson rump and tail. Tiny size. Red bill. Hawaiian introduced species.

Lawrences_Goldfinch.Description: Male has black face, gray body with yellow wing bars and yellow on breast. Female is grayish-yellow.
Lawrences_Goldfinch.Behavior: Highly nomadic, following seed crops. Often forages on the ground for seeds.
Lawrences_Goldfinch.Habitat: Dry chaparral and open woodlands of California and Baja California.
Lawrences_Goldfinch.Similar Looking Birds: American and Lesser Goldfinches have different patterns; Lawrence's has gray body with yellow.
Lawrences_Goldfinch.Best Ways to Identify: Gray body with black face and yellow wing bars — nomadic and unpredictable in California.

Laysan_Albatross.Description: Large albatross, white body and head, dark brown-black back and wings, pink bill. Dark smudge around eye. About 32 inches.
Laysan_Albatross.Behavior: Breeds on Hawaiian Northwestern Islands; forages across North Pacific. Regular winter visitor offshore Pacific coast.
Laysan_Albatross.Habitat: North Pacific Ocean. Breeds primarily on Midway and other Hawaii Northwestern Islands. Offshore Pacific coast in winter.
Laysan_Albatross.Similar Looking Birds: Black-footed Albatross is all dark. Laysan has white body and head with dark back.
Laysan_Albatross.Best Ways to Identify: White head and body with dark back and wings. Pink bill with dark smudge around eye. Common North Pacific albatross.

Laysan_Duck.Description: Small brown dabbling duck, Mallard relative. Males and females similar mottled brown. White eye ring distinctive. About 16 inches.
Laysan_Duck.Behavior: Feeds on brine flies, shrimp, and plants. Highly terrestrial. One of world's rarest ducks; only about 1,000 remain on Hawaiian atolls.
Laysan_Duck.Habitat: Endemic to low-lying Hawaiian atolls. Lives near hypersaline lagoons and freshwater seeps on Laysan Island and Midway Atoll.
Laysan_Duck.Similar Looking Birds: Hawaiian Duck very similar; both are Mallard relatives. Distinguished by range and white eye ring.
Laysan_Duck.Best Ways to Identify: Mottled brown plumage with distinctive white eye ring. Found only on Laysan Island and Midway Atoll.

Laysan_Finch.Description: Large Hawaiian honeycreeper, yellow head and breast, streaked brown back, massive finch bill. About 6.5 inches.
Laysan_Finch.Behavior: Omnivorous, eating seeds, insects, eggs, and carrion. Bold and inquisitive. Found only on Laysan Island.
Laysan_Finch.Habitat: Laysan Island in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands. Open grassland, shrubs, and beach strand vegetation.
Laysan_Finch.Similar Looking Birds: Nihoa Finch similar but island-specific. No other large yellow finch on Laysan Island.
Laysan_Finch.Best Ways to Identify: Large yellow-headed finch with massive bill on Laysan Island. Bold behavior. No similar bird on its island.

Laysan_Honeycreeper.Description: Small Hawaiian honeycreeper, crimson-red with dark wings and tail, curved bill. About 5 inches.
Laysan_Honeycreeper.Behavior: Fed on flowers for nectar on Laysan Island. Extinct in 1923 when last three individuals died in a sandstorm.
Laysan_Honeycreeper.Habitat: Laysan Island in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands. Extinct.
Laysan_Honeycreeper.Similar Looking Birds: Apapane nearly identical but survives on main Hawaiian Islands. Iiwi larger with longer curved bill.
Laysan_Honeycreeper.Best Ways to Identify: Extinct. Nearly identical to Apapane but from Laysan Island only. No longer exists. Last died 1923.

Laysan_Rail.Description: EXTINCT tiny flightless rail. Brown with gray head, short red bill, and streaked upperparts. Flightless and very small. About 6 inches.
Laysan_Rail.Behavior: Ran rapidly through low vegetation on Laysan Island. Omnivorous; ate insects, carrion, and bird eggs. Extinct due to rabbit habitat destruction and WWII.
Laysan_Rail.Habitat: Endemic to Laysan Island in Hawaiian archipelago. Last recorded 1944. Extinct due to introduced rabbits that destroyed its habitat.
Laysan_Rail.Similar Looking Birds: Other small rails. Flightless behavior and Laysan Island range were unique.
Laysan_Rail.Best Ways to Identify: Only known from museum specimens and historical photos. Extinct since 1944. Flightless small rail of Laysan Island, Hawaii.

Lazuli_Bunting.Description: Male has turquoise-blue head and back, white wing bars, orange-buff breast, and white belly.
Lazuli_Bunting.Behavior: Males sing from exposed perches in brushy areas. Migrates in flocks.
Lazuli_Bunting.Habitat: Brushy hillsides, chaparral, and riparian shrubs in western North America.
Lazuli_Bunting.Similar Looking Birds: Indigo Bunting lacks wing bars; Lazuli Bunting has two white wing bars and orange breast.
Lazuli_Bunting.Best Ways to Identify: Turquoise-blue with white wing bars and orange breast — western counterpart to Indigo Bunting.

LeContes_Sparrow.Description: Small marsh sparrow with orange-buff face and breast, purple-gray nape, and streaked back.
LeContes_Sparrow.Behavior: Runs mouse-like through grass rather than flushing. Very secretive.
LeContes_Sparrow.Habitat: Wet meadows and grassy marshes of the central and eastern United States.
LeContes_Sparrow.Similar Looking Birds: Nelson's Sparrow has orange face but duller; Grasshopper Sparrow lacks purple nape.
LeContes_Sparrow.Best Ways to Identify: Orange face and breast with purple-gray nape patch in wet grass.

LeContes_Thrasher.Description: Pale sandy-gray thrasher with pale underparts, downcurved bill, and rufous undertail coverts.
LeContes_Thrasher.Behavior: Runs rapidly on the ground through sparse desert vegetation. Rarely flies.
LeContes_Thrasher.Habitat: Very sparse desert with saltbush and cholla in southwestern California and Arizona.
LeContes_Thrasher.Similar Looking Birds: Curve-billed and Sage Thrashers are darker; LeConte's is palest of all thrashers.
LeContes_Thrasher.Best Ways to Identify: Palest thrasher — sandy gray with rufous undertail in very sparse desert habitat.

Leachs_Storm-Petrel.Description: Medium dark storm-petrel with white rump divided by dark central stripe, forked tail, erratic bounding flight. About 8 inches.
Leachs_Storm-Petrel.Behavior: Breeds on North Atlantic islands; common offshore. Erratic bounding flight distinctive. Comes to land only at night.
Leachs_Storm-Petrel.Habitat: North Atlantic and North Pacific. Breeds on offshore islands; forages over open ocean.
Leachs_Storm-Petrel.Similar Looking Birds: Wilson's Storm-Petrel has square tail and more direct flight. Leach's has forked tail.
Leachs_Storm-Petrel.Best Ways to Identify: Erratic bounding flight with white rump split by dark stripe. Forked tail. Common North Atlantic seabird.

Least_Auklet.Description: Tiny alcid, smallest in North America. Black above with white scapular streaks, variable white below, stubby reddish bill. About 6 inches.
Least_Auklet.Behavior: Breeds in enormous colonies on Alaskan islands. Dives for copepods. Forms massive flocks at sea. Joins mixed auklet flocks.
Least_Auklet.Habitat: Breeds in huge colonies on rocky Alaskan and Siberian islands. Winters in Bering Sea and North Pacific.
Least_Auklet.Similar Looking Birds: Other auklets much larger. Least Auklet tiny size unique.
Least_Auklet.Best Ways to Identify: Extremely small size among alcids. Stubby red bill. White scapular streaks. Breeds in vast colonies on Aleutian Islands.

Least_Bittern.Description: Tiny heron with tan and black back, chestnut sides of neck, and buffy wing patches showing in flight.
Least_Bittern.Behavior: Climbs through cattail reeds rather than wading. Very secretive and rarely seen.
Least_Bittern.Habitat: Dense freshwater marshes with tall cattails and reeds across eastern North America.
Least_Bittern.Similar Looking Birds: American Bittern is much larger and brown-streaked; Least Bittern is tiny.
Least_Bittern.Best Ways to Identify: Smallest heron — tiny size, buffy wing patches, and climbing through cattails.

Least_Flycatcher.Description: Small Empidonax with bold white eye ring, two white wing bars, and short primary projection.
Least_Flycatcher.Behavior: Sings emphatic che-BEK song from perch. Often in loose colonies in deciduous forests.
Least_Flycatcher.Habitat: Open deciduous forests and forest edges across northern North America.
Least_Flycatcher.Similar Looking Birds: Similar Empidonax species best separated by song — che-BEK is distinctive.
Least_Flycatcher.Best Ways to Identify: Bold eye ring, short primary projection, and loud emphatic che-BEK song.

Least_Grebe.Description: Smallest North American grebe. Dark sooty gray with bright yellow eye and dark bill. White wing patch in flight. About 10 inches.
Least_Grebe.Behavior: Dives from surface to catch small fish and aquatic invertebrates. Quickly dives when alarmed. Found in Texas, Florida, and Caribbean.
Least_Grebe.Habitat: Small ponds, lakes, and slow rivers with emergent vegetation in south Texas, southern Florida, and throughout the Caribbean.
Least_Grebe.Similar Looking Birds: Pied-billed Grebe larger with striped bill. Least Grebe much smaller and darker overall.
Least_Grebe.Best Ways to Identify: Tiny size, bright yellow eye, and dark sooty plumage. White wing patches visible in flight.

Least_Sandpiper.Description: Tiniest sandpiper with yellow-green legs, brown-streaked back, and streaked buff-brown breast.
Least_Sandpiper.Behavior: Forages on mudflats and marsh edges for tiny invertebrates, often crouching.
Least_Sandpiper.Habitat: Mudflats, marshes, and shorelines throughout North America during migration.
Least_Sandpiper.Similar Looking Birds: Semipalmated Sandpiper has black legs and gray back; Least has yellow legs.
Least_Sandpiper.Best Ways to Identify: Smallest sandpiper — yellowish legs and brown overall coloring distinguish it.

Least_Storm-Petrel.Description: Smallest storm-petrel in North America. All dark brown-black, rounded wedge tail, rapid direct flight. About 6 inches.
Least_Storm-Petrel.Behavior: Breeds on islands off Baja California. Very small size and rapid direct flight distinguish it from other Pacific storm-petrels.
Least_Storm-Petrel.Habitat: Eastern Pacific off California and Baja California. Breeds on San Benito and other Baja California islands.
Least_Storm-Petrel.Similar Looking Birds: Black Storm-Petrel much larger. Least Storm-Petrel very tiny with rapid wingbeats.
Least_Storm-Petrel.Best Ways to Identify: Smallest storm-petrel. Very tiny all-dark bird with rapid direct flight. Wedge-shaped tail. Eastern Pacific.

Least_Tern.Description: Smallest tern with yellow bill with black tip, yellow feet, white forehead patch, and gray-and-white plumage.
Least_Tern.Behavior: Nests on sandy beaches and gravel bars. Hovers and dives for small fish.
Least_Tern.Habitat: Coastal beaches and river sandbars across North America.
Least_Tern.Similar Looking Birds: Other small terns have orange or red bills; Least Tern has yellow bill with black tip.
Least_Tern.Best Ways to Identify: Tiniest tern — yellow bill with black tip and yellow feet on sandy beaches.

Lesser_Akialoa.Description: Small Hawaiian honeycreeper, very long strongly curved bill, yellow-olive body. Extinct since approximately 1940.
Lesser_Akialoa.Behavior: Probed bark and flowers with long curved bill. Extinct from Oahu due to deforestation and avian disease.
Lesser_Akialoa.Similar Looking Birds: Other akialoa species on different islands. No similar birds survive on Oahu.
Lesser_Akialoa.Best Ways to Identify: Extinct. Very long curved bill, yellow-olive. Oahu native forest. No longer exists.

Lesser_Black-backed_Gull.Description: Large gull, dark gray back (nearly as dark as Great Black-backed), yellow legs, yellow bill. About 22 inches.
Lesser_Black-backed_Gull.Behavior: European species; increasingly common winter visitor to Atlantic coast North America. Frequents coastlines and inland areas.
Lesser_Black-backed_Gull.Habitat: North Atlantic coast; regular and increasing winter visitor from Europe. Atlantic coast, Great Lakes, and inland reservoirs.
Lesser_Black-backed_Gull.Similar Looking Birds: Great Black-backed Gull larger and has pink legs. Lesser has yellow legs and smaller size.
Lesser_Black-backed_Gull.Best Ways to Identify: Yellow legs with dark gray back. Medium-large size. Increasing winter visitor to Atlantic coast from its European range.

Lesser_Frigatebird.Description: Small frigatebird. Male black with white axillary spurs under wings; female has white belly and breast band. Long forked tail. About 30 inches.
Lesser_Frigatebird.Behavior: Kleptoparasite that steals food from other seabirds. Rare vagrant from tropical Pacific to Hawaiian and Pacific waters.
Lesser_Frigatebird.Habitat: Tropical Pacific and Indian Oceans. Rare vagrant to Hawaiian waters and North American Pacific coast.
Lesser_Frigatebird.Similar Looking Birds: Magnificent Frigatebird larger. Lesser Frigatebird's white axillary spurs diagnostic in male.
Lesser_Frigatebird.Best Ways to Identify: Smallest frigatebird. Male has white axillary spurs. Female has white belly and breast. Rare Pacific vagrant.

Lesser_Goldfinch.Description: Male has black back (in eastern range), yellow underparts, and white wing patches. Female is dull olive-yellow.
Lesser_Goldfinch.Behavior: Forages in weedy fields and scrub for seeds. Often hangs upside down on seed heads.
Lesser_Goldfinch.Habitat: Weedy fields, gardens, and open scrub of the western United States.
Lesser_Goldfinch.Similar Looking Birds: American Goldfinch male has yellow back and black wings; Lesser has black back and yellow.
Lesser_Goldfinch.Best Ways to Identify: Black back, bright yellow underparts, and white wing patches in male.

Lesser_Koa-Finch.Description: Medium Hawaiian honeycreeper, male with orange-yellow head, olive-green body, large bill. About 6 inches.
Lesser_Koa-Finch.Behavior: Fed on koa seeds and pods in native forest. Extinct since approximately 1891 on Big Island.
Lesser_Koa-Finch.Habitat: Native koa forests of the Big Island of Hawaii. Extinct due to deforestation and introduced species.
Lesser_Koa-Finch.Similar Looking Birds: Greater Koa-Finch similar but larger. No similar birds survive in Hawaiian koa forest.
Lesser_Koa-Finch.Best Ways to Identify: Extinct Hawaiian species from Big Island koa forest. Orange-yellow head, olive body, large bill. No longer exists.

Lesser_Nighthawk.Description: Nightjar with cryptic brown mottled plumage, long wings with white bar, and small bill.
Lesser_Nighthawk.Behavior: Active at dawn and dusk rather than fully nocturnally like Common Nighthawk.
Lesser_Nighthawk.Habitat: Dry open country, desert scrub, and arid lowlands of the southwestern United States.
Lesser_Nighthawk.Similar Looking Birds: Common Nighthawk has white bar further from wingtip; Lesser has bar close to wingtip.
Lesser_Nighthawk.Best Ways to Identify: White wing bar close to wingtip, active at dusk in desert lowlands — crepuscular not nocturnal.

Lesser_Prairie-Chicken.Description: Smaller and paler than Greater Prairie-Chicken; heavily barred brown and buff with orange-red air sacs on neck.
Lesser_Prairie-Chicken.Behavior: Males boom and dance on leks in spring; flocks forage for seeds and insects in shrubby grasslands.
Lesser_Prairie-Chicken.Habitat: Shortgrass and mixed-grass prairies with shinnery oak and sand sagebrush in southern Great Plains.
Lesser_Prairie-Chicken.Similar Looking Birds: Greater Prairie-Chicken is darker and larger; Sharp-tailed Grouse has pointed tail and less barring.
Lesser_Prairie-Chicken.Best Ways to Identify: Pale barred pattern; rose-red neck sacs inflated in display; pinnae feathers on neck; short rounded tail.

Lesser_Scaup.Description: Diving duck with peaked head, blue-gray bill, and white-and-black pattern. Purple gloss on head.
Lesser_Scaup.Behavior: Dives for mollusks and aquatic plants. Forms large flocks on lakes and bays.
Lesser_Scaup.Habitat: Freshwater lakes, reservoirs, and coastal bays across North America.
Lesser_Scaup.Similar Looking Birds: Greater Scaup has rounded head and green gloss; Lesser has peaked head and purple gloss.
Lesser_Scaup.Best Ways to Identify: Peaked head with purple gloss and shorter white wing stripe than Greater Scaup.

Lesser_White-fronted_Goose.Description: A small, compact goose with a white forehead patch, yellow eye-ring, and orange legs. Smaller than the Greater White-fronted Goose.
Lesser_White-fronted_Goose.Behavior: Grazes on grasses and sedges. Highly migratory, forming mixed flocks with other goose species during migration and winter.
Lesser_White-fronted_Goose.Habitat: Breeds in shrubby tundra and alpine areas of northern Eurasia. Winters in wetlands, grasslands, and agricultural fields.
Lesser_White-fronted_Goose.Similar Looking Birds: Easily confused with Greater White-fronted Goose. The Bean Goose is also similar but larger with no white forehead.
Lesser_White-fronted_Goose.Best Ways to Identify: Distinctive yellow eye-ring visible at close range, smaller size, and white forehead extending higher on crown than in Greater White-fronted Goose.

Lesser_Whitethroat.Description: Small warbler, gray-brown above with darker mask, white throat, pale gray-white underparts. About 5 inches.
Lesser_Whitethroat.Behavior: Skulking in dense scrub but sings from exposed perch. Rare vagrant to western and eastern North America.
Lesser_Whitethroat.Habitat: Dense scrub, hedgerows, and thickets in Europe and Asia. Rare vagrant to both coasts of North America.
Lesser_Whitethroat.Similar Looking Birds: Common Whitethroat larger with rusty wing panel. Garden Warbler rounder and lacks mask.
Lesser_Whitethroat.Best Ways to Identify: Dark gray mask, white throat, plain gray-brown back. Small skulking warbler. Very rare vagrant from Eurasia.

Lesser_Yellowlegs.Description: Medium shorebird with bright yellow legs, straight thin bill, and white-spotted gray upperparts.
Lesser_Yellowlegs.Behavior: Forages gracefully in shallow water bobbing head as it walks. Two-note call.
Lesser_Yellowlegs.Habitat: Wetlands, mudflats, and marshes across North America during migration.
Lesser_Yellowlegs.Similar Looking Birds: Greater Yellowlegs is larger with longer uptilted bill and three-note call.
Lesser_Yellowlegs.Best Ways to Identify: Smaller than Greater with straight shorter bill and soft two-note tu-tu call.

Lessons_Seedeater.Description: Tiny finch. Male black above with white below and white wing spot. Female plain brown. About 4.5 inches.
Lessons_Seedeater.Behavior: Forages for grass seeds in open areas. Rare vagrant to Trinidad and occasionally farther north.
Lessons_Seedeater.Habitat: Grasslands and open areas of Trinidad and northeastern South America. Rare vagrant to southern North America.
Lessons_Seedeater.Similar Looking Birds: Morelet's Seedeater similar black-and-white pattern. Variable Seedeater similar. Small black-and-white finch.
Lessons_Seedeater.Best Ways to Identify: Male tiny black-and-white with white wing spot. Very rare vagrant from Caribbean and South America.

Lewiss_Woodpecker.Description: Unique woodpecker with dark greenish back, red face, pink belly, and gray collar. Crow-like flight.
Lewiss_Woodpecker.Behavior: Catches insects in aerial sorties like a flycatcher. Stores acorns in bark crevices.
Lewiss_Woodpecker.Habitat: Open ponderosa pine forests and burned areas of western North America.
Lewiss_Woodpecker.Similar Looking Birds: No other woodpecker has this combination of greenish back and pink belly.
Lewiss_Woodpecker.Best Ways to Identify: Dark greenish back, pink belly, red face, and crow-like flapping flight style.

Light-mantled_Albatross.Description: Elegant sooty albatross with pale silvery-gray mantle contrasting with dark head and wings. Long narrow wings. About 35 inches.
Light-mantled_Albatross.Behavior: Graceful flier with very narrow wings. Breeds on Southern Ocean subantarctic islands. Very rare vagrant.
Light-mantled_Albatross.Habitat: Southern Ocean. Very rare vagrant to North Pacific and Atlantic coasts of North America.
Light-mantled_Albatross.Similar Looking Birds: Sooty Albatross very similar. Light-mantled has pale gray mantle contrasting with dark head.
Light-mantled_Albatross.Best Ways to Identify: Pale silvery-gray back contrasting with dark sooty head and wings. Very long narrow wings. Southern Ocean species.

Lilac-crowned_Amazon.Description: Medium parrot, green with lilac-blue crown, red lores, green cheeks. Long rounded tail. About 13 inches.
Lilac-crowned_Amazon.Behavior: Endangered in Mexico; established feral population in Southern California. Loud calls.
Lilac-crowned_Amazon.Habitat: Feral in Los Angeles and San Diego area of Southern California. Endangered in Mexico.
Lilac-crowned_Amazon.Similar Looking Birds: Red-crowned Amazon has brighter red lores. Lilac-crowned has lilac-blue crown.
Lilac-crowned_Amazon.Best Ways to Identify: Lilac-blue crown, red lores. Green parrot. Feral in Southern California. Endangered Mexican species.

Limpkin.Description: Large brownish wading bird densely spotted white; long neck and legs; long slightly downcurved bill; heron-like appearance.
Limpkin.Behavior: Specializes in extracting apple snails from shells; gives loud wailing screams; walks with limping gait.
Limpkin.Habitat: Freshwater marshes, swamps, and river edges in Florida and expanding into southeastern US coastal states.
Limpkin.Similar Looking Birds: Immature Night-Herons lack white spots; ibises have curved bills and different body proportions.
